school-c6-science.title: Class 6 Science · Curiosity
school-c6-science.description: Every chapter of Class 6 Science (Curiosity, NCERT 2024 edition onward) explained in original words with activities, solved examples, common mistakes, quizzes, chapter tests and mock papers.

courses.title: Ch 1 · The Wonderful World of Science
courses.summary: What science is, why curiosity matters, the scientific method (observe, question, guess, test, conclude), fair tests, and how science shows up in everyday life in India.
outcomes: Learners can explain science as a way of finding out about the world
Learners can list and use the steps of the scientific method
Learners can design a simple fair test changing only one thing
Learners can give everyday examples of science at home, in farms and in technology

story.title: Why does the dal boil over?

scenes.text: Aarav watches dal bubbling and foaming over the pot.
He asks, 'Why does it rise when the lid is on?'
Grandma says, 'Lift the lid and see.' The foam drops.
Asking and checking — that is science!

steps.title: Science is a way of knowing
steps.body: **Science** is a way of understanding the world by asking questions, observing carefully, testing ideas and changing our mind when evidence says so. It covers living things (biology), matter (chemistry), energy and forces (physics), Earth and space.

steps.title: Curiosity
steps.body: Every scientific discovery began with someone wondering 'why?' or 'what if?'. Asking questions is the first skill of a scientist.

steps.title: Example 1 — a question becomes an investigation
steps.body:
Question: Do plants need light to stay green?

- Keep two pots of the same plant, one in a dark cupboard, one by a window, both watered.
- After a week, the dark one is pale and yellow.
- Conclusion: light is needed to stay green (to make food).

steps.title: Example 2 — science in the kitchen
steps.body: Curd setting: a spoon of curd added to warm milk turns it into curd overnight because tiny living things (bacteria) multiply in the warmth. Cold milk sets slowly — temperature matters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking science is only what happens in a lab. It is all around us.
- Believing a single observation 'proves' something; scientists repeat tests.

statements.s: Science happens only in laboratories.
statements.why: Kitchens, farms and parks are full of science.

statements.s: Asking questions is an important part of science.
Scientists never change their minds.
statements.why: They update ideas with new evidence.

statements.s: Curd setting involves living things.

options: a list of facts to memorise
a way of finding out by observing and testing
quiz.why: Science is a way of finding out about the world by observing, asking questions and testing ideas. It is not magic, guessing or just memorising facts.

quiz.q: The first step of discovery is usually …
quiz.why: Discovery usually begins with a question that comes from curiosity. Tests, results and books come later.
Biology is the study of living things, since 'bio' means life. Physics, chemistry and astronomy study other things.

options: to check the result is reliable
quiz.why: Repeating an experiment checks that the result is reliable and not a one-off. Getting the same result again gives more confidence.
Curd is made by bacteria, and they grow faster in a warm place. Cold or frozen milk slows them down.

story.title: The mystery of the wilting tulsi

scenes.text: Meera's tulsi plant is drooping.
She wonders: too little water, or too much sun?
She moves it to shade but waters it the same — no change. Then she waters more — it recovers.
Her test showed water was the problem.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
- **Observe**: notice something (the plant droops).
- **Question**: why is it drooping?
- **Hypothesis** (a testable guess): it needs more water.
- **Experiment / test**: change only water, keep others same.
- **Analyse** results.
- **Conclude** and **share**; if wrong, make a new hypothesis.

steps.title: Example 1 — Does salt dissolve faster in hot water?
steps.body:
- Hypothesis: yes.
- Test: same amount of salt in equal cups of hot and cold water, stir equally.
- Result: hot water dissolves it sooner.
- Conclusion: hypothesis supported.

steps.title: Example 2 — A wrong hypothesis is useful
steps.body: Hypothesis: heavier stones sink faster in water than lighter ones of the same shape. Test shows small differences only; the shape matters more. You learn something either way.

steps.title: Write it down
steps.body: Keep a science notebook: date, what you did, what you saw, measurements.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing two things at once — you can't tell which one caused the change.
- Calling a guess a 'fact' before testing.

activity.prompt: Put the steps of the scientific method in order.
items: Draw a conclusion and share it

quiz.why: A hypothesis is a guess about what will happen that can be tested by an experiment. It is not yet proven.
After testing, a scientist analyses the results to see whether they support the idea. Hiding data or guessing without looking is not scientific.

quiz.q: If a hypothesis is wrong, the scientist …
quiz.why: If the results do not support the hypothesis, the scientist makes a new hypothesis and tests it. Science corrects itself in this way.
Observation comes first, because we notice something and then ask questions. Experiments, conclusions and sharing follow.

options: results can be checked and repeated
quiz.why: Notes let us check and repeat results later. Without records, we may forget or others cannot verify what we found.

scenes.text: Kabir wants to know which brand of paper towel soaks more water.
His first try: one towel big, one small — unfair!
He cuts equal sizes, uses equal water, same time.
Now his comparison is fair.

steps.title: Fair test
steps.body: A **fair test** changes only **one** thing (the thing being tested) and keeps everything else the same. Then any difference in the result is due to that one change.

steps.title: Words to know
steps.body:
- The thing you change: e.g. brand of towel
- The thing you measure: e.g. water soaked (mL)
- Things kept the same: size, water amount, time

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Does a ball bounce higher on floor or carpet?

- Change: surface. Measure: bounce height. Keep same: ball, drop height, how it is dropped.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Do seeds sprout faster with more water?

- Change: amount of water. Keep same: seed type, number, soil, light, temperature.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing only once — repeat 3 times and compare.
- Comparing different-sized samples.

activity.prompt: For 'Does sugar dissolve faster in hot water?', sort each item.

quiz.why: A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same. Then we know that thing caused the difference.

quiz.q: Testing which ball bounces highest, keep the same …
quiz.why: To compare balls fairly, drop them all from the same height. Only the ball type should change.
Repeating tests makes the results more reliable, as a single result might be a mistake or luck.

quiz.q: In a seed test, what is measured?
quiz.why: In a seed test, the outcome we measure is how many days the seeds take to sprout. Soil, water and seed type are conditions.
Using different-sized towels makes the test unfair because the size also changes. A fair test keeps the towels, time and water the same.

scenes.text: Morning: Riya's mother checks the weather forecast on the phone.
Riya cycles to school — gears and brakes at work.
On the way, farmers use drip irrigation to save water.
At night, she sees a satellite pass overhead.

steps.title: At home and in the world
steps.body:
- Kitchen: cooking, pressure cooker, fridge
- Health: vaccines, clean water, nutrition
- Farming: better seeds, soil testing
- Technology: phones, satellites (ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023)

steps.title: Indian scientists
steps.body: C. V. Raman (Nobel Prize in Physics, 1930, for the Raman effect), Janaki Ammal (botanist, plant breeding), A. P. J. Abdul Kalam (rockets and missiles), Kalpana Chawla (astronaut).

steps.title: Science with care
steps.body: Science can help or harm. Good scientists think about safety, honesty and the environment.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why is a pressure cooker faster?

- Trapped steam raises the pressure, so water boils at a higher temperature and food cooks faster.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why do we wash hands with soap?

- Soap helps lift away dirt and germs so they rinse off — preventing illness.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Believing everything labelled 'scientific' in ads — ask for evidence.

activity.prompt: Match the scientist to the work.

quiz.why: Chandrayaan-3 landed in August 2023 near the Moon's south pole. It was the first mission to land that close to the pole.

quiz.q: C. V. Raman won the Nobel Prize in …
quiz.why: C. V. Raman won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for his work on the scattering of light, known as the Raman effect.

options: water boils at a higher temperature
quiz.why: A pressure cooker raises the pressure, which makes water boil at a higher temperature. The hotter water cooks food faster.
Soap helps lift dirt and germs from the skin so water can wash them away. It does not instantly kill every germ.
A good scientist is careful and honest, and reports what was really found. Hiding data or being careless spoils the science.

questions.q: Science is a way of …
options: finding out by observing and testing
questions.why: Science is a way of finding out by observing and testing. It is not magic, memorising or random guessing.

questions.q: A testable guess is called a …
questions.why: A testable guess is called a hypothesis. A result comes after testing, and a law is something already well established.

questions.q: Which comes right after asking a question?
questions.why: After a question, we make a hypothesis, a testable guess. Conclusions and sharing come after the test.

questions.q: A fair test changes …
questions.why: In a fair test only one thing is changed and the rest are kept the same. That way any difference is due to that one change.

questions.q: Who discovered the Raman effect?
questions.why: The Raman effect was discovered by C. V. Raman, who won the Nobel Prize in Physics for it. The others are other famous Indian scientists.

questions.q: Curd sets because of …
questions.why: Curd sets because bacteria turn milk into curd. Salt and sugar are not what makes it set.

questions.q: To test if light affects plant colour, keep the same …
questions.why: To test the effect of light, only light should change. Water and pot size must be the same so they do not affect the colour.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Changing two things at once makes a test unfair. Reason (R): We can't tell which change caused the result.
questions.why: Both are true: changing two things at once makes a test unfair, because we cannot tell which change caused the result. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: Tina tests whether a toy car goes further on a steeper ramp. She uses different cars for each ramp. Problem?
options: The car is not kept the same
questions.why: Using different cars means the car also changes, so we cannot tell whether the ramp or the car caused the difference. The car should be kept the same.

questions.q: Why do scientists share results?
options: so others can check and build on them
questions.why: Scientists share results so others can check them and build on them. Science grows through many people working together.

questions.q: What should Tina measure in the ramp test?
questions.why: In the ramp test, Tina should measure how far the car travels, since that is the outcome. Ramp colour and car name do not affect it.

questions.q: A result that cannot be repeated by others is …
questions.why: If others cannot repeat a result, we cannot trust it, so it is weak evidence. Strong evidence can be repeated.

questions.q: Case: Sugar dissolved in 30 s in hot water and 90 s in cold water (same amount, stirring). How many times faster in hot water?
questions.why: Hot water took 30 s and cold water 90 s. 90 ÷ 30 = 3, so it was 3 times faster in hot water.

questions.q: Which is NOT a step of the scientific method?
questions.why: Ignoring data that disagree is not part of the scientific method, since all evidence must be considered. Observation, hypothesis and conclusion are steps.

questions.q: Case: Seeds A (watered daily) sprouted in 4 days, B (watered once) in 7, C (not watered) none. Best conclusion?
questions.why: Seeds watered daily sprouted fastest, those watered once were slower and those with no water did not sprout. So water helps seeds sprout.

questions.q: In the seed case, one more thing to strengthen the conclusion?
options: Use different seed types in each pot
questions.why: Repeating the test with more seeds under the same conditions makes the conclusion stronger. Changing soil or seed type would make the test unfair.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Diversity in the Living World
courses.summary: The variety of plants and animals around us, grouping plants (herbs, shrubs, trees, climbers, creepers), leaf venation and root types, seeds with one or two cotyledons, grouping animals, adaptations to habitats like deserts, mountains and water, and why biodiversity must be conserved.
outcomes: Learners can classify plants as herbs, shrubs, trees, climbers and creepers
Learners can link leaf venation to root type and seed type
Learners can group animals by features and habitat
Learners can explain adaptations and why conserving biodiversity matters

lessons.title: Grouping plants by stem and height

scenes.text: Class 6 walks around the school garden with notebooks.
They see a tall neem, a hibiscus bush and tiny grass.
A money plant climbs the wall; a pumpkin vine spreads on the ground.
They group them and discover five kinds!

steps.title: Groups
steps.body:
- **Herbs**: small, soft green stems (tulsi, wheat, grass, mint)
- **Shrubs**: medium, many hard woody branches near the base (hibiscus, rose, lemon)
- **Trees**: tall, one thick woody trunk, branches higher up (neem, mango, peepal)
- **Climbers**: weak stems that climb using support (money plant, pea, grapevine)
- **Creepers**: weak stems that spread on the ground (pumpkin, watermelon, sweet potato)

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Classify: banana, rose, tomato, coconut.

- Banana: very large herb (soft, non-woody 'stem')
- Rose: shrub · Tomato: herb · Coconut: tree

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why do climbers need support?

- Their stems are too weak to stand up; climbing helps them reach sunlight.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every big plant a tree — banana has no woody trunk.
- Mixing up climbers (go up) and creepers (spread on ground).

quiz.why: A rose has several woody stems branching near the base and is of medium height, so it is a shrub. Herbs have soft stems and trees have a tall trunk.
A pumpkin has a weak stem that spreads along the ground, so it is a creeper. A climber grows up a support.
Herbs are small plants with soft, green stems. Thick woody trunks belong to trees.
A pea plant has a weak stem and climbs using tendrils that coil around a support. It does not use thorns or air roots.
Neem is a tall plant with a thick, woody trunk and many branches, so it is a tree.

scenes.text: Zoya pulls out a grass plant and a mustard plant after rain.
Grass has a bunch of thin roots; mustard has one thick main root.
Grass leaves have straight parallel lines; mustard leaves have a net.
Teacher says their seeds differ too!

steps.title: Leaf venation
steps.body:
- **Parallel venation**: veins run side by side (grass, maize, banana, wheat)
- **Reticulate venation**: veins form a net (mustard, hibiscus, mango, rose)

steps.title: Roots
steps.body:
- **Taproot**: one main root with side roots (mustard, carrot, neem)
- **Fibrous roots**: bunch of similar thin roots (grass, wheat, maize, onion)

steps.title: Seeds
steps.body:
- **Dicot**: seed with **two** cotyledons (seed leaves) — gram, pea, bean, mango
- **Monocot**: seed with **one** cotyledon — maize, wheat, rice

Usual pattern: dicots → reticulate venation + taproot; monocots → parallel venation + fibrous roots.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
A plant has net-like veins. Predict its roots and seed.

- **Taproot** and **two cotyledons** (dicot).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Soak gram and maize seeds overnight. Open them.

- Gram splits into **2 halves** (dicot); maize does not split (monocot).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking venation and roots are unrelated — they usually go together.
- Calling the cotyledon a leaf that does photosynthesis right away; it mainly stores food for the young plant.

quiz.why: Wheat is a grass, and its leaves have veins running side by side. That is parallel venation.
A carrot's main root grows deep and is thick, which we eat. That is a taproot.

quiz.q: A seed with two cotyledons is a …
quiz.why: A seed with two cotyledons (seed leaves) is a dicot, because 'di' means two. A monocot has one.

quiz.q: Plant with fibrous roots probably has …
quiz.why: Plants with fibrous roots are usually monocots, and these usually have parallel venation in their leaves. Net venation goes with taproots.
Rice is a monocot, with one seed leaf, parallel veins and fibrous roots. Pea, bean and mango are dicots.

scenes.text: At a lake near Bhopal, Dev sees ducks, fish, frogs and buffaloes.
Frogs move between land and water.
Fish never leave the water.
He groups them by where they live and how they move.

steps.title: Ways to group animals
steps.body:
- **By habitat**: land (terrestrial), water (aquatic), both (amphibians like frogs), air/trees (birds, monkeys)
- **By body features**: backbone or not; body covering (scales, feathers, fur)
- **By food**: herbivores (cow), carnivores (tiger), omnivores (crow, bear)

steps.title: Habitat
steps.body: The place where an organism lives and finds food, water, shelter. Habitats: forest, desert, grassland, mountain, pond, ocean.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Group: crow, fish, frog, earthworm, eagle.

- Air/land: crow, eagle · Water: fish · Both: frog · Soil (land): earthworm

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why can't a fish live on land?

- Fish breathe using **gills** that take oxygen from water; in air, gills dry and fail.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a whale a fish — it is a mammal that breathes with lungs.
- Using only one feature to group; different features give different groups.

activity.prompt: Where does each animal mainly live?

quiz.why: A habitat is the place where an organism lives, and it provides food, water and shelter. It gives more than light only.
A frog lives both on land and in water, so it is an amphibian. It is not only land or only aquatic.
Fish breathe using gills, which take oxygen from the water. Lungs are used by most land animals.
Omnivores eat both plants and animals. Herbivores eat only plants and carnivores only animals.
A whale breathes with lungs and feeds its young on milk, so it is a mammal even though it lives in water. A fish breathes with gills.

scenes.text: In Rajasthan, Chetan rides a camel across hot sand.
His cousin in Ladakh tends yaks in snow.
Why can't they swap homes?
Each has special features — adaptations — for its home.

steps.title: Adaptation
steps.body: Special features that help an organism survive in its habitat are **adaptations**. They develop over a very long time.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- **Camel**: long legs keep the body away from hot sand; broad padded feet don't sink; can go long without water; little urine and dry dung
- **Yak / mountain goat**: thick fur; strong hooves for rocky slopes
- **Fish**: streamlined body, fins, gills, scales
- **Desert plants (cactus)**: spines instead of leaves (less water loss), thick fleshy stem stores water, waxy coat, deep roots
- **Mountain trees (pine/deodar)**: cone shape, sloping branches so snow slides off

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why is a fish's body pointed at both ends?

- Streamlined shape lets water flow past easily, so it swims with less effort.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why does a cactus have spines?

- Spines are modified leaves; less surface means less water loss, and they protect from animals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking an animal 'decides' to adapt in its lifetime. Adaptations develop over many generations.
- Thinking all desert plants have no leaves; many have small or waxy leaves.

activity.prompt: Match the living thing to its adaptation.

options: keep body away from hot sand
quiz.why: A camel's long legs keep its body away from the hot desert sand, so it stays cooler. They are not for climbing or swimming.
A cactus stores water in its thick, fleshy stem, so it can survive in the desert. Its spines are leaves.
Cone-shaped trees with sloping branches let snow slide off. This stops branches from breaking under heavy snow.
A streamlined body has a smooth, narrow shape that lets a fish move through water with less resistance.
Adaptations develop slowly over many generations. Animals cannot choose to change them or grow them overnight.

scenes.text: Nani says sparrows chirped in every courtyard when she was young.
Now Ishaan rarely sees one in the city.
His class puts up nest boxes and grows native plants.
A few sparrows return — every effort counts.

steps.title: Biodiversity
steps.body: **Biodiversity** is the variety of all living things — plants, animals, microbes — in an area. India is one of the world's most biodiverse countries (Western Ghats, Himalayas, Sundarbans …).

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Living things depend on each other for food, pollination, clean air and water, medicines. Losing one species can affect many others.

steps.title: Threats and protection
steps.body:
- Threats: cutting forests, pollution, hunting, plastic, climate change
- Protection: national parks and sanctuaries, planting native trees, saving water, reducing plastic, not disturbing wildlife

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why are bees important to farmers?

- Bees **pollinate** many crops (fruits, vegetables), helping them form seeds and fruit.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body: Project Tiger (1973) helped protect tigers by creating tiger reserves.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking only big animals matter — insects, worms and microbes are vital too.

activity.prompt: Biodiversity actions I can take this month
items: Grow a native plant or herb
Keep a water bowl for birds in summer
Say no to single-use plastic bags
Learn the names of 5 birds or trees near home
Never disturb nests or catch wild animals

quiz.why: Biodiversity is the variety of living things on Earth, including plants, animals and microbes. It is not just tigers or only plants.
Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make seeds and fruits. This is pollination.
Cutting forests destroys habitats and so threatens biodiversity. National parks, planting trees and saving water protect it.
Project Tiger began in 1973 to protect tigers and their habitats in India.
Native plants provide food and shelter for local insects and birds. They are part of the local food web.

questions.q: Mango is a …
questions.why: A mango plant grows tall with a thick woody trunk, so it is a tree. Herbs and creepers have soft, weak stems.

questions.q: Which plant is a climber?
questions.why: A money plant has a weak stem that climbs up a support, so it is a climber. A pumpkin spreads on the ground and neem and rose are not climbers.

questions.q: Parallel venation is seen in …
questions.why: Grass is a monocot, and its leaves have parallel veins. Mustard, rose and hibiscus have net-like veins.

questions.q: Taproot is found in …
questions.why: A carrot has a taproot, with one main root going deep. Wheat, maize and onion have fibrous roots.

questions.q: Gram seed has … cotyledons
questions.why: Gram is a dicot, so its seed has 2 cotyledons (it splits into two halves).

questions.q: Frogs are …
questions.why: Frogs live both on land and in water, so they are amphibians. They are not fish or birds.

questions.q: Camel's broad padded feet help it to …
questions.why: A camel's broad, padded feet spread its weight so it does not sink into soft sand. They are not for climbing or swimming.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Maize has fibrous roots. Reason (R): Maize leaves show parallel venation.
options: Both true; R is a related clue, not a cause
questions.why: Both are true: maize has fibrous roots and parallel leaf veins. They usually occur together in monocots, but one does not cause the other.

questions.q: A plant has a taproot. Its leaves most likely show …
questions.why: A plant with a taproot is usually a dicot, which has net-like (reticulate) venation. Parallel venation goes with fibrous roots.

questions.q: Spines of cactus are modified …
questions.why: The spines of a cactus are modified leaves, which lose less water than flat leaves. The thick stem does the food-making and stores water.

questions.q: Case: A student finds a plant with a weak stem spreading on the ground with big leaves and yellow flowers; fruit is a big round vegetable. It is most likely a …
questions.why: A weak stem spreading on the ground, with a big round vegetable as fruit, fits a creeper like pumpkin. A climber would grow up a support.

questions.q: Which feature of fish is NOT an adaptation for water?
questions.why: Fins, gills and a streamlined body help a fish live in water. The ability to fly is not a fish feature.

questions.q: Case: Deodar trees in Himachal are cone-shaped with sloping branches. Main benefit?
options: Snow slides off and branches don't break
questions.why: The cone shape and sloping branches let snow slide off. This stops the weight of snow from breaking the branches.

questions.q: Why is a whale not a fish?
options: It breathes with lungs and feeds young on milk
questions.why: A whale breathes with lungs and feeds its young on milk, so it is a mammal. Being big, living in water or having fins does not make it a fish.

questions.q: Case: In an area, frogs disappear because a pond is filled. Insects increase. Why?
questions.why: Frogs eat insects, so when frogs disappear, the insects have fewer predators and increase. This is a link in the food chain.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: Pea is a dicot, and dicots have reticulate (net-like) venation. Maize and wheat are monocots, and mustard is a dicot.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
courses.summary: Food across India, the nutrients in food (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and water), simple tests for starch, protein and fat, the balanced diet, deficiency diseases, millets, and mindful habits like avoiding junk food and food waste.
outcomes: Learners can name the nutrients and their main sources and roles
Learners can perform and explain the iodine, copper sulphate and paper tests
Learners can plan a balanced plate for a day
Learners can link deficiency diseases to missing nutrients and explain mindful eating

lessons.title: Food across India and its nutrients

scenes.text: In class, Anu has idli-sambar, Harpreet has rajma-chawal, Dipika has fish-rice.
'Our food is so different!' says Harpreet.
Teacher: 'Different dishes, but the same nutrients inside.'
They list what each lunch gives the body.

steps.title: Why food differs
steps.body: Food habits depend on climate, local crops and traditions: rice in the east and south, wheat in the north, millets in dry areas, fish near coasts.

steps.title: Nutrients
steps.body:
- **Carbohydrates** (energy): rice, wheat, potato, millets, sugar
- **Proteins** (body-building, repair): dals, pulses, milk, eggs, paneer, fish, soya
- **Fats** (concentrated energy, stored): ghee, oil, butter, nuts
- **Vitamins** (protection, growth): fruits, vegetables, milk
- **Minerals** (bones, blood, etc.): iron, calcium, iodine — leafy vegetables, milk, iodised salt
- **Dietary fibre** (roughage, helps digestion): whole grains, vegetables, fruit peels
- **Water**: transports substances, controls body temperature

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Name the main nutrients in rajma-chawal.

- Rice: **carbohydrate**; rajma: **protein** and **fibre**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why is ghee called an energy-rich food?

- Fats give about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking fats are always bad — we need some fat; too much is the problem.
- Forgetting water and fibre as parts of a healthy diet.

activity.prompt: Which nutrient is each food richest in?

quiz.why: Dal is rich in protein, which helps the body grow and repair. Sugar and oil give energy, and water is needed for many jobs.
Carbohydrates, such as rice, roti and sugar, are the body's main source of energy. Minerals and vitamins protect the body.
Roughage is dietary fibre, which helps food move through the gut. It is not a fat, protein or vitamin.
Iodised salt has iodine added, which the body needs to make thyroid hormone. It does not give vitamin C, calcium or iron.
Water helps control body temperature, for example by sweating, and carries substances around the body. It also helps digestion.

lessons.title: Testing food for starch, protein and fat

scenes.text: Madam gives each group iodine, copper sulphate, caustic soda and paper.
A drop of iodine on potato turns it blue-black!
Milk with copper sulphate and caustic soda turns violet.
Groundnut rubbed on paper leaves an oily patch.

steps.title: Starch test
steps.body: Put 2–3 drops of dilute **iodine** solution on the food. **Blue-black** colour → starch present (potato, rice, bread).

steps.title: Protein test
steps.body: Make a paste/solution of food in water. Add 2 drops **copper sulphate** solution and 10 drops **sodium hydroxide (caustic soda)** solution; shake. **Violet/purple** colour → protein present (milk, egg white, dal).

steps.title: Fat test
steps.body: Rub or wrap the food in plain paper. A **translucent oily patch** (light passes through) that doesn't dry away → fat present (groundnut, butter).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Results: food X — iodine blue-black, no violet, no oily patch. Conclusion?

- X has **starch only** among the three (e.g., boiled potato).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Paneer: no blue-black, violet colour, slight oily patch.

- **Protein and fat**, little starch.

steps.title:
- Copper sulphate and caustic soda are harmful — use only under a teacher's supervision, wear gloves, never taste.
- A wet patch from water dries away; only a fat patch stays.
steps.body: Safety and common mistakes

activity.prompt: Match the test to its positive result.
pairs: Copper sulphate + caustic soda on protein

quiz.why: Iodine solution turns starch blue-black. This is the test for starch.
A violet colour in the copper sulphate and caustic soda test shows protein.

quiz.q: An oily patch on paper shows …
quiz.why: Food rubbed on paper leaves an oily patch if it contains fat. Starch and protein do not do this.
Caustic soda is a harmful chemical and can burn skin. It must be used only with care and an adult's supervision.

quiz.q: Which will give blue-black with iodine?
quiz.why: Rice is rich in starch, so it turns blue-black with iodine. Egg white has protein, oil has fat and water has neither.

scenes.text: Ravi feels tired and pale, and gets breathless climbing stairs.
The doctor finds he has anaemia — too little iron.
He starts eating spinach, jaggery, dates, dals and fruit.
A few weeks later he has more energy.

steps.title: Balanced diet
steps.body: A **balanced diet** has all nutrients in the right amounts, plus fibre and water. Eat a variety: cereals/millets, pulses, vegetables, fruits, milk, some fat. Needs differ by age, activity and health.

steps.title: Deficiency diseases
steps.body:
- **Vitamin A** → poor vision, night blindness (carrots, papaya, milk)
- **Vitamin B1** → beriberi, weak muscles (whole grains)
- **Vitamin C** → scurvy, bleeding gums (amla, lemon, guava)
- **Vitamin D** → rickets, soft bent bones (sunlight, milk)
- **Calcium** → weak bones and teeth
- **Iron** → anaemia, tiredness (green leafy vegetables, jaggery)
- **Iodine** → goitre, swelling of the neck (iodised salt)
- **Protein (lack of food)** → poor growth

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
A child's gums bleed often. Which fruit helps?

- Likely vitamin C deficiency → **amla, guava, lemon, orange**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Plan a balanced lunch.

- Roti/rice (carbs) + dal (protein) + sabzi and salad (vitamins, minerals, fibre) + curd (protein, calcium) + water.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Eating only one favourite food daily.
- Self-diagnosing — always see a doctor for symptoms; this is general education, not medical advice.

quiz.why: Bleeding gums can be a sign of lack of vitamin C, which causes scurvy. Citrus fruits and amla give vitamin C.

quiz.q: Rickets is due to lack of …
quiz.why: Rickets, which softens and bends bones, is caused by lack of vitamin D (along with calcium). Sunlight and some foods give vitamin D.
Goitre, a swelling in the neck, is caused by lack of iodine. Using iodised salt helps prevent it.
A balanced diet has all the nutrients in the right amounts. Only sweets, only proteins or only fruits would miss some nutrients.
Anaemia is linked to lack of iron, which the body needs to make healthy red blood cells.

lessons.title: Millets, junk food and mindful eating

scenes.text: Grandma in Karnataka makes ragi mudde every day.
Grandson Arjun prefers chips and cola.
His teacher explains why millets are 'nutri-cereals' and junk food is risky.
Arjun tries ragi dosa — and likes it!

steps.title: Millets — Shree Anna
steps.body: Millets like ragi (finger millet), jowar (sorghum), bajra (pearl millet) and others are rich in fibre and minerals (ragi is high in calcium), grow with little water and suit dry areas. The United Nations declared **2023 the International Year of Millets**, proposed by India.

steps.title: Junk food
steps.body: Chips, fried snacks, sugary drinks and many packaged foods are high in salt, sugar or fat and low in fibre and vitamins. Too much over time can lead to obesity, tooth decay and other health problems.

steps.title: Mindful eating
steps.body:
- Eat slowly and when hungry; stop when full
- Read food labels (sugar, salt, fat)
- Prefer home-cooked, seasonal, local food
- Don't waste food; take only what you can eat
- Wash hands before eating

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Label: 100 g chips contain 35 g fat and 1.5 g salt. Is it a good daily snack?

- No — very high fat and salt; an occasional treat at most.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why are millets good for farmers in dry regions?

- They need less water and survive heat, so crops don't fail easily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'fruit drinks' are the same as fruit — many are mostly sugar water.
- Skipping breakfast and then overeating junk later.

items: Ate a millet dish at least twice
Read the label on one packaged food
Drank water instead of a sugary drink
Finished my plate without wasting food

quiz.why: The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets, after a proposal by India. Millets are healthy and grow in dry areas.
Ragi (finger millet) is especially rich in calcium, which is good for bones and teeth.

quiz.q: Junk food is usually high in …
quiz.why: Junk food is usually high in salt, sugar or fat and low in fibre and vitamins. Eating it often is not healthy.

options: eating slowly and stopping when full
eating while watching TV for hours
quiz.why: Eating slowly and stopping when full is a mindful habit, as it helps us listen to our body. Wasting food or eating very fast is not mindful.

quiz.q: Millets suit dry areas because they …
quiz.why: Millets need less water than many crops, so they grow well in dry areas. They do not need lots of fertiliser or snow.

questions.q: Rice is rich in …
questions.why: Rice is rich in carbohydrate, mainly starch, which gives energy. It has little fat or vitamin C.

questions.q: Iodine turns starch …
questions.why: Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present. This is the test for starch.

questions.q: Lack of vitamin C causes …
questions.why: Lack of vitamin C causes scurvy. Rickets is from vitamin D, anaemia from iron and goitre from iodine.

questions.q: Which is a body-building food?
questions.why: Eggs are rich in protein, which is a body-building food. Jaggery, sugar and oil mainly give energy.

questions.q: Oily patch on paper indicates …
questions.why: An oily patch on paper shows the food has fat. Starch and protein do not leave an oily patch.

questions.q: Goitre is linked to lack of …
questions.why: Goitre is linked to lack of iodine, which the thyroid gland needs. Iodised salt helps prevent it.

questions.q: Dietary fibre helps …
questions.why: Dietary fibre helps digestion and the movement of waste through the gut. It does not directly help eyesight or clotting.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Sunlight helps prevent rickets. Reason (R): The skin makes vitamin D in sunlight.
questions.why: Both are true: the skin makes vitamin D in sunlight, and vitamin D helps bones, so sunlight helps prevent rickets. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: Food Y gives violet with copper sulphate–caustic soda test, no blue-black, no oily patch. Y is most likely …
questions.why: Violet shows protein, with no starch and no fat. Boiled egg white is mostly protein, while sugar, potato and butter would give other results.

questions.q: Which meal is most balanced?
options: Roti, dal, sabzi, curd and salad
questions.why: Roti, dal, sabzi, curd and salad give carbohydrates, proteins, fibre, vitamins and minerals. The other meals miss many nutrients.

questions.q: Night blindness is linked to …
questions.why: Night blindness, difficulty seeing in dim light, is linked to lack of vitamin A. Carrots and green leafy vegetables give vitamin A.

questions.q: Case: Chirag eats only polished white rice and gets weak muscles and swelling. Possible deficiency?
questions.why: Polishing rice removes the outer layer that holds vitamin B1, and lack of it causes beriberi. Weak muscles and swelling fit this, though a doctor must diagnose it.

questions.q: Why should copper sulphate tests be supervised?
questions.why: Copper sulphate and caustic soda are harmful chemicals, so the tests should be done with adult supervision and never tasted.

questions.q: Fats give per gram about … energy compared with carbohydrates.
questions.why: Fats give about 9 kcal per gram while carbohydrates give about 4, so fats give about twice as much energy per gram.

questions.q: Case: A packet says 'Sugar 45 g per 100 g'. What fraction is sugar?
questions.why: 45 g per 100 g is 45/100, which is a little less than half. So about 1/2 of the packet is sugar.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason millets are promoted?
questions.why: Millets do contain nutrients such as fibre and minerals, so 'no nutrients' is false. They are promoted because they suit dry regions and need less water.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Exploring Magnets
courses.summary: Magnets and their discovery, magnetic and non-magnetic materials, poles of a magnet, finding directions with a freely suspended magnet and a compass, attraction and repulsion, making a magnet, and caring for magnets.
outcomes: Learners can sort materials into magnetic and non-magnetic
Learners can locate poles and explain why a magnet always has two poles
Learners can find directions using a freely suspended magnet or compass
Learners can predict attraction or repulsion and make a simple magnet

scenes.text: Grandma drops her needle in a basket of rice.
Tanya swings a fridge magnet over the rice.
Click! The needle jumps up to the magnet.
Magnets attract iron things.

steps.title: Discovery
steps.body: Long ago, people found natural stones (**lodestone**, magnetite) that attracted iron. Today magnets are made in many shapes: bar, horseshoe (U-shaped), ring, disc, button.

steps.title: Magnetic vs non-magnetic
steps.body:
- **Magnetic materials** are attracted by magnets: iron, nickel, cobalt, steel.
- **Non-magnetic**: wood, plastic, rubber, glass, paper, aluminium, copper, gold, silver, brass.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which will a magnet pick up: steel pin, aluminium foil, iron nail, copper coin?

- **Steel pin and iron nail**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How to separate iron filings from sand?

- Move a magnet (wrapped in thin paper) through the mixture; filings stick and can be peeled off.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all metals are magnetic — aluminium, copper and gold are not.
- Thinking a magnet attracts all coins; it depends on the metal.

quiz.why: A naturally occurring magnet is called lodestone, made of the mineral magnetite. Chalk, granite and marble are not magnetic.
Copper is not attracted by a magnet. Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials.
Magnets attract magnetic materials such as iron, nickel and cobalt. They do not attract plastic, wood or all metals.
Magnets are made in solid shapes like bar, horseshoe and ring. A liquid is not a common shape for a magnet.

quiz.q: To separate iron filings from sand use …
quiz.why: Iron filings are attracted by a magnet and sand is not. So a magnet can separate them.

scenes.text: Rohan dips a bar magnet into a box of pins.
Most pins cling to the two ends; very few in the middle.
'Why the ends?' he asks.
The ends are the poles — the strongest parts.

steps.title: Poles
steps.body: Magnetic attraction is strongest at the two ends of a magnet, called **poles** — the **North pole (N)** and **South pole (S)**.

steps.title: Always two poles
steps.body: If you break a bar magnet, each piece becomes a new magnet with its own N and S pole. You can never get a single isolated pole.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
A bar magnet is cut into 3 pieces. How many poles in all?

- Each piece has 2 → **6 poles**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet gather most at …

- **The two ends** (poles).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the middle is strongest.
- Thinking breaking a magnet separates N from S.

statements.s: Attraction is strongest at the poles.
Breaking a magnet gives a separate N piece and S piece.
A ring magnet has poles too.
The middle of a bar magnet attracts most strongly.

quiz.why: Every magnet has a north pole (N) and a south pole (S).

quiz.q: Break a magnet in two: each piece has …
quiz.why: If you break a magnet, each piece becomes a complete magnet with two poles. You cannot get a single pole.

quiz.q: Strongest part of a bar magnet?
quiz.why: The magnetic force is strongest at the ends, which are the poles. The middle is weak.

quiz.q: 4 pieces of a magnet: total poles?
quiz.why: Each piece of a broken magnet has two poles. So 4 pieces have 4 × 2 = 8 poles.

quiz.q: Can we have a magnet with only a north pole?
quiz.why: No. A magnet always has two poles, and a single pole has never been found by breaking a magnet.

scenes.text: Scouts on a trek in Uttarakhand lose the trail on a cloudy day.
Their leader pulls out a small compass.
The needle settles pointing north.
They walk east as planned and find their camp.

steps.title: Freely suspended magnet
steps.body: A bar magnet hung freely from a thread comes to rest along the **north–south** direction. The end pointing north is the **north-seeking pole (N)**.

steps.title: Compass
steps.body: A **magnetic compass** has a small magnetised needle on a pivot inside a case with directions marked. Turn the case so 'N' lines up with the needle's north end; then read directions. The needle's north end is usually painted red.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Sun rises on your right while the compass needle points ahead of you. Which way do you face?

- Needle (north) ahead → you face **north**, east is on your right ✓.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why must a compass be kept away from other magnets or iron?

- They pull the needle and give wrong directions.

steps.title: History
steps.body: Sailors and travellers have used magnetic compasses for hundreds of years to navigate at sea when stars or the Sun were hidden.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the compass near a steel almirah or phone speaker.
- Turning the needle instead of the case.

activity.prompt: Steps to find east using a compass.
items: Hold the compass flat away from iron objects
Wait for the needle to settle
Turn the case until 'N' is under the needle's north end
Read the 'E' mark on the case

quiz.q: A freely suspended magnet rests along …
quiz.why: A freely hanging magnet turns and comes to rest along the north–south direction. This is how a compass works.
The north-seeking end of a freely suspended magnetic needle points to the north.

quiz.q: If you face north, west is on your …
quiz.why: If you face north, east is on your right and west is on your left.
A compass needle is a small magnet that can turn freely. It points in the north–south direction.
Iron objects and magnets near a compass pull its needle away from the true direction, so it gives a wrong reading.

lessons.title: Attraction, repulsion and making a magnet

scenes.text: Simran slides ring magnets onto a pencil.
One ring floats above the other in mid-air!
She flips it — now they snap together.
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- **Unlike** poles attract (N–S).
- **Like** poles repel (N–N or S–S).
- **Repulsion** is the sure test of a magnet: a piece of iron is attracted by both poles, but only another magnet can repel.

steps.title: Making a magnet (stroke method)
steps.body: Take an iron nail. Place one pole of a bar magnet at one end of the nail and move it to the other end. Lift it up, bring it back to the start, and repeat in the **same direction** with the **same pole** 30–40 times. The nail becomes a weak magnet; test it on pins.

steps.title: Caring for magnets
steps.body: Magnets lose magnetism if heated, hammered or dropped. Store bar magnets in pairs with unlike poles side by side, with wooden pieces between, and soft iron 'keepers' across the ends. Keep away from phones, cards and computers.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Two bar magnets: you bring end A of magnet 1 near the N pole of magnet 2 and they repel. What is A?

- Like poles repel → **A is N**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How do you know if an iron bar is a magnet?

- Bring each end near the N pole of a compass/known magnet; if one end **repels**, it is a magnet.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using attraction to test for a magnet — iron is also attracted.
- Stroking back and forth in both directions when making a magnet.

pairs: Either pole near an iron nail

quiz.why: Like poles (N–N or S–S) push each other away, so they repel. Unlike poles attract.
Only a magnet can repel another magnet, while an iron bar is attracted by both poles. So repulsion is the sure test, but attraction alone is not.

options: in one direction with the same pole
quiz.why: To make a magnet, stroke the iron piece in one direction with the same pole of a magnet. Stroking back and forth or with both poles cancels the effect.
Heating or hammering a magnet can destroy its magnetism. So we should not heat, drop or hammer magnets.

options: unlike poles side by side and keepers
quiz.why: Bar magnets are stored in pairs with unlike poles side by side and wooden spacers, with soft iron keepers across the ends. This helps them keep their strength.

questions.q: Which is magnetic?
questions.why: Iron is a magnetic material, so a magnet attracts it. Copper, glass and wood are not magnetic.

questions.q: Poles of a magnet are named …
questions.why: The two poles of a magnet are called north (N) and south (S).

questions.q: Like poles …
questions.why: Like poles repel each other. Unlike poles attract.

questions.q: A compass needle points …
questions.why: A compass needle is a small magnet that settles along the north–south direction. It does not point towards the Sun.

questions.q: Which coin material would NOT be attracted?
questions.why: Aluminium is non-magnetic, so a magnet does not attract it. Iron, nickel and steel are attracted.

questions.q: A magnet broken into 5 pieces has … poles in all
questions.why: Each piece of a broken magnet has two poles. So 5 pieces have 5 × 2 = 10 poles.

questions.q: Attraction is strongest at …
questions.why: The pull of a magnet is strongest at its poles, which are near the ends. It is weak in the middle.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Repulsion is the sure test for a magnet. Reason (R): An iron bar is attracted by both poles.
questions.why: Both are true: repulsion is the sure test, because an iron bar is attracted by both poles but can never repel. So only a magnet can repel.

questions.q: Case: End P of rod X repels the S pole of a magnet. P is …
questions.why: Like poles repel. Since P repels the S pole of the magnet, P must also be a south pole.

questions.q: Facing north, the sun sets on your …
questions.why: The Sun sets in the west. If you face north, west is on your left.

questions.q: Why store magnets with keepers?
questions.why: Keepers (soft iron pieces) are placed across the ends of stored magnets to help them keep their magnetism. Without them, magnets slowly weaken.

questions.q: Case: A ring magnet floats above another on a pencil. If the top one is flipped, it will …
questions.why: If the top ring is flipped, unlike poles now face each other, so it is pulled down and attracts. Before flipping, like poles repel and make it float.

questions.q: Iron filings + sawdust + salt: which is removed first with a magnet?
questions.why: Only iron is magnetic, so a magnet pulls out the iron filings first. Sawdust and salt are not attracted.

questions.q: A student strokes a nail 40 times but alternately with N and S poles. Result?
questions.why: Stroking with N and S poles alternately cancels the effect of each stroke. The nail ends up weak or not magnetised at all.

questions.q: Case: In a test, rod A attracts both ends of rod B; rod B attracts both ends of rod A. Which is true?
options: Neither can be a magnet repelling the other — at most one is a magnet
questions.why: If both rods were magnets, some of their ends would repel, since each has an N and an S pole. Since they only attract, at most one of them is a magnet.

questions.q: A compass placed near a strong magnet points …
questions.why: Near a strong magnet, the magnet's field is stronger than Earth's, so the needle points towards or away from the magnet's poles. It no longer shows north.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Measurement of Length and Motion
courses.summary: Why we need standard units, traditional Indian units, the SI unit metre and conversions, measuring length correctly with a scale and measuring curved lines, and describing motion with a reference point — linear, circular and oscillatory (periodic) motion.
outcomes: Learners can explain why standard units are needed and use the metre and its multiples
Learners can measure length correctly avoiding common errors
Learners can measure curved lengths with a thread
Learners can define motion using a reference point and classify types of motion

scenes.text: Neha measures cloth with her handspan: 8 spans.
Her father measures it: 6 spans.
Same cloth, different numbers!
A measuring tape gives 160 cm for both — a standard unit settles it.

steps.title: Measurement
steps.body: **Measurement** = comparing an unknown quantity with a known fixed quantity called a **unit**. A measurement has a **number** and a **unit** (e.g., 25 cm).

steps.title: Traditional units
steps.body: In India, people used body-based units: *angul* (finger width), *mutthi* (fist), *bitta*/handspan, cubit (elbow to fingertip), *kadam* (step), *dhanush*, *yojan* for long distances. They vary from person to person.

steps.title: Standard units
steps.body:
To be fair everywhere, the world uses the **International System of Units (SI)**. The SI unit of length is the **metre (m)**.

- 1 cm = 10 mm
- 1 m = 100 cm
- 1 km = 1000 m

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Convert 3.5 m to cm.

- 3.5 × 100 = **350 cm**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing only the number without the unit.
- Multiplying when you should divide (big unit → small unit: multiply; small → big: divide).

quiz.why: The SI unit of length is the metre. Centimetre and kilometre are related units, and foot is not an SI unit.
1 kilometre is 1000 metres, since 'kilo' means thousand.

options: they vary from person to person
quiz.why: Handspans differ from person to person, so measurements would not agree. We need a standard unit that is the same for everyone.
A measurement needs a number and a unit. '7' alone does not say whether it is 7 cm or 7 m.

scenes.text: Sameer's ruler is broken at the 0 end.
'I can't measure!' he says.
His friend starts from the 1 cm mark and subtracts 1 at the end.
Problem solved!

steps.title: Rules for a correct reading
steps.body:
- Place the scale **along** (parallel to) the length, touching the object.
- Start from the 0 mark (or any clear mark and subtract).
- Keep your eye **directly above** the point you read — looking from the side gives a wrong reading (parallax).
- Repeat and take the most common or average value.

steps.title: Example 1 — broken scale
steps.body:
Object's ends are at 1.0 cm and 8.4 cm.

- Length = 8.4 − 1.0 = **7.4 cm**

steps.title: Example 2 — average
steps.body:
Three readings of a pencil: 12.3, 12.4, 12.2 cm.

- Average = 36.9 ÷ 3 = **12.3 cm**

steps.title: Choose the right tool
steps.body: Ruler for books (cm, mm); measuring tape for cloth and body; long tape for a field; odometer for vehicles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting from the edge of the ruler instead of 0.
- Reading at an angle.
- Holding the scale tilted away from the object.

activity.prompt: Ends of a leaf read 2.5 cm and 9.3 cm on a scale. Length?

quiz.why: The eye should be directly above the mark being read. Looking from an angle gives a wrong reading, known as parallax error.

quiz.q: Broken ruler from 3 cm to 10.5 cm: length?
quiz.why: When the start of the object is at 3 cm and the end at 10.5 cm, the length is 10.5 − 3 = 7.5 cm.
A measuring tape is flexible, so it can go round the waist. A rigid ruler cannot.
The average is the sum of readings divided by their number: (15.1 + 15.3 + 15.2) ÷ 3 = 45.6 ÷ 3 = 15.2.
The scale should lie along the object, touching it, so we measure its true length. A tilted or raised scale gives errors.

scenes.text: Pari wants to know the length of a winding road on a map.
She lays a thread along the curves, marking start and end.
She straightens the thread on a scale: 14 cm.
On the map's scale (1 cm = 2 km) the road is 28 km!

steps.title: Thread method
steps.body:
- Put a knot at one end of a thread on the start of the curve.
- Lay the thread along the curve, pressing at each bend.
- Mark the thread at the end of the curve.
- Straighten the thread and measure the marked length with a scale.

steps.title: Divider method
steps.body: A divider can be 'walked' along a gentle curve in small equal steps; length ≈ number of steps × step size.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Circumference of a bangle: thread mark measures 19.5 cm. Circumference?

- **19.5 cm**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Map scale 1 cm = 5 km. Thread along a river measures 7.2 cm. Real length?

- 7.2 × 5 = **36 km**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Letting the thread stretch or slip off the curve.
- Forgetting to use the map scale.

items: Tie or hold one end of the thread at the start of the curve
Lay the thread along every bend
Mark the thread at the end point
Measure the marked length with a scale

quiz.q: To measure a curved line, use …
quiz.why: A thread can be laid along a curved line, then straightened and measured with a ruler. A ruler alone cannot follow curves.

quiz.q: Thread length 12 cm; map 1 cm = 3 km. Real?
quiz.why: On the map 1 cm stands for 3 km, so 12 cm stands for 12 × 3 = 36 km.
The thread must not stretch, because stretching would make it longer and the length wrong.
A divider measures a curved line by stepping along it in small equal steps. The number of steps then gives the length.

quiz.q: Circumference of a bottle can be found with …
quiz.why: The distance around a bottle is its circumference, which we can find by wrapping a thread or tape around it. A straight ruler cannot bend around it.

scenes.text: At a mela, Vikram rides the giant wheel.
His sister rides a toy train along a straight track.
Their cousin swings back and forth on a jhula.
Three rides, three kinds of motion!

steps.title: What is motion?
steps.body: An object is **in motion** if its position changes with time compared with a **reference point** (a fixed object). Whether something moves depends on the reference: a passenger in a bus is at rest relative to the bus but moving relative to trees.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Linear (rectilinear) motion**: along a straight line — a train on a straight track, a falling stone, march-past.
- **Circular motion**: along a circle, keeping the same distance from a centre — giant wheel seat, blades of a fan (a point on them), a stone whirled on a thread.
- **Oscillatory motion**: to and fro about a fixed position — swing, pendulum, guitar string.
- **Periodic motion**: repeats after a fixed time — pendulum, Earth around the Sun, clock hands. Oscillatory and many circular motions are periodic.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Classify: sewing-machine needle, ceiling fan blade tip, a car on a straight highway.

- Needle: **oscillatory** · Fan tip: **circular** · Car: **linear**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
A child on a merry-go-round says the friend beside her is 'not moving'. Explain.

- Relative to her (reference point on the ride), the friend's position doesn't change; relative to the ground both move in circles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the reference point.
- Calling every repeating motion oscillatory — the Earth's orbit is periodic and nearly circular, not to-and-fro.

items.text: Tip of a clock's second hand

quiz.q: Motion is decided by comparing with …
quiz.why: Whether something moves depends on a reference point. If its position changes compared to that point, it is in motion.
A swing moves to and fro about a fixed position, which is oscillatory motion. It is not linear or circular.
A soldier marching in a straight line shows linear motion, which is movement along a straight path.

quiz.q: Earth going around the Sun is …
quiz.why: Earth goes round the Sun and repeats this after a fixed time, one year. So it is periodic motion.

quiz.q: A passenger sitting in a moving bus is at rest relative to …
quiz.why: A passenger sitting in a moving bus has the same motion as the bus, so is at rest relative to the bus. Compared to the road, trees and houses, the passenger is moving.

questions.q: SI unit of length?
questions.why: The SI unit of length is the metre. Inch, mile and yard are other units.

questions.q: 1 m = ? cm
questions.why: 1 metre is 100 centimetres, since 'centi' means one hundredth.

questions.q: Swing motion is …
questions.why: A swing moves to and fro, which is oscillatory motion.

questions.q: Why are standard units needed?
questions.why: Standard units make measurements the same for everyone, so they are uniform and reliable everywhere. Body parts differ from person to person.

questions.q: Correct eye position while reading a scale?
questions.why: The eye should be directly above the mark to avoid parallax error. Looking at an angle shifts the reading.

questions.q: Giant wheel seat shows … motion
questions.why: A seat on a giant wheel moves along a circle, so it shows circular motion.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A sleeping passenger in a moving train is in motion. Reason (R): Motion depends on the reference point.
options: Both true, R explains A (relative to the ground)
questions.why: Both are true: a sleeping passenger is at rest relative to the train but moving relative to the ground, because motion depends on the reference point. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: A pencil's ends are at 2.0 cm and 13.7 cm. Length?
questions.why: The length is the difference of the two readings: 13.7 − 2.0 = 11.7 cm.

questions.q: Map scale 1 cm = 4 km; thread along road 6.5 cm. Distance?
questions.why: Each cm on the map is 4 km, so 6.5 cm is 6.5 × 4 = 26 km.

questions.q: Which is periodic but NOT oscillatory?
questions.why: The Moon going around the Earth repeats after a fixed time, so it is periodic, but it moves in a circle and not to and fro. A swing, pendulum and guitar string are oscillatory.

questions.q: Case: Readings of a table length: 120.4, 120.6, 120.5, 120.5 cm. Best value?
Case: A cubit is about 45 cm. A rope is 8 cubits long. About how long in metres?
questions.why: 8 × 45 cm = 360 cm, and 100 cm = 1 m, so the rope is 3.6 m.

questions.q: A wheel of circumference 2 m turns 750 times. Distance covered?
questions.why: Each turn covers 2 m, so 750 turns cover 750 × 2 = 1500 m = 1.5 km.

questions.q: Case: A bus moves on a straight road while its wheels turn. The bus body shows … motion and a point on the wheel rim shows … relative to the axle.
questions.why: The bus body moves along a straight road, so it shows linear motion. A point on the rim moves in a circle around the axle, which is circular motion relative to the axle.
Convert to metres: 750 mm = 0.75 m and 30 cm = 0.30 m. So 0.75 + 1.25 + 0.30 = 2.3 m.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Materials Around Us
courses.summary: Objects and the materials they are made of, and grouping materials by properties: appearance and lustre, hardness and roughness, solubility in water, floating and sinking, and transparency (transparent, translucent, opaque) — and why we choose a material for a job.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish an object from the material it is made of
Learners can group materials by lustre, hardness, solubility, floating and transparency
Learners can test and record properties fairly
Learners can explain why certain materials are chosen for certain uses

scenes.text: Anaya lists kitchen things: steel plate, glass tumbler, wooden spoon, plastic box.
'Spoons can be steel, wood or plastic!' she notices.
One material can make many objects; one object can be made of many materials.
She groups them by material.

steps.title: Object vs material
steps.body: An **object** is a thing (chair, spoon). A **material** is what it is made of (wood, steel, plastic, glass, cloth, paper, clay). Some objects use several materials: a pencil has wood, graphite, paint, rubber, metal.

steps.title: Why group materials?
steps.body: Grouping makes it easy to study, find and use them; shopkeepers arrange goods in groups too. We group by **properties**.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Name materials in a bicycle.

- Steel (frame), rubber (tyres), plastic (seat cover/handle grips), leather or foam (seat).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Which objects can be made of clay?

- Pots (matka), diyas, cups (kulhad), bricks, toys.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling 'spoon' a material.
- Thinking each object can only be made of one material.

quiz.why: Plastic is a material that things are made from. A pen, bottle and table are objects.
A tumbler and a window pane are made of glass. A tyre, shirt and book are made of other materials.
A pencil is made of several materials, such as wood, graphite, paint and rubber.
We group materials by their properties, such as hardness, shine or whether they dissolve. The name or the shop does not matter.
A kulhad is a small cup made of clay, baked hard. It is not made of steel, glass or plastic.

scenes.text: A new steel tumbler shines under the light.
A wooden block looks dull.
Teacher scratches chalk with a key — it marks easily; a steel spoon doesn't.
Shine and hardness are properties.

steps.title: Appearance and lustre
steps.body: Materials differ in colour, texture and shine. Freshly cut or polished **metals** (iron, copper, aluminium, gold) have **lustre** — they shine. Many lose shine on exposure to air and moisture (iron rusts, copper darkens); scrubbing restores it. Wood, paper, chalk are non-lustrous.

steps.title: Hardness
steps.body: **Hard** materials are difficult to compress or scratch (iron, stone, diamond). **Soft** ones are easily compressed or scratched (cotton, sponge, chalk, wax).

steps.title: Rough and smooth
steps.body: Sandpaper and bark are rough; glass and polished marble are smooth.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why does an old copper vessel look dull?

- Air and moisture form a dull layer on its surface; cleaning it with tamarind or lemon restores lustre.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Which is harder: chalk or a steel nail? Test.

- Scratch chalk with the nail — chalk gets a mark → **nail is harder**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking a shiny plastic toy is a metal — shine alone doesn't tell; test other properties too.

quiz.why: Lustre is the shine of a material, like the shine of a polished metal. It is not colour or softness.
A sponge is soft because it can be pressed easily. Iron, diamond and stone are hard.

quiz.q: Old iron loses lustre due to …
quiz.why: Iron reacts with air and moisture and rusts, so its shine goes. Cutting and painting do not cause rust.
Sandpaper has a rough surface. Mirror, glass and marble are smooth.
Metals generally have a shiny surface, which is lustre. They are not transparent or soluble in water.

scenes.text: Rani stirs sugar into water for nimbu-pani.
The sugar vanishes but the drink tastes sweet.
Sand stirred into water just settles at the bottom.
Sugar is soluble; sand is insoluble.

steps.title: Soluble and insoluble
steps.body:
- **Soluble**: mixes completely and disappears in water — sugar, salt, lemon juice (liquid), vinegar.
- **Insoluble**: does not dissolve — sand, chalk powder, sawdust, oil (floats as a layer), wax.

steps.title: Gases dissolve too
steps.body: Some oxygen dissolves in water — fish and water plants use it.

steps.title: Example 1 — fair test
steps.body:
Which dissolves: salt, sand, sugar, chalk?

- Take equal water in 4 glasses, add one spoon each, stir same time.
- Salt and sugar disappear → **soluble**; sand settles, chalk makes water milky then settles → **insoluble**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Oil and water — what happens?

- Oil forms a separate layer on top → oil is **insoluble (immiscible)** in water and lighter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'disappeared' means gone — the sugar is still there (taste it, or evaporate the water).
- Not stirring equally when comparing.

quiz.why: Salt dissolves in water, so it is soluble. A soluble substance mixes completely with water.
Oil does not mix with water, so it forms a separate layer, usually on top. It does not dissolve.
Fish breathe the oxygen gas that is dissolved in water, using their gills. They cannot use the oxygen in the water molecules.

quiz.q: Which proves dissolved sugar is still there?
quiz.why: Sugar mixed in water seems to disappear, but the water tastes sweet. So it is still there, dissolved.
Sand does not dissolve in water. It settles at the bottom.

story.title: Leaves and stones in the pond

scenes.text: Kids drop a leaf, a stone and a plastic ball in a pond.
The stone sinks; the leaf and ball float.
Back home, they look through glass, butter paper and cardboard.
Clear, blurry, and nothing at all!

steps.title: Float or sink
steps.body: Objects that are lighter than the water they push aside float (wood, dry leaf, plastic ball, ice, oil); heavier ones sink (stone, iron nail, coin). Shape also matters: a ship of steel floats because its shape pushes aside a lot of water.

steps.title: Transparency
steps.body:
- **Transparent**: you can see clearly through it — clear glass, clean water, air, some plastics.
- **Translucent**: you can see, but not clearly — butter paper, frosted glass, oiled paper, thin cloth.
- **Opaque**: you cannot see through at all — wood, cardboard, metal, stone.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Torch test: shine a torch through each sheet; on a wall, glass lets a bright patch, butter paper a dim patch, cardboard none.

- Transparent, translucent, opaque.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why are bathroom windows often frosted?

- Frosted glass is **translucent**: light comes in but people can't see clearly inside.

steps.title: Choosing materials
steps.body:
- Cooking pots: metal (good conductor, hard)
- Windows: glass (transparent)
- Raincoat: plastic (waterproof)
- Wires: copper with plastic cover

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking heavy things always sink — a big wooden log floats.
- Calling butter paper opaque.

quiz.why: Clean water lets light pass so we can see clearly through it, so it is transparent. Opaque materials block light.
Butter paper lets some light through but we cannot see clearly through it. So it is translucent.
Dry wood floats on water. An iron nail, stone and coin sink.

options: shape pushes aside lots of water
quiz.why: A steel ship is shaped to push aside a lot of water, so the water pushes it up enough to float. Steel itself is heavier than water.
Bathroom windows are often translucent, since they let light in but give privacy because you cannot see through clearly.

questions.q: Which is a material?
questions.why: Glass is a material, while ball, chair and cup are objects.

questions.q: Freshly cut metals are …
questions.why: Freshly cut metals are shiny, which is lustre. Metals are not transparent or soluble in water.

questions.q: Sugar in water is …
questions.why: Sugar dissolves in water, so it is soluble. Insoluble things do not dissolve.

questions.q: Cardboard is …
questions.why: Cardboard does not let light pass, so it is opaque. Transparent and translucent materials let light through.

questions.q: Which sinks in water?
questions.why: An iron nail is denser than water, so it sinks. A plastic ball, leaf and cork float.

questions.q: Which is hard?
questions.why: Iron is hard, as it cannot be pressed or scratched easily. Wax, sponge and cotton are soft.

questions.q: Oil poured into water …
questions.why: Oil does not dissolve in water and is lighter, so it forms a layer on top.

questions.q: Assertion (A): We use glass for windows. Reason (R): Glass is transparent.
questions.why: Both are true: glass is used for windows because it is transparent. So light passes through, which explains the use.

questions.q: Case: A material is shiny, hard, does not dissolve and sinks. It is most likely …
questions.why: A shiny, hard solid that does not dissolve and sinks fits a metal such as iron. Sugar dissolves, wax is soft and wood floats.

questions.q: Why do copper vessels get dull?
questions.why: Copper vessels get dull because copper reacts with air and moisture, forming a layer on the surface. They do not melt or dissolve.

questions.q: Frosted glass is … because …
options: translucent; light passes but not a clear image
questions.why: Frosted glass lets light pass but not a clear image, so it is translucent. Transparent glass gives a clear view.

questions.q: Case: Ravi tests solubility of 4 powders using different amounts of water in each. What's wrong?
questions.why: A fair test keeps everything the same except one thing. Using different amounts of water changes two things, so the test is unfair.

questions.q: Which property makes steel suitable for cooking pots?
questions.why: Steel is hard, so it does not bend or dent, and it conducts heat, so it cooks food. Its use matches its properties.

questions.q: Why does a heavy wooden log float but a small iron nail sinks?
options: Floating depends on the material and shape, not just weight
questions.why: Floating depends on the material and its shape, not on weight alone. Wood is less dense than water, while an iron nail is denser.

questions.q: Case: A sheet lets a dim blurry patch of torchlight through. It is …
questions.why: A sheet that lets some light through but gives only a blurry patch is translucent. Transparent gives a clear image and opaque gives none.

questions.q: Best material for a raincoat?
questions.why: Plastic is waterproof and keeps rain out. Wool, cotton and paper soak up water.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Temperature and its Measurement
courses.summary: Hot and cold, why touch is unreliable, temperature and the Celsius scale, clinical, laboratory and digital thermometers, how to read them safely, normal body temperature, and everyday uses of temperature measurement.
outcomes: Learners can explain why our sense of touch cannot measure temperature reliably
Learners can read clinical and laboratory thermometers correctly
Learners can state the ranges and precautions of each thermometer
Learners can relate temperature to health, weather and cooking

lessons.title: Hot, cold and the trouble with touch

scenes.text: Teacher sets out three bowls: cold, lukewarm, warm.
Ishita puts her left hand in cold and right hand in warm for a minute.
Then both hands in the lukewarm bowl: left feels warm, right feels cold!
'Same water, two feelings — we need a thermometer.'

steps.title: Hot and cold
steps.body: How hot or cold something is is its **temperature**. Touch tells us roughly, but it depends on what our skin felt just before, so it is **not reliable** — and touching very hot things is dangerous.

steps.title: Temperature unit
steps.body: We measure temperature in **degrees Celsius (°C)**. Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C (at normal air pressure). The SI unit is the kelvin (K) — used by scientists.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Explain the three-bowls result.

- The hand from cold water feels the lukewarm water as warm; the hand from warm water feels it as cold. Our sense compares, it doesn't measure.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Is 35 °C weather hot or cold?

- Hot (a warm summer day); 5 °C would be cold.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing a child's fever only by touching the forehead — use a thermometer.
- Mixing °C and °F numbers.

statements.s: Our sense of touch reliably measures temperature.
Water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure.
Water freezes at 0 °C.
Temperature tells how hot or cold something is.

quiz.why: A common unit of temperature is the degree Celsius (°C). Kilogram, litre and metre measure other things.

quiz.q: Why not judge temperature by touch?
options: it is unreliable and can be unsafe
quiz.why: Touch is unreliable because how hot something feels depends on what you touched before. It can also be unsafe for very hot objects.
Water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure. 212 is the same temperature in °F.
Water freezes at 0 °C. 32 is the same temperature in °F.
The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin. Celsius and Fahrenheit are other scales.

scenes.text: Little Arnav feels hot at night.
Papa uses a digital thermometer under his tongue.
It beeps: 38.6 °C — a fever.
They call the doctor and give fluids.

steps.title: Clinical thermometer
steps.body: Used to measure **body temperature**. Range usually **35 °C to 42 °C** (human body temperature stays in this range). **Normal body temperature** is about **37 °C** (98.6 °F); it varies a little between people and through the day.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Digital thermometer**: battery-powered, shows the number on a screen; safe and easy. Recommended.
- **Mercury thermometer**: glass with mercury; has a **kink** (narrow bend) that stops mercury falling back so you can read it. Mercury is toxic — many places now discourage its use. If one breaks, don't touch the mercury; ask an adult.

steps.title: How to use a digital thermometer
steps.body:
- Clean the tip with soap water or spirit.
- Switch on; place under the tongue (or armpit) with lips closed.
- Wait for the beep; read the value.
- Clean and store.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
A reading of 39.2 °C means …

- Above 37 °C → **fever**; consult a doctor if it continues or is high.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why does a clinical thermometer only go to 42 °C?

- Body temperature doesn't go far outside 35–42 °C, so a short range gives finer, easier reading.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a clinical thermometer for hot water — it can break (it's not made for above 42 °C).
- Reading immediately without waiting. General education, not medical advice: see a doctor for high or lasting fever.

bands.text: Lower than usual — re-check; if the person feels unwell or very cold, see a doctor.
Fever — rest, drink fluids, inform an adult/doctor.
High fever — seek medical help promptly.

quiz.why: Normal human body temperature is about 37 °C. 42 °C would be dangerously high.
A clinical thermometer reads from about 35 °C to 42 °C, the range of human body temperature.

quiz.q: The kink in a mercury thermometer …
quiz.why: The kink in a mercury clinical thermometer stops the mercury from falling back quickly, so the reading can be taken after removing it.
A digital thermometer has no mercury, so it is safer. A broken mercury thermometer can release toxic mercury.

quiz.q: Should you measure boiling water with a clinical thermometer?
quiz.why: No. The scale stops at about 42 °C, and boiling water at 100 °C would break it.

scenes.text: In the lab, Kiran puts a thermometer in melting ice: 0 °C.
She heats water; the liquid column climbs steadily.
At boiling it stays near 100 °C.
She records readings every minute and plots a graph.

steps.title: Laboratory thermometer
steps.body: Used for measuring temperatures of liquids, air, experiments. Range usually **−10 °C to 110 °C**. No kink — the reading changes as soon as it is removed, so read it **while it is in the liquid**. Usually contains coloured alcohol or mercury.

steps.title: Reading the scale
steps.body:
- Find the value of each small division: between 0 and 10 there may be 10 divisions → each = 1 °C (or 5 → each = 2 °C).
- Keep your eye level with the top of the liquid column.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body:
- Hold it upright; don't let the bulb touch the bottom or sides of the container.
- Bulb must be surrounded by the substance.
- Handle with care, don't shake hard.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Between 20 and 30 there are 5 divisions; the liquid is 3 divisions above 20.

- Each = 2 °C → 20 + 6 = **26 °C**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why can't you use a laboratory thermometer to measure fever?

- It has no kink; the reading drops before you read it after removing it. It's also not designed for the mouth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the thermometer out to read.
- Letting the bulb touch the hot beaker bottom.

activity.prompt: Match the thermometer to the job.

quiz.why: A laboratory thermometer typically reads from about −10 °C to 110 °C. This is wider than a clinical thermometer's range.
A lab thermometer has no kink, so the mercury falls as soon as the temperature drops. So we read it while it is in the liquid.

options: surrounded by the liquid, not touching container
quiz.why: The bulb should be in the middle of the liquid, surrounded by it and not touching the sides or bottom. Otherwise the container's temperature affects it.

quiz.q: 10 divisions between 30 and 40; liquid at 7th division. Reading?
