quiz.why: Between 30 and 40 there are 10 divisions, so each is 1 °C. The 7th division is 30 + 7 = 37 °C.
The reading must be taken while the bulb is still in the liquid, since the mercury drops quickly when it is taken out.

lessons.title: Temperature in daily life and weather

scenes.text: News: 'Delhi 44 °C, Shimla 18 °C, Leh −5 °C.'
Aditi in Delhi drinks lots of water and stays indoors at noon.
Her cousin in Leh wears layers.
Knowing the temperature helps us stay safe.

steps.title: Uses
steps.body:
- **Health**: fever check, vaccine and medicine storage (fridges at about 2–8 °C)
- **Weather**: maximum and minimum temperatures; heatwave warnings
- **Cooking**: ovens, milk boiling, setting curd in warmth
- **Farming**: frost warnings, seed germination

steps.title: Heat safety
steps.body: In a heatwave: drink water often, wear light cotton clothes, avoid going out in the hottest hours (about 12–4 pm), never leave children or pets in parked cars.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
A fridge reads 12 °C inside. Is it fine for storing milk?

- No — a fridge should be cold (about 4 °C). Milk may spoil faster.

steps.title: Celsius and Fahrenheit
steps.body: Some thermometers show °F. 37 °C = 98.6 °F; 0 °C = 32 °F; 100 °C = 212 °F.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Ignoring heatwave warnings; heatstroke is an emergency — call 112.

items: I check fever with a thermometer, not touch
I drink water often in hot weather
I avoid the midday sun in a heatwave
I never touch mercury from a broken thermometer
I tell an adult if someone feels very hot, confused or faint

quiz.why: The range is the difference between maximum and minimum: 39 − 24 = 15 °C.
37 °C is about 98.6 °F, which is normal body temperature in Fahrenheit.
In a heatwave, drink plenty of water and stay in the shade to avoid heat illness. Exercising at noon or skipping water is risky.
Vaccines are kept in fridges at about 2–8 °C. This is called the cold chain, and it keeps them effective.
Water boils at 100 °C, which is 212 °F.

questions.q: Unit °C stands for …
questions.why: The symbol °C stands for degree Celsius, the unit of temperature.

questions.q: Normal human body temperature?
questions.why: Normal human body temperature is about 37 °C. Anything near 100 °C would be boiling water.

questions.q: Water freezes at …
questions.why: Water freezes at 0 °C. Boiling is at 100 °C.

questions.q: Clinical thermometer range?
questions.why: A clinical thermometer reads about 35–42 °C, the range of body temperature.

questions.q: Which has a kink?
questions.why: The mercury clinical thermometer has a kink that holds the reading. Lab, room and digital thermometers do not need it.

questions.q: Why is touch unreliable?
options: Our feeling depends on what we touched before
questions.why: How hot or cold something feels depends on what we touched just before, so touch can fool us. A thermometer gives a reliable number.

questions.q: A lab thermometer should be read …
options: while it is in the liquid
questions.why: A lab thermometer has no kink, so the mercury falls quickly after removal. So read it while it is in the liquid.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A clinical thermometer must not be used for boiling water. Reason (R): Its scale goes only up to about 42 °C.
questions.why: Both are true: a clinical thermometer's scale ends at about 42 °C, so boiling water at 100 °C could break it. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Between 0 and 10 there are 5 divisions; reading is 4 divisions past 10. Value?
questions.why: Between 0 and 10 there are 5 divisions, so each is 2 °C. 4 divisions past 10 is 10 + 4 × 2 = 18 °C.

questions.q: Case: A child's digital thermometer reads 38.4 °C. Best action?
options: Take a cold bath in ice
Inform an adult, rest, fluids, consult a doctor if needed
questions.why: 38.4 °C is a fever. A child should tell an adult, rest and drink fluids, and see a doctor if needed. An ice bath or exercise would be unsafe.

questions.q: Why are digital thermometers preferred over mercury ones?
options: Mercury is toxic if the glass breaks
questions.why: If a mercury thermometer breaks, the mercury is toxic. Digital ones have no mercury, so they are safer.

questions.q: Case: Max temperatures on 5 days: 34, 36, 39, 41, 40 °C. Rise from day 1 to day 4?
questions.why: The rise from day 1 (34 °C) to day 4 (41 °C) is 41 − 34 = 7 °C.

questions.q: Why does a lab thermometer have no kink?
options: It must show changing temperatures continuously
questions.why: A lab thermometer has no kink, so it follows the temperature up and down as it changes. That helps readings during an experiment.

questions.q: Case: Ice in a beaker reads 0 °C; after heating 5 minutes it reads 60 °C. Average rise per minute?
questions.why: The rise is 60 °C in 5 minutes, so the average is 60 ÷ 5 = 12 °C per minute.

questions.q: A temperature of 104 °F is about …
Case: A student's bulb touches the bottom of a heated beaker. Reading will likely be …
options: higher than the water's real temperature
questions.why: If the bulb touches the bottom of a heated beaker, it reads the hot glass and not the water, so the reading is too high. The bulb should stay in the middle of the liquid.

courses.title: Ch 8 · A Journey through States of Water
courses.summary: Water as solid, liquid and gas; melting, freezing, evaporation, boiling and condensation; factors that speed up evaporation; the cooling effect of evaporation (sweat, matka); and the water cycle that moves water around the Earth.
outcomes: Learners can describe the three states of water and changes between them
Learners can explain factors affecting evaporation using fair tests
Learners can explain cooling by evaporation in daily life
Learners can describe the water cycle and its importance

scenes.text: Anil leaves an ice cube on a plate in the sun.
It melts into a puddle.
By evening the puddle has vanished into the air.
Ice → water → vapour: one substance, three states.

steps.title: States
steps.body:
- **Solid** — ice: fixed shape and volume
- **Liquid** — water: fixed volume, takes the shape of its container, flows
- **Gas** — water vapour: no fixed shape or volume, spreads out; invisible

steps.title: Changes of state
steps.body:
- **Melting**: ice → water (on heating; ice melts at 0 °C)
- **Freezing**: water → ice (on cooling; at 0 °C)
- **Evaporation**: water → vapour at any temperature, from the surface
- **Boiling**: rapid change to vapour throughout, at 100 °C (normal pressure)
- **Condensation**: vapour → water (on cooling)

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why do clothes dry on a line?

- Water in them **evaporates** into the air.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why does a cold glass of water get droplets outside?

- Water vapour in air touches the cold glass, cools and **condenses**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling steam from a kettle 'vapour' — the white cloud you see is tiny condensed droplets; true vapour is invisible.
- Thinking evaporation happens only at 100 °C.

quiz.why: Water vapour is water in the gas state. Ice is the solid and water the liquid.

quiz.q: Droplets on a cold glass come from …
quiz.why: Water vapour in the air touches the cold glass, cools and turns into droplets. This is condensation.
Evaporation can happen at any temperature, from the surface of a liquid. It is only faster when it is hotter.
Ice melts at 0 °C. 100 °C is the boiling point of water.
A liquid has a fixed volume but no fixed shape, so it takes the shape of its container. A solid has a fixed shape.

scenes.text: Monsoon week: Seema's uniform won't dry.
Mother spreads it wide under the fan.
On a sunny, breezy day it dries in an hour.
Heat, wind and spreading out speed up drying.

steps.title: Factors
steps.body:
- **Temperature**: warmer → faster evaporation
- **Surface area**: spread out (wide plate) → faster than a narrow bottle
- **Wind**: moving air carries vapour away → faster
- **Humidity**: when air already holds lots of vapour (humid, rainy days) → slower

steps.title: Example 1 — fair test of surface area
steps.body:
Pour 50 mL water into a plate and into a glass; keep both side by side in the same place.

- After some hours, the plate has less water left → larger surface area evaporates faster.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why do clothes dry slowly in Mumbai's monsoon?

- The air is very **humid**, so evaporation is slow.

steps.title: Salt from sea water
steps.body: In coastal Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, sea water is let into shallow pans; the Sun evaporates the water and salt is left behind.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing two factors at once in a test.
- Forgetting humidity — even a warm day can be slow drying if humid.

quiz.why: Clothes dry slowest on a humid, rainy day, since air already full of vapour takes in more only slowly. Sun and wind speed drying.
A bigger surface area exposes more water to the air, so evaporation is faster.

quiz.q: Salt is made from sea water by …
quiz.why: Salt is obtained from sea water by evaporation. The Sun's heat turns the water to vapour and leaves the salt behind.
Wind carries water vapour away from the surface, so more water can evaporate. So it speeds evaporation.

quiz.q: A fair test of temperature changes …
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one factor changes. To test temperature, change only the temperature and keep wind and the rest the same.

scenes.text: In summer, Dadi's clay matka keeps water cool without a fridge.
Its outside feels damp.
Why is the water cool?
Water seeps out and evaporates from the surface, taking heat away.

steps.title: Evaporation cools
steps.body: When water evaporates, it takes heat from the surface it leaves. So the surface cools down.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- **Sweating**: sweat evaporating from skin cools the body.
- **Matka/surahi**: tiny pores let water seep out and evaporate, cooling the water inside.
- **Wet cloth** on the forehead during fever (with doctor's advice).
- **Desert coolers**: air passes through wet pads.
- Sprinkling water on a hot courtyard floor in the evening.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why does a matka cool better on a dry windy day?

- Faster evaporation → more cooling.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why do we feel cold after a swim even on a warm day?

- Water on the skin evaporates, taking heat from the body.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the clay itself is 'cold' — the cooling comes from evaporation.
- Expecting a matka to cool much on a humid day.

statements.s: Evaporation makes a surface cooler.
A glazed (non-porous) pot cools water as well as a matka.
Sweating helps cool the body.
Desert coolers work best in humid weather.
statements.why: Work best when air is dry.

quiz.why: The water seeps through the pores of the clay pot and evaporates from the outside. Evaporation takes away heat, so the water inside stays cool.
We sweat more when it is hot or when we exercise. Sweat evaporates and cools the body.
Coolers work best in dry air, because water evaporates quickly there and cools the air. In very humid air evaporation is slow.

quiz.q: After a swim we feel cold because …
quiz.why: Water on the skin evaporates and takes heat from the body, so we feel cold after a swim.

quiz.q: Sprinkling water on a hot floor cools it by …
quiz.why: Water sprinkled on a hot floor evaporates, taking heat from the floor and cooling it.

scenes.text: A drop of water in the Bay of Bengal is warmed by the Sun.
It rises as vapour, cools high up and becomes part of a cloud.
Months later it falls as rain over the Western Ghats.
It flows down a river and back to the sea — a never-ending journey.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
- **Evaporation** from oceans, rivers, lakes, soil
- **Transpiration**: plants release water vapour from leaves
- **Condensation**: vapour cools high above, forming tiny droplets → clouds
- **Precipitation**: droplets join and fall as rain, snow or hail
- **Collection/run-off**: water flows into rivers, seas; some soaks into the ground (groundwater)

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: The water cycle supplies fresh water for drinking, farming and ecosystems, and fills rivers and groundwater. In India, the monsoon brings most of the year's rain.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why are clouds formed high up?

- Air cools as it rises; vapour condenses on dust particles at low temperatures.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How does cutting forests affect rain locally?

- Fewer trees → less transpiration and more run-off; soil holds less water.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the water cycle creates new water — the same water keeps moving.
- Forgetting plants' role (transpiration).

activity.prompt: Order the water cycle starting from the sea.
items: It condenses into droplets forming clouds
Droplets join and fall as rain
Rainwater flows through rivers back to the sea

quiz.q: Water vapour released by plants is …
quiz.why: Plants lose water vapour from their leaves, which is called transpiration. Condensation is vapour turning into liquid.
Clouds form when water vapour cools high in the air and condenses into tiny droplets. This is condensation.
Rain, snow and hail are forms of water falling from clouds, which is called precipitation.

quiz.q: Most rain in India comes during …
quiz.why: Most of India's rainfall comes during the monsoon season, which usually lasts from June to September.

quiz.q: Water soaking into the ground becomes …
quiz.why: Water that soaks into the ground collects as groundwater. We get it from wells and borewells.

questions.q: Ice is water in the … state
questions.why: Ice is the solid state of water. Liquid water and water vapour (gas) are the other states.

questions.q: Water → vapour at surface is …
questions.why: Water changing into vapour from its surface is evaporation. Condensation is the opposite.

questions.q: Clouds are formed by …
questions.why: Clouds form when water vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets. They do not form by melting or freezing.

questions.q: Which speeds up drying?
questions.why: Wind speeds up drying because it carries water vapour away. High humidity and cold slow it down.

questions.q: Droplets outside a cold bottle come from …
questions.why: Water vapour in the air cools on touching the cold bottle and condenses into droplets. The water does not come from inside the bottle.

questions.q: Matka water is cool because of …
questions.why: Water seeps through the pores of the matka and evaporates, which cools the water inside. This is evaporative cooling.

questions.q: Water boils at … at normal pressure
questions.why: At normal pressure water boils at 100 °C. 0 °C is its freezing point.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Clothes dry slowly on humid days. Reason (R): Air already full of vapour takes in vapour slowly.
questions.why: Both are true: on humid days the air already holds much vapour, so more water evaporates only slowly. The reason explains why clothes dry slowly.

questions.q: Case: 100 mL water in a plate and in a bottle kept side by side. After 6 h which has less water?
questions.why: The plate has a bigger surface area, so more water evaporates from it. After 6 hours the plate has less water than the bottle.

questions.q: Transpiration happens through …
questions.why: Plants lose water vapour mainly through their leaves, through tiny pores called stomata. This is transpiration.

questions.q: Sweating cools us because …
questions.why: Sweat evaporates from the skin and takes heat from the body, which cools us. Sweat itself is not cold.

questions.q: Case: In salt pans, why choose sunny, windy months?
questions.why: Sunny and windy months make evaporation faster, so salt forms sooner. Rain and cold slow it down.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of the water cycle?
questions.why: Evaporation, condensation and precipitation are steps of the water cycle. Photosynthesis making salt is not.

questions.q: A desert cooler cools less in Kolkata's monsoon than in Jaipur's dry summer. Why?
questions.why: A cooler works by evaporation, which is slow in humid air. Kolkata in the monsoon is very humid, so cooling is weaker than in Jaipur's dry summer.

questions.q: Case: A puddle of 2 L evaporates at 250 mL/hour on a sunny day. Time to dry?
questions.why: 2 L is 2000 mL. At 250 mL per hour, the time is 2000 ÷ 250 = 8 hours.

questions.q: The 'steam' cloud seen above a kettle is …
questions.why: Water vapour itself is invisible. The cloud we see above a kettle is made of tiny droplets formed when the vapour cools and condenses.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
courses.summary: Mixtures and why we separate them; handpicking, threshing, winnowing and sieving; sedimentation, decantation and filtration; evaporation; magnetic separation and churning — with real examples from Indian homes and farms.
outcomes: Learners can explain what a mixture is and why components are separated
Learners can choose a suitable method based on differences in size, weight, solubility or magnetism
Learners can describe sedimentation, decantation, filtration and evaporation step by step
Learners can use more than one method in sequence for a complex mixture

lessons.title: Mixtures and simple methods: handpicking, threshing, winnowing

scenes.text: At harvest, Gurpreet's family beats bundles of wheat stalks.
Then they drop the grain from a height in the breeze.
Light husk blows away; heavy grain falls in a heap.
At home, Mother picks tiny stones out of the dal.

steps.title: Mixtures
steps.body: A **mixture** has two or more substances mixed together that keep their own properties (sand + salt, dal + stones). We separate them to remove harmful or unwanted parts or to get a useful part.

steps.title: Methods based on visible differences
steps.body:
- **Handpicking**: picking out by hand items that differ in size, colour or shape — stones from rice or dal.
- **Threshing**: beating stalks to separate grains from them — by hand, bullocks or a thresher machine.
- **Winnowing**: dropping a mixture from a height in wind; light husk blows away, heavy grain falls close — using a *soop*/winnowing basket.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which method removes small stones from rice?

- **Handpicking** (they differ in colour/shape and are few).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why must winnowing be done in a breeze?

- Wind carries the light husk away from the heavier grains.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using handpicking for very fine or very many particles — it's too slow.
- Thinking threshing and winnowing are the same — threshing loosens grain, winnowing separates husk.

activity.prompt: Match the method to the job.

quiz.why: A mixture contains two or more substances mixed together. A pure substance has only one kind of matter.
Winnowing separates heavier grains from lighter husk using wind. The lighter husk blows away.
Threshing separates grains from the stalks by beating them. Winnowing then removes the husk.

quiz.q: Handpicking is used when unwanted parts are …
quiz.why: Handpicking is used when the unwanted parts are few and big enough to see and pick by hand. It does not work for tiny or dissolved things.

quiz.q: Husk is removed in winnowing because it is …
quiz.why: Husk is lighter than grain, so wind blows it away during winnowing while the heavier grains fall down.

scenes.text: Dadi sifts atta through a chalni before making rotis.
Bran and small lumps stay on top.
At a building site, workers sieve sand to remove pebbles.
Same idea, different sizes!

steps.title: Sieving
steps.body: Separating particles of **different sizes** by passing the mixture through a mesh: smaller particles pass, bigger ones stay. Used for flour (bran stays), sand (pebbles stay), tea leaves from tea (a strainer).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
How are pebbles removed from sand for construction?

- Pass it through a large slanting wire **sieve**; fine sand goes through.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Mixture of rice grains and fine flour?

- Sieve with a mesh smaller than rice grains but bigger than flour particles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a sieve when parts are the same size.
- Choosing too large a mesh.

statements.s: Sieving separates by size.
A tea strainer is a sieve.
Sieving can separate salt from water.
Bran stays on the sieve when flour is sifted.

quiz.why: Sieving separates particles of different sizes. Smaller ones pass through the holes, and bigger ones stay on the sieve.

quiz.q: At a construction site, sieving removes …
quiz.why: At a construction site, sieving removes pebbles and stones from sand. The sand passes through and the pebbles stay behind.
A tea strainer holds back the tea leaves while the liquid tea passes through. So it separates leaves from tea.
Bran particles are bigger than the holes in the sieve, so they stay on it. The fine flour passes through.
No. Dissolved sugar is spread through the water in tiny particles that pass through any sieve.

scenes.text: After heavy rain, the village tap gives muddy water.
Ritu lets a bucket stand; mud settles at the bottom.
She gently pours the clear water into another vessel.
Then she filters it through a clean cloth and boils it.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
- **Sedimentation**: heavier insoluble particles settle down when a mixture is left undisturbed; the settled layer is **sediment**.
- **Decantation**: gently pouring off the clearer liquid without disturbing the sediment.
- **Filtration**: passing the liquid through a filter (filter paper, cloth, sand layers) that holds back fine insoluble particles. The clear liquid is the **filtrate**; what stays is the **residue**.

steps.title: Making a filter-paper cone
steps.body: Fold a filter paper in half, then again into a quarter; open one side to make a cone and place it in a funnel. Wet it slightly so it sticks.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Separate sand from water.

- Sedimentation → decantation → filtration of the rest.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How is paneer separated from whey?

- Milk is curdled with lemon juice; the mixture is **filtered** through a muslin cloth — paneer stays (residue), whey passes (filtrate).

steps.title: Safe drinking water
steps.body: Filtration removes visible particles but not all germs. Boil water or use a safe purifier; this is why municipal water is also treated (e.g., chlorine).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stirring during decantation — sediment mixes again.
- Thinking filtration removes dissolved salt — it does not.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to clean muddy water.
items: Decant the upper clear water gently
Filter it through a clean cloth or filter paper

quiz.q: Settled particles at the bottom are …
quiz.why: Particles that settle at the bottom of a liquid are called sediment. The residue is what stays on a filter.

quiz.q: Pouring off liquid without disturbing sediment is …
quiz.why: Gently pouring off the clear liquid without disturbing the settled sediment is decantation.

quiz.q: Liquid that passes through a filter is …
quiz.why: The clear liquid that passes through a filter is the filtrate. What stays on the filter is the residue.
Paneer is separated from the whey by passing the curdled milk through a cloth, which is filtration. The paneer stays on the cloth.
No. Dissolved salt is in tiny particles that pass through the filter with the water. To get the salt we must evaporate the water.

story.title: Salt from the sea, butter from curd

scenes.text: At Rann of Kutch, workers collect white salt from shallow pans.
At a scrapyard, a big crane magnet lifts iron from mixed junk.
At home, Grandma churns curd with a mathani.
Butter floats up — another separation!

steps.title: Evaporation
steps.body: To get a dissolved solid from a liquid, heat or leave it in the sun until the liquid evaporates; the solid remains (salt from sea water).

steps.title: Magnetic separation
steps.body: A magnet pulls out iron or steel pieces (iron filings from sand, iron scrap from waste).

steps.title: Churning
steps.body: Rapid stirring/spinning separates lighter parts from heavier: churning curd/cream gives butter, which floats on buttermilk. (Machines called centrifuges use the same idea.)

steps.title: Example 1 — mixture of salt, sand and iron filings
steps.body:
- Magnet removes **iron filings**
- Add water, stir: salt dissolves
- **Filter**: sand stays as residue
- **Evaporate** filtrate: salt remains

steps.title: Example 2 — mixture of sand and sawdust
steps.body:
- Add water: sawdust floats, sand sinks
- Skim off sawdust; decant/filter sand; dry both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Evaporating before filtering when sand is present — sand stays mixed with salt.
- Using a magnet on aluminium or copper — they aren't attracted.

quiz.q: Salt is obtained from sea water by …
quiz.why: Salt is obtained from sea water by evaporation. The Sun evaporates the water and the salt is left behind.
Butter is separated from cream or curd by churning. The spinning separates the fat from the liquid.

quiz.q: Iron filings from sulphur powder: method?
quiz.why: Iron is magnetic and sulphur is not, so a magnet pulls out the iron filings. The other methods would not separate them.

quiz.q: For salt + sand, after dissolving, next step is …
quiz.why: After dissolving the salt in water, the sand stays undissolved, so filter to remove it. Then evaporate the water to get the salt.
A centrifuge spins fast to separate parts of a mixture, like churning does. Heavier parts go outward and lighter parts stay inside.

questions.q: Removing stones from rice by hand is …
questions.why: Picking out stones from rice by hand is handpicking. It works because the stones are few and easy to see.

questions.q: Husk is separated from grain by …
questions.why: Winnowing uses wind to blow the light husk away from the heavier grain.

questions.q: Butter from curd: method?
questions.why: Butter is separated by churning. Filtration, threshing and sieving do not separate butter.

questions.q: Separation by size uses …
questions.why: A sieve separates particles by size, since small particles pass through its holes. Magnets and evaporation use other properties.

questions.q: Clear liquid after filtration is …
questions.why: The clear liquid that passes through a filter is the filtrate. The solid left on the filter is the residue.

questions.q: Grains from stalks: method?
questions.why: Threshing separates grains from the stalks by beating. Winnowing removes the husk later.

questions.q: Salt from salt water: method?
questions.why: To get salt from salt water, evaporate the water. The salt stays behind, because filtration cannot remove dissolved salt.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Filtration cannot separate salt from water. Reason (R): Dissolved salt passes through filter paper.
questions.why: Both are true: dissolved salt is in tiny particles that pass through the filter paper with the water. So filtration cannot separate salt from water.

questions.q: Case: Muddy water — correct order?
questions.why: First let the mud settle (sedimentation), then pour off the water (decantation), then filter it to remove fine particles. That is the right order.

questions.q: Iron pins mixed with wooden beads: quickest method?
questions.why: Iron pins are magnetic and wooden beads are not, so a magnet picks the pins out quickly.

questions.q: Why is boiling needed after filtering water?
questions.why: Filtering removes particles but not all germs, so boiling is used to kill them. This makes the water safer to drink.

questions.q: Case: Mixture of sand, salt and iron filings. First step?
questions.why: Use a magnet first, while the mixture is dry, to pull out the iron filings. Then add water to dissolve the salt, filter out the sand and evaporate the water.

questions.q: Case: Mixture of sawdust and sand. Best method?
options: Add water: sawdust floats, sand sinks
questions.why: Sawdust floats on water and sand sinks, so adding water separates them. Skim off the sawdust and the sand remains.

questions.q: Paneer from curdled milk is the …
questions.why: When curdled milk is passed through a cloth, the paneer stays on the cloth. What remains on the filter is the residue.

questions.q: Case: 1 L sea water contains about 35 g salt. Salt from 20 L by evaporation?
questions.why: 20 L of sea water has about 20 × 35 g = 700 g of salt. This is 0.7 kg.

questions.q: Which pair of methods is used to get clear water and dry sand from a sand–water mixture?
options: Sedimentation/decantation and then drying the sand
questions.why: Let the sand settle and pour off the clear water (sedimentation and decantation), then dry the sand. Churning, magnets, handpicking and winnowing do not suit this mixture.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Living Creatures: Exploring their Characteristics
courses.summary: How to tell living from non-living: movement, food and growth, breathing (respiration), response to stimuli, excretion, reproduction and life cycles, and the conditions seeds need to germinate.
outcomes: Learners can list and explain the characteristics of living things
Learners can show that plants are living using evidence
Learners can describe what seeds need to germinate using fair tests
Learners can describe a simple life cycle (e.g., frog) and the idea of a life span

scenes.text: Little Mihir says, 'The car moves and drinks petrol — it's alive!'
His sister asks: does it grow? Have babies? Breathe?
A tiny plant does grow, take in air and make seeds.
Movement alone doesn't make something alive.

steps.title: Characteristics of living things
steps.body:
- **Need food** (energy)
- **Grow** (become bigger, change)
- **Respire** (breathe/use air to get energy from food)
- **Respond to stimuli** (changes around them)
- **Excrete** (remove waste)
- **Reproduce** (make young ones like themselves)
- **Move** (animals move from place to place; plants show movement of parts)
- Have a **life span** and **die**

steps.title: Non-living things
steps.body: May show one or two features (a car moves, a cloud grows), but never all together.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Is a seed living?

- A dry seed shows little activity but when it gets water, air and warmth it germinates and grows → it is **living** (resting).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Is fire living?

- It 'grows' and 'uses air', but doesn't reproduce like living things, respond like them or have cells → **non-living**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using movement as the only test.
- Thinking plants are not living because they don't walk.

quiz.q: Which is a feature of all living things?
quiz.why: All living things reproduce, making new living things of their kind. Colour, moving from place to place or wheels are not common to all.
A car moves but does not grow, breathe or reproduce, so it is non-living.
Plants grow, breathe, respond and reproduce, so they are living.

quiz.q: Removing waste from the body is …
quiz.why: Removing waste from the body is excretion. Growth, movement and respiration are other life processes.
A dry seed is alive but resting. When it gets water, air and warmth, it can germinate and grow.

scenes.text: Ananya touches a touch-me-not (Mimosa) plant.
Its leaves fold up instantly!
Her sunflower turns to face the morning Sun.
Plants respond too.

steps.title: Respiration
steps.body: Living things take in air (oxygen) and give out carbon dioxide to release energy from food. Animals breathe through lungs (humans), gills (fish), skin (earthworm); plants exchange gases through tiny pores (stomata) in leaves.

steps.title: Growth
steps.body: A puppy becomes a dog; a seedling becomes a tree. Growth is from inside. (Non-living things like a pile of sand 'grow' only by adding from outside.)

steps.title: Response to stimuli
steps.body: A **stimulus** is a change around a living thing that brings a response: touching a hot plate → we pull the hand back; Mimosa leaves fold on touch; plants bend towards light; cockroaches run when lights come on.

steps.title: Example 1 — lime-water test
steps.body: Blow air through a straw into lime water; it turns milky → exhaled air has **carbon dioxide**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
A potted plant on a windowsill bends towards the window. Why?

- The shoot **responds** to light (grows towards it).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing breathing with respiration: breathing is taking air in and out; respiration releases energy from food in cells.
- Thinking plants don't respire at night — they respire all the time.

activity.prompt: Match the living thing to how it breathes or responds.

quiz.why: Lime water turns milky when carbon dioxide is passed through it. So it is a test for carbon dioxide.
Plants take in and give out gases through tiny pores called stomata, mostly on their leaves.

quiz.q: Pulling your hand from a hot pan is a …
quiz.why: Pulling your hand away from a hot pan is a response to a stimulus. The heat is the stimulus.
Earthworms breathe through their moist skin, since they have no lungs or gills.
Plants respire all the time, day and night, to get energy. They also make food by photosynthesis in light.

scenes.text: Sonal sets up three cups of moong seeds.
Cup A: dry. Cup B: moist cotton. Cup C: seeds under water.
After 3 days only Cup B sprouts.
Seeds need water AND air.

steps.title: Germination
steps.body: When a seed starts growing into a seedling it **germinates**. It needs **water**, **air** and suitable **warmth**. Most seeds do not need light to germinate (but the seedling needs light to make food and stay green).

steps.title: Example 1 — the three cups
steps.body:
- Dry: no water → no germination
- Moist cotton: water + air → **germinates**
- Fully under water: no air → little/no germination

steps.title: Example 2 — warmth
steps.body: Put two moist-cotton cups, one in the fridge and one in the room. Only the room cup sprouts → seeds need **warmth**.

steps.title: Sprouts at home
steps.body: Soaked moong or chana sprouts overnight in a warm kitchen — a nutritious snack.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing more than one condition at a time.
- Concluding 'seeds need light' without testing light separately.

items.text: Moist cotton in a warm room
Moist cotton in a dark warm cupboard

quiz.why: Seeds need water, air and warmth to germinate. Most seeds do not need light or soil to start.

quiz.q: Seeds under water fail because of lack of …
quiz.why: Seeds under water fail to germinate because they cannot get air (oxygen). They need it to respire.

quiz.q: Seeds in a fridge fail because …
quiz.why: Seeds in a fridge are too cold, and germination needs warmth. So they do not sprout.

quiz.q: Do most seeds need light to germinate?
quiz.why: Most seeds do not need light to germinate. They can sprout in the dark soil.
A germinating seed grows into a young plant called a seedling. It later becomes a full plant.

lessons.title: Reproduction, life cycles and life span

scenes.text: In July, Raju sees jelly-like eggs in a pond.
Soon, tiny tadpoles with tails wriggle out.
Weeks later, they grow legs and lose their tails.
They hop out as frogs — a life cycle!

steps.title: Reproduction
steps.body: Living things make more of their own kind: animals give birth or lay eggs; plants grow from seeds, and some from stems, leaves or roots (potato, money plant, rose cuttings).

steps.title: Life cycle of a frog
steps.body: **Egg** → **tadpole** (lives in water, breathes with gills, has a tail) → **froglet/tadpole with legs** → **adult frog** (lungs and skin breathing, lives on land and in water). The change in body form is called **metamorphosis**.

steps.title: Life span
steps.body: Every living thing has a typical life span and then dies: some insects live days, a dog 10–15 years, humans 70+ years, some trees hundreds of years.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Name two ways plants reproduce.

- By **seeds** (mango) and by **parts** like stem cuttings (rose) or tubers (potato).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why do frogs lay eggs in water?

- Eggs and tadpoles need water to survive (tadpoles have gills).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a tadpole is a fish.
- Thinking all animals lay eggs — mammals mostly give birth to young.

quiz.why: A tadpole lives in water and breathes using gills. An adult frog breathes with lungs and skin.

quiz.q: Change of body form in the life cycle is …
quiz.why: A change of body form during the life cycle, like a tadpole becoming a frog, is called metamorphosis.
Potato plants grow from tubers, which are underground parts of the stem. So a new plant can grow without a seed.
Frogs lay their eggs in water, where tadpoles hatch and grow.
Every living thing has a life span, the time it lives. Fuel tanks, wheels and batteries belong to machines.

questions.q: Which is living?
questions.why: A mushroom is a fungus and is alive. A cloud, stone and robot are non-living.

questions.q: Germination needs …
questions.why: Germination needs water, air and warmth. It does not need salt, plastic or only sunlight.

questions.q: A tadpole becomes a …
questions.why: A tadpole grows into a frog through metamorphosis. It does not become a fish, snake or bird.

questions.q: Exhaled air turns lime water milky because it contains …
questions.why: Exhaled air turns lime water milky because it contains carbon dioxide. Oxygen and nitrogen do not do this.

questions.q: Touch-me-not folding its leaves shows …
questions.why: Touch-me-not folds its leaves when touched, which is a response to a stimulus. The touch is the stimulus.

questions.q: Fish breathe through …
questions.why: Fish breathe through gills, which take oxygen dissolved in water. They do not use lungs or stomata.

questions.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of all living things?
questions.why: Having legs is not a feature of all living things, as plants and fish do not have them. Growth, reproduction and respiration are common to all.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A car is non-living though it moves. Reason (R): It does not grow or reproduce.
questions.why: Both are true: a car moves but does not grow or reproduce, so it is non-living. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: Seeds on dry cotton (A), moist cotton (B), under boiled cooled water with oil layer (C). Which germinates?
questions.why: Seeds in moist cotton get water and air, and warmth from the room, so they germinate. Dry cotton has no water, and the oil layer cuts off air.

questions.q: In case above, cup C fails because …
questions.why: In cup C the oil layer on boiled, cooled water blocks air. Boiling also removes dissolved air, so the seeds get no oxygen.

questions.q: Change from tadpole to frog is …
questions.why: The change from a tadpole to a frog involves a big change in body form, which is metamorphosis.

questions.q: Case: A plant in a dark room grows long, thin and yellow towards a crack of light. This shows …
questions.why: A plant growing towards a crack of light shows a response to light. Its growth is directed by the stimulus.

questions.q: Why is a dry seed considered living?
options: It can germinate and grow when conditions are right
questions.why: A dry seed can germinate and grow when it gets the right conditions, so it is alive but resting. Being green, moving or eating are not needed.

questions.q: Plants exchange gases through …
questions.why: Plants exchange gases through tiny pores called stomata, mainly on the leaves. Flowers and fruits do not do this.

questions.q: Case: Moist seeds in a fridge didn't sprout in 4 days; same seeds in a warm room did. The variable tested?
questions.why: The only difference was temperature, as both sets were moist, so the variable tested is warmth. The cold fridge stopped germination.

questions.q: Which correctly lists the frog's life stages?
questions.why: The frog's life cycle is egg, tadpole, froglet (a young frog with legs) and then adult frog. The other orders are wrong.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Nature's Treasures
courses.summary: Natural resources that sustain life — air, water, soil, sunlight, forests, minerals and fossil fuels; renewable (inexhaustible) and non-renewable (exhaustible) resources; and how to use them wisely through conservation and the 3 Rs.
outcomes: Learners can list natural resources and their uses
Learners can state the composition of air and the importance of water and soil
Learners can classify resources as renewable or non-renewable
Learners can suggest practical conservation actions

scenes.text: Teacher lights a candle and covers it with a glass tumbler.
After a short while, the flame goes out.
'What did it use up?' asks Farhan.
Part of the air — oxygen — is needed for burning.

steps.title: What is air?
steps.body: Air is a **mixture** of gases: about **78% nitrogen**, **21% oxygen**, and about 1% other gases (argon, carbon dioxide ≈ 0.04%, others) plus water vapour and dust.

steps.title: Uses
steps.body:
- Oxygen for breathing and burning
- Carbon dioxide for plants to make food
- Moving air (wind) for windmills, drying, sailing, pollination and seed dispersal
- Nitrogen is used by plants via soil bacteria

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why does the covered candle go out?

- It uses up the oxygen inside the glass; without enough oxygen, burning stops.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why is air called a mixture?

- Its gases are not chemically joined; proportions can vary slightly, and parts can be separated.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking air is mostly oxygen — it is mostly nitrogen.
- Thinking air has no weight; it does.

activity.label: Share of a gas in air (%)

bands.text: About 1%: argon, carbon dioxide (~0.04%) and other gases together.
About 21%: oxygen — for breathing and burning.
Not a single gas sits here — check again!
About 78%: nitrogen — the largest part of air.

quiz.why: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of air, the largest part. Oxygen is about 21%.
Oxygen makes up about 21% of air. Nitrogen is about 78%.

quiz.q: Plants need … from air to make food
quiz.why: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air and use it with water and sunlight to make food, in photosynthesis.

quiz.q: A covered candle goes out because …
quiz.why: A candle needs oxygen to burn. In a covered jar the oxygen gets used up, so the flame goes out.
Windmills use the energy of moving air (wind) to turn their blades. They do not need fire or still water.

scenes.text: Every village in Rajasthan Nani visited once had a pond (johad) to catch rain.
Farmers depend on soil, water and sunshine for crops.
Solar panels now light the school.
These three treasures make life possible.

steps.title: Water
steps.body: Covers about 70% of Earth's surface, but most is salty sea water; only a small fraction is fresh water available to use. Needed for drinking, farming, industry, and all life. Saving it: fix leaks, harvest rainwater, reuse water for plants.

steps.title: Soil
steps.body: Top layer of Earth formed over thousands of years from rocks broken by weather, mixed with **humus** (decayed plant/animal matter). Supports plant growth; home to earthworms, microbes. Soil erosion is reduced by trees and grass.

steps.title: Sunlight
steps.body: Main source of energy for Earth: plants use it to make food; it drives the water cycle and winds; solar cookers and panels use it.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why is rainwater harvesting useful?

- It stores rain to recharge groundwater and supply water in dry months.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How do tree roots prevent soil erosion?

- Roots bind soil so wind and water carry less of it away.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking fresh water is unlimited because the Earth has lots of water.
- Burning crop stubble harms soil organisms and air.

activity.prompt: Match the resource to a way to conserve it.
pairs: Using paper wisely and planting saplings

quiz.why: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans, which is salty. Only a small part is fresh water.
Humus is the dark, rich material made from decayed plants and animals. It makes soil fertile.

quiz.q: Main source of energy for Earth?
quiz.why: The Sun is the main source of energy for Earth. It gives light and heat that support life.
Plant roots hold the soil together, which helps prevent soil erosion by wind and water.
A johad is a traditional pond that collects rainwater, as in Rajasthan. It helps recharge groundwater.

scenes.text: Ankit's uncle works in a coal mine in Jharkhand.
'Coal formed from plants buried millions of years ago,' he explains.
Petrol and natural gas also come from deep underground.
'Once used up, they are gone for a very long time.'

steps.title: Forests
steps.body: Give wood, fruits, medicines, gum, honey; homes for animals; clean air; rain and soil protection. Cutting forests (deforestation) harms all these.

steps.title: Minerals
steps.body: Iron ore, bauxite (aluminium), copper, mica, limestone are dug from the Earth by mining — used for tools, buildings, vehicles, electronics.

steps.title: Fossil fuels
steps.body: **Coal**, **petroleum** and **natural gas** formed from remains of ancient plants and animals buried under the Earth over millions of years. Burning them gives energy but releases smoke and carbon dioxide, polluting air and warming the climate.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why are fossil fuels called non-renewable?

- They take millions of years to form; we are using them far faster.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Give two cleaner alternatives to petrol and coal.

- **Solar** and **wind** energy (also hydro, biogas, electric vehicles charged from clean power).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking coal is a rock that will always be there.
- Forgetting that mining also changes land and forests.

quiz.why: Fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient plants and animals buried underground.
Bauxite is the ore from which aluminium is obtained. Copper and iron come from other ores.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and smoke, which pollute the air and add to global warming.
Forests give us wood, medicines, fruits and many other products. They do not give coal directly or petrol.
Solar energy comes from the Sun and does not run out or give much pollution. Diesel, kerosene and petrol are fossil fuels.

scenes.text: Class 6C starts a 3R challenge for a month.
They carry cloth bags (Reduce), turn bottles into planters (Reuse), and sort waste (Recycle).
School waste drops by a third.
They win the eco-club trophy.

steps.title: Two kinds
steps.body:
- **Renewable / inexhaustible**: naturally replenished or practically unlimited — sunlight, wind, (also water and forests if used wisely)
- **Non-renewable / exhaustible**: limited, take very long to form — coal, petroleum, natural gas, minerals

steps.title: Conservation
steps.body:
- **Reduce** use (switch off lights and fans, use buses/cycles)
- **Reuse** things (jars, bags, notebooks' blank pages)
- **Recycle** paper, glass, metal, some plastics
- Plant trees, harvest rain, avoid wasting food and water

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Classify forests.

- Renewable **if** regrown and used carefully; cutting faster than they grow makes them run out.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
A tap leaks 1 drop per second (~0.05 mL). About how much water per day?

- 86,400 s × 0.05 mL ≈ 4,320 mL ≈ **4.3 litres**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'renewable' means we can waste it.
- Thinking recycling alone solves everything — reducing comes first.

quiz.why: Sunlight is inexhaustible, as the Sun keeps shining for billions of years. Coal, petrol and natural gas can run out.
Reduce comes first, because using less avoids making waste in the first place. Reuse and recycle come after.

quiz.q: Turning a bottle into a planter is …
quiz.why: Using a bottle again as a planter, without breaking it down, is reuse. Recycling would melt or process it into new material.
Coal took millions of years to form and cannot be replaced quickly once used. So it is non-renewable.
Forests are renewable only if trees are regrown and used wisely, so they are not used faster than they regrow. Cutting quickly or burning ends this.

questions.q: Air is a …
questions.why: Air is a mixture of gases such as nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide. It is not a single gas.

questions.q: Which is a fossil fuel?
questions.why: Coal is a fossil fuel formed from ancient plants over millions of years. Sunlight, water and wind are not fossil fuels.

questions.q: Which is inexhaustible?
questions.why: Sunlight is inexhaustible because the Sun keeps giving energy. Coal, petroleum and iron ore can run out.

questions.q: Percentage of nitrogen in air?
questions.why: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of air. Oxygen is about 21%.

questions.q: Humus makes soil …
questions.why: Humus is made from decayed plants and animals and is rich in nutrients. So it makes soil fertile.

questions.q: Bauxite is an ore of …
questions.why: Bauxite is the ore from which aluminium is obtained. Zinc, iron and copper come from other ores.

questions.q: Reusing a jam jar to store spices is …
questions.why: Using a jam jar again for storing spices, without changing it, is reuse. Recycling means processing it into new material.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Fossil fuels are non-renewable. Reason (R): They take millions of years to form.
questions.why: Both are true: fossil fuels take millions of years to form, so we use them far faster than they form. That is why they are non-renewable.

questions.q: Case: A candle under a large jar burns longer than under a small jar. Why?
options: More air (oxygen) in the large jar
questions.why: A larger jar holds more air, and so more oxygen. So the candle can keep burning longer before the oxygen is used up.

questions.q: Which helps groundwater most?
questions.why: Rainwater harvesting collects rain and lets it soak into the ground, which recharges groundwater. Paving the ground or cutting trees reduces that.

questions.q: Why is fresh water precious though Earth has lots of water?
options: Most water is salty or frozen
questions.why: Most of Earth's water is salty sea water or frozen in ice, so only a small share is fresh water we can use. That is why fresh water is precious.

questions.q: Case: A school replaces 20 bulbs of 60 W with 9 W LEDs, used 5 h a day. Power saved at any time when all are on?
questions.why: Each bulb saves 60 − 9 = 51 W. For 20 bulbs, the saving is 20 × 51 = 1,020 W.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide is about … of air
questions.why: Carbon dioxide is a very small part of air, about 0.04%. Nitrogen is 78% and oxygen 21%.

questions.q: Which is the best order of preference?
questions.why: The 3 Rs are in order of preference: Reduce first, then Reuse, then Recycle. Reducing avoids waste altogether.

questions.q: Case: A tap leaks 10 mL per minute. Water lost in a day?
questions.why: A day has 24 × 60 = 1440 minutes. 1440 × 10 mL = 14,400 mL, which is 14.4 L.

questions.q: Forests are renewable resources only when …
options: trees are replanted and harvested slower than they grow
questions.why: Forests are renewable only when trees are replanted and cut more slowly than they grow. Clearing or burning them faster destroys that.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Beyond Earth
courses.summary: The night sky: stars and constellations (Saptarishi/Ursa Major, Orion, the Pole Star), nakshatras, the Sun and our Solar System's eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets, artificial satellites and India's space missions, and dark skies vs light pollution.
outcomes: Learners can identify common constellations and find the Pole Star
Learners can list the eight planets in order and key facts about them
Learners can distinguish stars, planets, moons, asteroids, comets and satellites
Learners can describe India's space missions and the problem of light pollution

scenes.text: During a power cut, Aarohi's family lies on the terrace.
Without city lights, thousands of stars appear.
Grandpa points out seven bright stars shaped like a ladle — the Saptarishi.
He follows two of them to find the Pole Star.

steps.title: Stars
steps.body: Stars are huge, very hot balls of glowing gas that make their own light. They look tiny because they are extremely far away. The **Sun** is a star — the nearest one to us. Stars seem to twinkle because their light passes through moving layers of air.

steps.title: Constellations
steps.body:
Groups of stars that seem to form patterns are **constellations**. Examples:

- **Saptarishi** (Big Dipper, part of Ursa Major): seven bright stars like a ladle; the two 'pointer' stars point towards the **Pole Star (Dhruva Tara)**.
- **Orion** (Mriga): a hunter with three stars in a row forming his belt; seen well in winter evenings.

The Pole Star stays almost fixed above the northern horizon — useful for finding north at night.

steps.title: Nakshatras
steps.body: Ancient Indian astronomers divided the Moon's path across the sky into **27 nakshatras** (star groups), used in calendars.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
How can you find north at night?

- Locate the Saptarishi; extend the line through the two end 'pointer' stars about five times their gap → Pole Star → its direction is **north**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why can't we see stars in the day?

- They are there, but sunlight scattered by air makes the sky too bright.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling planets 'stars' — planets don't make their own light.
- Thinking stars in a constellation are close together — they may be at very different distances.

statements.s: The Sun is a star.
Stars disappear during the day.
The Pole Star is useful to find north.
Stars in a constellation are always close to each other.
statements.why: They only look close from Earth.

quiz.why: The Sun is a star, and it is the nearest star to Earth. Other stars are very far away.
The Saptarishi (Big Dipper) has 7 bright stars. 'Sapta' means seven.

quiz.q: Pointer stars of Saptarishi point to …
quiz.why: The two pointer stars of Saptarishi point to the Pole Star (Dhruva Tara). This helps us find north.

quiz.q: Orion's belt has … stars in a row
quiz.why: Orion's belt is a row of 3 bright stars in the middle of the Orion constellation.
In Indian astronomy there are 27 nakshatras, which are star groups along the Moon's path.

lessons.title: The Sun and the Solar System

story.title: A model in the school ground

scenes.text: Class 6 places a football for the Sun at one end of the ground.
Tiny peppercorns for Earth are many steps away.
Jupiter is a big marble, much farther.
Space is mostly empty — and huge!

steps.title: The Solar System
steps.body: The **Sun** and everything that goes around it: **8 planets**, their moons, **dwarf planets** (like Pluto), **asteroids**, **comets** and dust. The Sun's pull (gravity) keeps them in orbit.

steps.title: The eight planets (from the Sun)
steps.body:
- **Mercury**: smallest, closest to Sun
- **Venus**: hottest planet, brightest in our sky (morning/evening 'star')
- **Earth**: only known planet with life; liquid water
- **Mars**: red planet
- **Jupiter**: largest planet, gas giant
- **Saturn**: beautiful rings (others have faint rings too)
- **Uranus**: spins on its side
- **Neptune**: farthest, very cold, windy

Memory trick: *My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos*.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which planets are rocky and which are giants?

- Rocky (inner): Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars
- Giants (outer): Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why is Pluto not called a planet now?

- In 2006, astronomers classed it as a **dwarf planet** because it hasn't cleared other bodies from its orbit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Mercury is the hottest — Venus is hotter because its thick air traps heat.
- Calling the Sun a planet.

activity.prompt: Order the planets from the Sun.

quiz.why: Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system. Saturn is second, and Earth is much smaller.
Venus is the hottest planet, because its thick atmosphere traps heat. Mercury is closer to the Sun but cooler.
Mars is called the Red Planet because of its reddish, iron-rich soil.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006. It is not a moon or a star.
Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun. Pluto is now a dwarf planet.

scenes.text: Kabir asks, 'Is the Moon a planet?'
Teacher: 'It goes around Earth, so it is a natural satellite.'
'And the satellites that give us TV and weather?'
'Those are artificial satellites — made by people.'

steps.title: Moons
steps.body: A **natural satellite** orbits a planet. Earth has one Moon; it reflects sunlight and shows phases. Mercury and Venus have none; Jupiter and Saturn have many.

steps.title: Asteroids and comets
steps.body:
- **Asteroids**: rocky pieces orbiting the Sun, mostly in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.
- **Comets**: lumps of ice and dust; when near the Sun they glow and show a long tail pointing away from the Sun (e.g., Halley's comet, seen about every 76 years).

steps.title: Artificial satellites
steps.body: Made by humans for communication (TV, phone), weather forecasting, navigation (India's NavIC), mapping and research. India's first satellite was **Aryabhata** (1975).

steps.title: India in space
steps.body: ISRO missions: **Chandrayaan-1** (2008) helped find signs of water on the Moon; **Mangalyaan** (Mars Orbiter Mission, 2013–14) reached Mars orbit on the first attempt; **Chandrayaan-3** soft-landed near the Moon's south pole (23 August 2023); **Aditya-L1** (2023) studies the Sun.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why does the Moon shine?

- It **reflects** sunlight; it has no light of its own.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a 'shooting star' a star — it is a small rock burning up in our air (a meteor).
- Thinking satellites stay still — they orbit continuously.

pairs: Rocky body, many between Mars and Jupiter
Icy body with a glowing tail near the Sun

quiz.why: The Moon has no light of its own. It shines because it reflects sunlight.
The asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, and it has many rocky bodies.
India's first satellite was Aryabhata, launched in 1975. Chandrayaan and Mangalyaan are later missions.
Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon on 23 August 2023, near the south pole.
A comet's tail always points away from the Sun, pushed by the solar wind and sunlight. This is true whichever way the comet moves.

scenes.text: In Mumbai, Zara can see only a few stars.
On a trip to Hanle in Ladakh, she sees the Milky Way!
Hanle has a Dark Sky Reserve that limits bright lights.
Zara wants her city to protect the night too.

steps.title: Light pollution
steps.body: Too much artificial light at night (bright streetlights, hoardings, lights pointing upward) brightens the sky and hides stars. It also disturbs birds, insects, sea turtles and our own sleep, and wastes electricity.

steps.title: Dark sky efforts
steps.body: India's first **Dark Sky Reserve** is at **Hanle, Ladakh** (2022), near an astronomical observatory. Shielded lights that point down, warm colours and switching off unneeded lights help.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Suggest two ways a housing society can reduce light pollution.

- Use shielded downward lamps; switch off decorative lights after a set time.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why do astronomers build observatories on high mountains?

- Less city light, thinner and drier air → clearer view.

steps.title: Stargazing tips
steps.body: Go to a dark place, wait 15–20 minutes for eyes to adjust, use a red torch, and a sky-map app or chart.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking light pollution only matters to astronomers — it affects wildlife and health too.

items: Find a dark spot away from bright lights (with an adult)
Let my eyes adjust for 15 minutes
Use the pointer stars to find the Pole Star
Look for Orion's belt (winter) or a bright planet

quiz.why: Light pollution is caused by too much artificial light at night. It makes the night sky bright and hides stars.
Hanle, in Ladakh, became India's first Dark Sky Reserve. Its dry, clear skies and little light make it good for stargazing.

quiz.q: Observatories are built on mountains because …
quiz.why: Observatories are on mountains for less light from towns and clearer, thinner air. This gives better views of the sky.

quiz.q: A way to reduce light pollution?
quiz.why: Shielded lamps that point their light down cut light that goes up into the sky. This reduces light pollution.
Light pollution also affects birds and insects, which can be confused by bright lights at night. It is not only a problem for telescopes.

questions.q: A star …
questions.why: A star makes its own light, like the Sun. Planets and moons only reflect light.

questions.q: Planet closest to the Sun?
questions.why: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun. Venus is next, then Earth and Mars.

questions.q: Largest planet?
questions.why: Jupiter is the largest planet. Saturn comes second.

questions.q: Earth's natural satellite?
questions.why: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite, as it circles Earth. Aryabhata is an artificial satellite.

questions.q: Pole Star is in the direction of …
questions.why: The Pole Star lies almost exactly above the North Pole, so it shows the direction north.

questions.q: Saturn is famous for its …
questions.why: Saturn is famous for its bright rings. Mars is red, and Venus is the hottest planet.

questions.q: Asteroids mostly lie between …
questions.why: Most asteroids lie in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Venus is hotter than Mercury. Reason (R): Venus's thick atmosphere traps heat.
questions.why: Both are true: Venus has a thick atmosphere that traps heat, making it hotter than Mercury though it is farther from the Sun. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is a dwarf planet?
questions.why: Pluto is a dwarf planet. Neptune, Mars and Venus are planets.

questions.q: Case: Riya sees a bright streak that lasts a second. It is a …
questions.why: A bright streak lasting a second or so is a meteor, or shooting star, a small rock burning in the atmosphere. A comet looks like a slow fuzzy patch.

questions.q: India's Mars Orbiter Mission is called …
questions.why: India's Mars Orbiter Mission is called Mangalyaan. Chandrayaan-3 went to the Moon and Aditya-L1 to the Sun.

questions.q: Which mission studies the Sun?
questions.why: Aditya-L1 is India's mission to study the Sun. Mangalyaan went to Mars and Chandrayaan-2 to the Moon.

questions.q: Case: City lights are replaced by shielded downward lamps. Main benefit for the night sky?
questions.why: Shielded downward lamps send less light up, so the sky is darker. So more stars become visible.

questions.q: Which group lists only rocky planets?
questions.why: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the four rocky inner planets. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are giant planets.

questions.q: Halley's comet is seen about every …
questions.why: Halley's comet returns about every 76 years. It is a periodic comet.

questions.q: Case: You find the two pointer stars 5° apart. About how far beyond them is the Pole Star?
questions.why: The Pole Star is roughly five times the gap between the pointer stars, so about 5 × 5° = 25° beyond them.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 6 Science
courses.summary: One-stop revision of all 12 Curiosity chapters: key-fact sheets, a table of tests and methods, exam tips, and two mock papers.
outcomes: Learners can recall key facts and definitions from every chapter
Learners can choose the right method, test or instrument for a situation
Learners can answer case-based and assertion–reason questions
Learners can self-assess with two mock papers

lessons.title: Fact sheet: living world and health (Ch 1, 2, 3, 10)

scenes.text: Leela writes one fact per card.
Her brother quizzes her until she gets every card right twice.
Wrong cards go back in the pile.
By bedtime the pile is empty.

steps.title: Science method (Ch 1)
steps.body: Observe → question → hypothesis → fair test (change one thing) → analyse → conclude → share.

steps.title: Diversity (Ch 2)
steps.body:
- Herbs, shrubs, trees, climbers, creepers
- Reticulate venation ↔ taproot ↔ dicot (2 cotyledons); parallel venation ↔ fibrous roots ↔ monocot (1 cotyledon)
- Adaptations: camel (long legs, padded feet), cactus (spines, fleshy stem), fish (gills, streamlined), pine (cone shape)

steps.title: Mindful eating (Ch 3)
steps.body:
- Nutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water
- Tests: iodine → blue-black (starch); CuSO₄ + NaOH → violet (protein); oily patch (fat)
- Vit A night blindness · B1 beriberi · C scurvy · D rickets · iron anaemia · iodine goitre
- 2023 International Year of Millets

steps.title: Living things (Ch 10)
steps.body:
- Food, growth, respiration, response, excretion, reproduction, life span
- Germination needs water, air, warmth
- Frog: egg → tadpole → froglet → frog (metamorphosis)

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body:
A plant has net veins. Predict roots and seed type.

- Taproot; dicot.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Breathing ≠ respiration
- Not all big plants are trees (banana is a herb)

quiz.why: The protein test gives a violet colour. Blue-black is the starch test.
The spines of a cactus are modified leaves. They reduce water loss in the desert.
Lack of iodine causes goitre, a swelling in the neck. Rickets, scurvy and anaemia have other causes.
Wheat is a monocot, with one seed leaf, parallel leaf veins and fibrous roots.
A hypothesis is a testable guess, which we check by experiment. It is not yet a conclusion or a law.

lessons.title: Fact sheet: matter, measurement and space (Ch 4–9, 11, 12)

scenes.text: Sanjay draws a giant mind-map on chart paper.
Magnets, measuring, materials, temperature, water, separation, resources, space.
He pins it above his desk.
A glance a day keeps forgetting away.

steps.title: Magnets (Ch 4)
steps.body: Magnetic: iron, nickel, cobalt, steel · two poles always · like repel, unlike attract · repulsion = sure test · compass needle points N–S

steps.title: Measurement & motion (Ch 5)
steps.body: SI unit metre; 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm · eye directly above mark · thread for curves · linear, circular, oscillatory; periodic repeats in equal time

steps.title: Materials (Ch 6) & temperature (Ch 7)
steps.body: Lustre, hardness, solubility, float/sink, transparent/translucent/opaque · clinical 35–42 °C, lab −10–110 °C; normal body ≈ 37 °C; water freezes 0 °C, boils 100 °C

steps.title: Water (Ch 8) & separation (Ch 9)
steps.body: Melting, freezing, evaporation (faster with heat, area, wind; slower with humidity), condensation · cooling by evaporation · water cycle · handpicking, threshing, winnowing, sieving, sedimentation, decantation, filtration, evaporation, magnet, churning

steps.title: Resources (Ch 11) & space (Ch 12)
steps.body: Air: 78% N₂, 21% O₂ · renewable vs non-renewable; fossil fuels: coal, petroleum, natural gas · Reduce–Reuse–Recycle · 8 planets MVEMJSUN · Saptarishi → Pole Star · Aryabhata 1975, Chandrayaan-3 2023

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body:
Separate salt, sand and iron filings.

- Magnet → dissolve → filter → evaporate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Clinical thermometer for boiling water ✗
- Filtration does not remove dissolved salt

activity.prompt: Match the instrument/method to the job.

quiz.why: A lab thermometer reads about −10 °C to 110 °C. A clinical thermometer is only 35–42 °C.
Frosted glass lets light through but gives no clear view, so it is translucent. Clear glass is transparent.
Clouds form when water vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets. This is condensation.
Oxygen is about 21% of air. Nitrogen is 78%.
Saturn is the planet with prominent rings. Venus, Mars and Mercury have no bright rings.

- Use correct terms (evaporation, not 'drying up')
- Name the method and the reason ("winnowing, because husk is lighter")
- For experiments: what you change, what you keep same, what you observe

steps.title: Q1. Why is a fair test important?

steps.body: 6 poles — each piece has N and S.

steps.title: Q3. Describe the frog life cycle.
steps.body: Egg → tadpole (gills, tail) → froglet (legs) → adult frog.

steps.title: Q4. Why does a matka cool water?

quiz.q: Mock: Best way to separate paneer from whey?
quiz.why: Paneer is separated from the whey by filtration through a cloth, which holds back the solid paneer. A magnet or winnowing would not work.

quiz.q: Mock: Which is periodic but not oscillatory?
quiz.why: Earth around the Sun repeats after a year, so it is periodic, but its path is a circle (orbit). A pendulum, guitar string and swing move to and fro, which is oscillatory.
Iodine solution is the reagent for testing starch, as it turns blue-black. Lime water tests for carbon dioxide.
Like poles repel each other, while unlike poles attract.
37 °C is about 98.6 °F, using °F = °C × 9/5 + 32. This is normal body temperature.
Venus is the hottest planet, as its thick atmosphere traps heat. Mercury is closer to the Sun but cooler.

scenes.text: Imran reviews his mock 1 mistakes.
He practises separation and magnets again.
He attempts mock 2 with a timer.
He scores much higher.

steps.title: Q1. Case: Seeds in three cups (dry, moist, under water). Which sprout and why?
steps.body: Only moist — it has water and air; dry has no water, under water lacks air.

steps.title: Q2. Name the nutrient and a source: (a) energy (b) body-building (c) prevents scurvy
steps.body: (a) carbohydrate — rice (b) protein — dal (c) vitamin C — amla

steps.title: Q3. Why do clothes dry faster on a windy day?
steps.body: Wind removes the vapour above the clothes, so more water evaporates.

steps.title: Q4. Classify as renewable or not: coal, wind, sunlight, natural gas
steps.body: Renewable: wind, sunlight; non-renewable: coal, natural gas.

steps.title: Q5. How to find north at night?
steps.body: Use Saptarishi's pointer stars to locate the Pole Star.

steps.title:
- Writing 'sieving' for husk (it's winnowing)
- Mixing transparent/translucent
- Forgetting the unit in conversions
steps.body: Frequent slips

activity.prompt: Write the three facts you keep forgetting and a trick to remember each.
activity.hint: E.g., 'My Very Educated Mother…' for planets.

quiz.why: Pebbles are bigger than sand grains, so a sieve separates them by size. Evaporation and churning do not apply.

options: a change that brings a response
quiz.why: A stimulus is a change in the surroundings that brings a response from a living thing, like heat making us pull our hand away.
Aluminium is not magnetic. Nickel, cobalt and iron are magnetic materials.

quiz.q: Mock: Fresh water is a small share because …
options: most water is salty or frozen
quiz.why: Most of Earth's water is salty or frozen, so only a small share is fresh water. Oceans are salty, not fresh.
India's first satellite was Aryabhata, launched in 1975. INSAT, Chandrayaan-1 and Aditya-L1 came later.
Wood does not let light pass, so it is opaque. Water, clear glass and air are transparent.

questions.q: SI unit of length?
questions.why: The SI unit of length is the metre. Kilometre and centimetre are derived units, and inch is not SI.

questions.q: Which is a shrub?
questions.why: A rose is a shrub, with several woody stems near the base. Neem is a tree, a pumpkin a creeper and grass a herb.

questions.q: Starch + iodine gives …
questions.why: Starch turns blue-black with iodine. Violet is the colour for protein.

questions.q: Which is magnetic?
questions.why: Iron is magnetic. Plastic, glass and copper are not attracted by a magnet.

questions.q: Water vapour → water is …
questions.why: Water vapour turning into liquid water is condensation. Evaporation is the opposite.

questions.q: Clinical thermometer range?
questions.why: A clinical thermometer reads about 35–42 °C, the range of body temperature.

questions.q: Nitrogen in air ≈ …
questions.why: Nitrogen is about 78% of air. Oxygen is 21%.

questions.q: Fourth planet from the Sun?
questions.why: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, after Mercury, Venus and Earth.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Monocots have fibrous roots. Reason (R): Monocot seeds have one cotyledon.
options: Both true; R is a related feature, not the cause
questions.why: Both are true: monocots have fibrous roots and seeds with one seed leaf. They are linked features that usually occur together, but one does not cause the other.

questions.q: Why does iron lose lustre over time?
options: It reacts with air and moisture (rust)
questions.why: Iron reacts with air and moisture to form rust, which dulls its shine. It does not melt or dissolve.

questions.q: Case: Mixture of chalk powder and water. Best method?
questions.why: Chalk powder does not dissolve in water, so it settles (sedimentation) and can be filtered out. A magnet, winnowing and threshing do not suit this.

questions.q: A swing is an example of …
questions.why: A swing moves to and fro about a point, which is oscillatory motion.

questions.q: Case: Child has bleeding gums and tires easily. Which food helps most?
questions.why: Bleeding gums can be a sign of lack of vitamin C, and amla and guava are rich in it. A doctor should check any health problem.

questions.q: Case: Ends of a rod at 3.5 cm and 15.1 cm on a scale. Length?
questions.why: The length is the difference between the two readings: 15.1 − 3.5 = 11.6 cm.

questions.q: Case: Rod P attracts both ends of a compass needle. P is most likely …
questions.why: A rod that attracts both ends of a compass needle is likely an unmagnetised piece of iron. A magnet would repel one end of the needle.

questions.q: Case: A tank loses water faster on a sunny, windy day than on a cloudy, still day. Which factors?
questions.why: Sun and wind make water evaporate faster, so the factors are temperature and wind. Humidity matters too, but magnetism and tank colour do not.

questions.q: Fossil fuels are exhaustible because …
options: they form over millions of years
questions.why: Fossil fuels take millions of years to form, so once used they are not replaced in a human lifetime. That is why they are exhaustible.

questions.q: Case: 3 L sea water at 35 g salt per litre is evaporated. Salt obtained?
questions.why: 3 L of sea water has about 3 × 35 g = 105 g of salt. Evaporating the water leaves this salt.

questions.q: Case: Mixture of sand, salt and sawdust. Best order?
options: Add water, skim sawdust, filter sand, evaporate filtrate
questions.why: Add water so the sawdust floats and can be skimmed off, filter out the sand, then evaporate the filtrate to get the salt. Evaporating first would not separate them.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
questions.why: The Moon has no light of its own and reflects sunlight. Planets do not make their own light, Pluto is a dwarf planet and stars are very far away.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Locating Places on the Earth
courses.summary: Maps and their components (distance/scale, direction, symbols), types of maps, the globe, latitudes and longitudes, the Equator, Tropics and Prime Meridian, finding places with coordinates, and time zones and Indian Standard Time — including Ujjain's place in ancient Indian astronomy.
outcomes: Learners can read a map using scale, directions and symbols
Learners can explain latitudes, longitudes and the major lines
Learners can locate places using coordinates
Learners can calculate time differences using longitudes and explain IST

scenes.text: Ananya draws a map to the picnic spot for her friends.
She adds an arrow for north, symbols for a temple, pond and school.
She writes '1 cm = 100 m' so they know distances.
Everyone reaches on time!

steps.title: What is a map?
steps.body: A **map** is a drawing of the whole or part of the Earth's surface on a flat sheet, drawn to scale. A **sketch** is drawn without exact scale (from memory); a **plan** shows a small area (a house) at a large scale.

steps.title: Three components
steps.body:
- **Distance (scale)**: ratio between map distance and real distance (1 cm = 1 km)
- **Direction**: four cardinal directions N, S, E, W; intermediate NE, SE, SW, NW; maps usually have an arrow pointing north
- **Symbols**: agreed signs and colours (blue = water, green = plains/forests, brown = mountains, black dots = settlements) explained in the **legend/key**

steps.title: Types of maps
steps.body:
- **Physical**: natural features — mountains, rivers, plains
- **Political**: countries, states, cities, boundaries
- **Thematic**: one theme — rainfall, roads, crops, population

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Scale 1 cm = 5 km. Two towns are 7.5 cm apart. Real distance?

- 7.5 × 5 = **37.5 km**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Which map shows Odisha's rice-growing areas?

- A **thematic** map (crops).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading map distances without the scale.
- Assuming the top of every map is north — check the arrow.

activity.prompt: Match the colour or symbol on a physical map.

quiz.q: A map drawn without exact scale is a …
quiz.why: A sketch is a rough drawing of an area that is not drawn to scale. A plan or map is drawn to scale.
A political map shows state and country boundaries. A physical map shows landforms.
With 1 cm = 2 km, 4 cm stand for 4 × 2 = 8 km.
North-East lies between North and East. It is an intermediate direction.
A legend (key) explains the symbols and colours used on the map. It is not the scale or title.

lessons.title: The globe and the lines of latitude

scenes.text: Teacher spins a globe on its tilted axis.
A red line runs around its middle — the Equator.
Dotted lines above and below are the Tropics.
Sanjay finds India just north of the Equator, crossed by the Tropic of Cancer.

steps.title: The globe
steps.body: A **globe** is a small model of the Earth. It shows shapes and sizes correctly but can't show much detail. The Earth spins on its **axis**, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles; the axis is tilted.

steps.title: Latitudes (parallels)
steps.body:
Imaginary circles running east–west, parallel to the **Equator (0°)**, which divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres. They get smaller towards the poles (90° N and 90° S are points).

- **Tropic of Cancer** 23½° N (passes through India)
- **Tropic of Capricorn** 23½° S
- **Arctic Circle** 66½° N, **Antarctic Circle** 66½° S

steps.title: Heat zones
steps.body:
- **Torrid zone**: between the Tropics — hottest, Sun overhead at some time of year
- **Temperate zones**: between the Tropics and the polar circles
- **Frigid zones**: beyond the polar circles — very cold

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which hemisphere is India in?

- About 8° N to 37° N → **Northern Hemisphere**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why is the Torrid zone hottest?

- The Sun's rays fall nearly vertically there, concentrating heat.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling latitudes 'vertical lines'. They run east–west.
- Thinking the Equator passes through India — it passes south of India.

statements.s: The Equator is 0° latitude.
The Tropic of Cancer passes through India.
Latitude circles are all the same size.
The Arctic Circle is 66½° S.

quiz.why: The Equator is the 0° line of latitude that divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
The Tropic of Capricorn is at 23½° South. The Tropic of Cancer is at 23½° North.
