The Torrid Zone, between the two tropics, gets the most direct sunlight, so it is the hottest heat zone.
90° N is the North Pole, the northernmost point on Earth.
Latitudes are circles that run east–west around the globe, parallel to the Equator.

scenes.text: A coast guard radio crackles: 'Ship at 15° N, 73° E!'
Officer Meera traces the latitude and longitude on her chart.
They cross near the coast of Goa.
Help reaches quickly because of coordinates.

steps.title: Longitudes (meridians)
steps.body: Imaginary half-circles running from the North Pole to the South Pole. All are equal in length. The **Prime Meridian (0°)** passes through **Greenwich** (London). Longitudes go 180° east and 180° west; 0° and 180° divide Earth into **Eastern** and **Western Hemispheres**.

steps.title: Coordinates
steps.body: Every place has a latitude and a longitude: e.g., New Delhi ≈ 28.6° N, 77.2° E. The point where they cross is the location — like a grid.

steps.title: Ujjain — an ancient prime meridian
steps.body: Centuries before Greenwich, Indian astronomers used a meridian through **Ujjain** as a reference line for calculations of time and planets' positions (it appears in texts like the *Surya Siddhanta*).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
A place is at 0° latitude, 0° longitude. Where is it?

- In the Atlantic Ocean, off West Africa (Gulf of Guinea).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
India lies roughly between 68° E and 97° E. Which hemisphere(s)?

- **Northern and Eastern** hemispheres.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up latitude (first, N/S) and longitude (second, E/W).
- Saying longitudes are parallel circles — they meet at the poles.

quiz.why: The Prime Meridian (0° longitude) passes through Greenwich in London. Ujjain was an ancient Indian reference.
Longitudes are lines from the North Pole to the South Pole, so they meet at the poles.

quiz.q: Coordinates of New Delhi are about …
quiz.why: New Delhi is at about 28.6° N and 77.2° E. North of the Equator and east of Greenwich fits India.
Ujjain was used in ancient Indian astronomy as a reference meridian.
All longitudes are half-circles of the same length, running from pole to pole.

lessons.title: Time zones and Indian Standard Time

scenes.text: India plays in Australia; the match starts at 9:30 am local time there.
In India, Rohan wakes at 4:00 am to watch!
Different places have different local times.
Longitudes explain why.

steps.title: Earth's rotation and time
steps.body: Earth turns 360° in 24 hours → **15° in 1 hour** → **1° in 4 minutes**. Places to the **east** see the Sun earlier, so their time is **ahead**.

steps.title: Standard time
steps.body: Each country chooses a standard meridian so the whole country uses one time. **Indian Standard Time (IST)** uses **82½° E** (passing near Mirzapur, Uttar Pradesh). IST = Greenwich time + **5 hours 30 minutes** (82.5 × 4 min = 330 min).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
It's 12 noon at Greenwich. Time at 60° E?

- 60 × 4 = 240 min = 4 h ahead → **4:00 pm**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
It's 10:00 am IST. Time at Greenwich?

- 10:00 − 5:30 = **4:30 am**

steps.title: Example 3
steps.body:
Two places differ by 30° of longitude. Time difference?

- 30 × 4 = 120 min = **2 hours**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting time for places to the east (east = ahead, add).
- Forgetting the extra 30 minutes in IST.

activity.prompt: It is 8:00 am at Greenwich. What is the hour in India (IST)? Enter as a decimal of hours, e.g. 1:30 pm = 13.5

quiz.why: Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so it turns 360 ÷ 24 = 15° each hour.
Indian Standard Time uses the 82½° E meridian.

quiz.q: IST is ahead of Greenwich by …
quiz.why: 82½° × 4 minutes per degree = 330 minutes, which is 5 hours 30 minutes. So IST is 5 h 30 min ahead of Greenwich.

quiz.q: Places east of Greenwich have time …
quiz.why: Earth rotates west to east, so places east see the Sun earlier. Their time is ahead of Greenwich.
Earth turns 15° in 60 minutes, so 1° takes 60 ÷ 15 = 4 minutes.

questions.q: A drawing of Earth's surface on a flat sheet to scale is a …
questions.why: A map is a drawing of the Earth's surface on a flat sheet, drawn to scale. A globe is a model of Earth.

questions.q: Equator latitude?
questions.why: The Equator is at 0° latitude.

questions.q: Prime Meridian passes through …
questions.why: The Prime Meridian passes through Greenwich, near London.

questions.q: Which map shows rainfall distribution?
questions.why: A map showing a single theme, such as rainfall, is a thematic map. Political maps show boundaries.

questions.q: Brown colour on physical map shows …
questions.why: On a physical map, brown shows mountains and highlands, green plains and blue water.

questions.q: Tropic of Cancer is at …
questions.why: The Tropic of Cancer is at 23½° North. 23½° South is the Tropic of Capricorn.

questions.q: Scale 1 cm = 25 km; 6 cm = ?
questions.why: 6 cm × 25 km per cm = 150 km.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Places east of Greenwich are ahead in time. Reason (R): Earth rotates west to east.
questions.why: Both are true: places east of Greenwich are ahead in time because Earth rotates from west to east. The Sun reaches the east first.

questions.q: Heat zone between the Tropics?
questions.why: The torrid zone lies between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. It is the hottest.

questions.q: India is in which hemispheres?
questions.why: India is north of the Equator and east of the Prime Meridian, so it is in the Northern and Eastern Hemispheres.

questions.q: Case: It is 6:00 pm IST. Greenwich time?
questions.why: IST is 5 h 30 min ahead of Greenwich. So 6:00 pm − 5:30 = 12:30 pm.

questions.q: Case: Place A is at 30° E, place B at 75° E. When it is noon at A, time at B?
questions.why: The two places are 75° − 30° = 45° apart. At 4 minutes per degree that is 180 minutes (3 hours), so B is 3 hours ahead: 3:00 pm.

questions.q: Which statement about longitudes is true?
options: All are equal half-circles meeting at the poles
They get smaller at the poles
questions.why: All longitudes are equal half-circles that run from pole to pole and meet at the poles. They are not parallel.

questions.q: Why is a standard meridian needed in a country?
options: So the country follows one time
questions.why: A standard meridian lets the whole country follow one time. Without it, each place would have its own local time.

questions.q: Case: A plane leaves Delhi (IST) at 2:00 am and lands in London after 9 hours. London time (Greenwich) on landing?
questions.why: 2:00 am + 9 h = 11:00 am IST. Subtract 5 h 30 min to get Greenwich time: 5:30 am.

questions.q: Time difference between 82½° E and 82½° W?
questions.why: The two meridians are 82.5° + 82.5° = 165° apart. At 4 minutes per degree that is 660 minutes, which is 11 hours.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Oceans and Continents
courses.summary: Land and water on Earth, the seven continents and five oceans with their key features, ocean movements — waves, tides and currents — and why oceans matter for climate, food, trade and India's coastline.
outcomes: Learners can name and locate the seven continents and five oceans
Learners can state key facts (largest, smallest, deepest) about them
Learners can explain waves, tides and ocean currents
Learners can describe the importance of oceans to India

lessons.title: A blue planet: land and water

scenes.text: Astronaut photos show Earth as a glowing blue ball.
Teacher says about 71% of the surface is water.
Only about 29% is land — the continents.
No wonder Earth is called the Blue Planet.

steps.title: Land and water
steps.body: About **71%** of Earth's surface is water (mostly oceans) and about **29%** is land. More land lies in the Northern Hemisphere; the Southern Hemisphere is mostly water.

steps.title: Continents and oceans
steps.body: Large landmasses are **continents** (7). The huge connected body of salt water is the **world ocean**, divided into **5 oceans**.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
If Earth's surface were 100 squares, how many would be water?

- About **71**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why is Earth called the 'Blue Planet'?

- Most of its surface is covered by oceans, which look blue from space.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking land and water are half-and-half.
- Calling the Caspian Sea an ocean — it is a large inland lake.

statements.s: About 71% of Earth's surface is water.
There are 7 continents and 5 oceans.
The Southern Hemisphere has more land.
All oceans are connected.

quiz.why: About 71% of Earth is covered by water, so land is about 29%.
There are 7 continents: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
There are 5 oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic.
The Northern Hemisphere has more land. The Southern Hemisphere has more water.
Earth is called the Blue Planet because oceans cover most of it, so it looks blue from space.

scenes.text: Class 6 builds a giant world-map jigsaw.
Asia is the biggest piece; Australia the smallest.
Antarctica is all white — covered in ice.
They place each piece and learn one fact about it.

steps.title: Continents (largest to smallest)
steps.body:
- **Asia**: largest and most populous; India is in South Asia; has Mount Everest (8,849 m), the highest peak
- **Africa**: second largest; the Equator runs through its middle; the Sahara (largest hot desert) and the Nile
- **North America**: connected to South America by a narrow strip (isthmus) of Panama
- **South America**: the Andes and the Amazon rainforest and river
- **Antarctica**: around the South Pole, covered with thick ice; no permanent residents, only research stations — India's are **Maitri** and **Bharati**
- **Europe**: joined with Asia (together 'Eurasia'), separated by the Ural Mountains
- **Australia**: smallest; an island continent

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which continent is crossed by the Equator and both Tropics?

- **Africa**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
India's research stations in Antarctica?

- **Maitri** and **Bharati** (earlier Dakshin Gangotri).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Antarctica an ocean or a country.
- Thinking Europe and Asia are separated by sea everywhere — they share land.

activity.prompt: Match the continent to its feature.
pairs: Separated from Asia by the Urals

quiz.why: Asia is the largest continent in both area and population.
Australia is the smallest continent.
Antarctica is covered with thick ice almost all year. It is the coldest continent.
The Amazon River and rainforest are in South America.

quiz.q: Europe and Asia are separated by …
quiz.why: The Ural Mountains form the boundary between Europe and Asia.

scenes.text: At the school quiz, the question is: 'Deepest ocean?'
Priya answers: 'Pacific — the Mariana Trench!'
Next: 'Only ocean named after a country?'
'The Indian Ocean!' she says, and wins.

steps.title: The oceans
steps.body:
- **Pacific**: largest and deepest; the **Mariana Trench** (about 11 km deep) is the deepest known point
- **Atlantic**: second largest; S-shaped; busy shipping routes between the Americas and Europe/Africa
- **Indian**: named after India; surrounds India on three sides with the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal
- **Southern**: surrounds Antarctica
- **Arctic**: smallest and shallowest; around the North Pole, mostly frozen

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which seas border India on the west and east?

- **Arabian Sea** (west), **Bay of Bengal** (east), **Indian Ocean** (south).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why does the Arctic Ocean have little shipping?

- It is frozen for much of the year.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Indian Ocean is the largest — it is third.
- Calling seas and bays separate oceans.

items.text: Bay of Bengal is part of it

quiz.why: The Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean. The Mariana Trench is in it.
The Arctic is the smallest ocean, around the North Pole.
The Indian Ocean is named after India, which juts into it. The others are not named after countries.
The Atlantic Ocean has an S-shape between the Americas and Europe and Africa.
The Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica.

lessons.title: Waves, tides and currents · Why oceans matter

scenes.text: In the morning, the sea at Mumbai's Marine Drive reaches the wall.
By afternoon, it has moved back, showing rocks.
Fisherfolk say, 'The Moon pulls the sea.'
They plan boat trips around the tides.

steps.title: Waves
steps.body: Rise and fall of the water surface, mostly caused by wind. Very large waves called **tsunamis** are caused by undersea earthquakes (the Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004 hit India's east coast).

steps.title: Tides
steps.body: Regular rise (**high tide**) and fall (**low tide**) of sea level, usually twice a day, caused mainly by the **gravitational pull of the Moon** (and the Sun). Tides help ships enter harbours and can be used for tidal energy.

steps.title: Ocean currents
steps.body: Streams of water moving in definite directions. **Warm currents** (from near the Equator) warm nearby coasts; **cold currents** (from polar regions) cool them. Where warm and cold currents meet, fishing grounds are rich.

steps.title: Oceans and India
steps.body: India has a very long coastline (long quoted as about 7,500 km; a 2024 re-measurement using finer methods gives about 11,000 km). Oceans give fish, salt, oil and gas, sea routes for trade (about 95% of India's trade by volume moves by sea), and the monsoon winds that bring rain.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why do fishers avoid low tide near some harbours?

- Water is shallow; boats may get stuck.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking tides are caused by wind — mainly the Moon's gravity.
- Confusing currents (flowing streams) with waves (up–down movement).

activity.prompt: Match the ocean movement to its cause or effect.
pairs: Pull of the Moon and Sun

quiz.why: Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, and also of the Sun, on the oceans.
Tsunamis are huge waves usually caused by undersea earthquakes. Tides and rain do not cause them.
High tides come about twice a day, roughly every 12 hours and 25 minutes.

quiz.q: Where warm and cold currents meet …
quiz.why: Where warm and cold currents meet, plankton thrive, so fish gather there. These are rich fishing grounds.

quiz.q: Most of India's trade by volume moves by …
quiz.why: Most of India's trade by volume goes by sea, because ships can carry huge loads cheaply.

questions.q: Largest ocean?
questions.why: The Pacific is the largest ocean, covering about a third of Earth's surface.

questions.q: Largest continent?
questions.why: Asia is the largest continent, ahead of Africa and North America.

questions.q: Water covers about … of Earth
questions.why: Water covers about 71% of Earth, and land the other 29%.

questions.q: Continent with the Sahara?
questions.why: The Sahara, the largest hot desert, is in Africa.

questions.q: India's research station in Antarctica?
questions.why: Maitri is India's research station in Antarctica. Another Indian station there is Bharati.

questions.q: Smallest ocean?
questions.why: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest ocean.

questions.q: Tides are mainly caused by …
questions.why: Tides are mainly caused by the Moon's gravity pulling on the oceans. Wind and earthquakes cause other waves.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Indian Ocean is named after India. Reason (R): India juts deep into it with a long coastline.
questions.why: Both are true: the Indian Ocean is named after India, which projects deep into it with a long coastline. The reason explains the name.

questions.q: Deepest known point on Earth is in the …
questions.why: The deepest known point is the Mariana Trench, in the Pacific Ocean, nearly 11 km deep.

questions.q: Which continent is crossed by the Equator and both Tropics?
questions.why: Africa is crossed by the Equator, the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. Other continents are crossed by fewer of them.

questions.q: Europe and Asia together are called …
questions.why: Europe and Asia form one connected landmass, called Eurasia.

questions.q: Case: A coastal town is unusually warm in winter for its latitude. A likely reason?
questions.why: Warm ocean currents bring warm water along the coast, so the coast stays warmer than other places at that latitude.

questions.q: Case: On 26 Dec 2004, huge waves struck Tamil Nadu. They were …
options: a tsunami caused by an undersea earthquake
questions.why: The 26 December 2004 waves were a tsunami caused by an undersea earthquake. They are different from tides or monsoon rain.

questions.q: Which correctly orders continents by size (largest first)?
questions.why: By size the order is Asia, Africa, North America, then others. So 'Asia, Africa, North America' is correct.

questions.q: Case: Two high tides occur in about 24 h 50 min. Approximate gap between them?
questions.why: Two high tides in about 24 h 50 min are about half of that apart. That is about 12 h 25 min.

questions.q: Why are fishing grounds rich where warm and cold currents meet?
options: Mixing supports plankton, food for fish
questions.why: Where warm and cold currents mix, nutrients rise and plankton grow. Fish feed on plankton, so fishing is good there.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Landforms and Life
courses.summary: The major landforms — mountains, plateaus and plains — how they form, examples in India and the world, and how people live, farm, travel and celebrate in each; plus deserts, coasts and islands, and caring for fragile landscapes.
outcomes: Learners can describe mountains, plateaus and plains with examples
Learners can explain how landforms shape people's lives and work
Learners can locate key Indian landforms
Learners can suggest how to protect fragile landforms

scenes.text: Kavya visits her aunt in a Himachal village.
Families keep sheep and goats and grow apples on terraced slopes.
Nights are cold even in June.
Pilgrims walk up to a temple at the top of the valley.

steps.title: What are mountains?
steps.body: Landforms that rise high above the surrounding land, usually with steep slopes and a narrow top (peak). Many form when Earth's plates push against each other (the Himalayas formed as the Indian plate pushed into the Eurasian plate). A series of mountains is a **range**.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- **Himalayas**: youngest and highest range; Mount Everest (8,849 m, Nepal–China border); Kangchenjunga is India's highest peak (8,586 m)
- **Western Ghats (Sahyadri)**, **Aravallis** (among the oldest ranges), **Vindhyas**
- World: Andes (S. America), Alps (Europe), Rockies (N. America)

steps.title: Life in the mountains
steps.body:
- Cold climate, thin air, steep land → terrace farming (apples, tea, potatoes), herding (yaks, sheep), tourism and pilgrimage
- Rivers start from glaciers (Ganga from Gangotri glacier)
- Challenges: landslides, few roads, harsh winters

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why are farms on mountains cut into steps?

- **Terraces** create flat strips that hold water and soil, reducing erosion.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why are the Himalayas important for north India?

- They feed rivers (Ganga, Yamuna, Brahmaputra), block cold winds from Central Asia, and stop monsoon winds so it rains in India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Mount Everest India's highest peak — it is in Nepal; India's highest is Kangchenjunga.
- Thinking all mountains are young — the Aravallis are very old.

statements.s: Himalayas are the youngest major range.
Kangchenjunga is India's highest peak.
Terrace farming increases soil erosion.
Ganga starts from the Gangotri glacier.

quiz.why: Mount Everest, at 8,849 m, is the highest peak in the world.
The Aravallis in Rajasthan are among the oldest fold mountains in the world. The Himalayas are much younger.
Cutting steps into slopes to grow crops is terrace farming. It slows soil erosion on mountain slopes.

quiz.q: A series of mountains is a …
quiz.why: A series of mountains in a line is a range. A plateau and a plain are different landforms.
The Andes are in South America, along its west coast.

story.title: The red earth of Chota Nagpur

scenes.text: Sunil's father works in a mine on the Chota Nagpur Plateau.
The soil is red, rich in iron.
Hundru Falls tumbles from the plateau's edge.
Tribal communities grow crops and gather forest produce.

steps.title: What is a plateau?
steps.body: A raised, fairly **flat-topped** highland with steep sides, standing above the land around. Sometimes called a 'tableland'.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- **Deccan Plateau** (peninsular India) — black soil good for cotton (formed from ancient lava)
- **Chota Nagpur Plateau** (Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal) — rich in coal, iron, mica
- **Tibetan Plateau** — highest plateau in the world
- **East African Plateau** — gold and diamonds

steps.title: Life on plateaus
steps.body:
- Mining of minerals
- Waterfalls (Hundru, Jog Falls on the edge of the Western Ghats/Deccan) for tourism and hydro-electricity
- Farming where soil is fertile (black soil for cotton); grazing in drier parts

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why is the Chota Nagpur Plateau called India's mineral heartland?

- It has large deposits of **coal, iron ore, mica, bauxite**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why is black soil good for cotton?

- It holds moisture well and is rich in minerals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking plateaus are always low — the Tibetan Plateau is very high.
- Confusing plateaus (flat top, raised) with plains (flat, low).

activity.prompt: Match the plateau to its feature.

quiz.why: A plateau is a flat-topped highland with steep sides, also called a tableland.
The Tibetan Plateau is the highest plateau in the world. It is called the 'roof of the world'.
Black soil, found on the Deccan Plateau, is well suited to cotton.
Plateaus often have rich minerals and waterfalls, since rivers drop over their edges. They are not just sand.
Hundru Falls is on the Chota Nagpur Plateau, in Jharkhand.

scenes.text: In Bihar, golden wheat fields stretch flat to the horizon.
The Ganga flows wide and slow, bringing fertile silt.
Big towns and railways have grown here.
Plains are home to many people.

steps.title: What are plains?
steps.body: Large stretches of **flat, low land**. Most are formed by rivers depositing fine soil (**silt/alluvium**) carried from mountains.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- **Indo-Gangetic Plain** (Punjab to West Bengal) — one of the most fertile and densely populated regions in the world
- **Brahmaputra Plain** (Assam)
- Coastal plains along India's east and west coasts

steps.title: Life in the plains
steps.body:
- Fertile soil and water → intensive farming (wheat, rice, sugarcane)
- Easy to build roads, railways, cities → dense population and industry
- Challenges: floods, overcrowding, pollution of rivers

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why are plains densely populated?

- Fertile land, water, flat ground for houses, farms and transport.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Where does the silt in the Ganga plain come from?

- Rivers carry eroded soil from the **Himalayas** and deposit it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking plains are all made the same way — some are coastal or formed by wind.
- Forgetting floods as a problem of river plains.

quiz.why: Plains are mostly formed by rivers depositing silt (alluvium) over many years.

quiz.q: Most fertile and densely populated plain in India?
quiz.why: The Indo-Gangetic Plain is very fertile and has many people, since rivers keep bringing fresh silt.
River plains can be flooded when rivers overflow. Landslides and snow belong to mountains.
Plains are flat and fertile, so they suit farming and building roads and railways.
Silt is fine soil eroded from mountains and carried down by rivers. Rivers then deposit it on plains.

lessons.title: Deserts, coasts, islands and caring for landforms

story.title: From the Thar to the Andamans

scenes.text: In Jaisalmer, Rahul's family stores rainwater in a taanka.
Camels carry goods across the sand dunes.
His pen-friend in Port Blair lives on an island with coral reefs.
Both places are beautiful — and fragile.

steps.title: Deserts
steps.body: Very dry areas with little rain. Hot deserts: **Thar** (Rajasthan), Sahara. Cold desert: **Ladakh**. People adapt: water harvesting (taankas, stepwells), camels, loose cotton clothes, thick-walled houses.

steps.title: Coasts and islands
steps.body:
- Coasts: fishing, ports, tourism, salt pans; risk of cyclones
- Islands: **Andaman & Nicobar** (Bay of Bengal), **Lakshadweep** (Arabian Sea, coral islands)

steps.title: Caring for landforms
steps.body: Mountains, deserts, coasts and islands are fragile. Avoid littering, follow trek rules, protect mangroves and forests, limit construction on slopes and beaches, respect local communities' knowledge.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why are houses in the Thar often thick-walled?

- Thick walls keep interiors cool by day and warm at night.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How do mangroves protect coasts?

- Their roots hold soil and reduce the force of waves and storm surges.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all deserts are hot — Ladakh is a cold desert.
- Thinking tourists' plastic doesn't matter in remote places.

items: I carry my waste back from hills and beaches
I don't break corals or shells
I respect local customs and ask before photographing people
I save water in dry places

quiz.why: Ladakh is a cold desert, since it is cold and receives very little rain.

options: coral islands in the Arabian Sea
quiz.why: Lakshadweep is a group of coral islands in the Arabian Sea.
A taanka is an underground tank in Rajasthan that stores rainwater. It is a traditional water-harvesting structure.
Mangroves protect coasts by breaking waves and holding the soil. They do not cause floods.
The Thar Desert is in Rajasthan.

questions.q: Highest mountain range in the world?
questions.why: The Himalayas are the highest mountain range, with Mount Everest in them.

questions.q: A flat-topped highland is a …
questions.why: A flat-topped highland is a plateau. A plain is low and flat land.

questions.q: Indo-Gangetic region is a …
questions.why: The Indo-Gangetic region is a vast, flat river plain.

questions.q: India's highest peak?
questions.why: Kangchenjunga (8,586 m) is the highest peak in India. Everest and K2 are not in India.

questions.q: Black soil region?
questions.why: The Deccan Plateau has black soil, formed from ancient lava rocks.

questions.q: Terrace farming is common in …
questions.why: Terrace farming is common on mountain slopes, where flat steps are cut to hold soil and water.

questions.q: Cold desert of India?
questions.why: Ladakh is India's cold desert. Thar and Kutch are hot or salty deserts.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Plains are densely populated. Reason (R): They have fertile soil and are easy for transport.
questions.why: Both are true: plains have fertile soil and are easy for transport, so many people settle there. The reason explains the high population.

questions.q: Chota Nagpur Plateau is known for …
questions.why: The Chota Nagpur Plateau is rich in minerals such as coal and iron ore. It has no glaciers or coral reefs.

questions.q: Himalayas help India by …
options: blocking cold winds and feeding rivers
questions.why: The Himalayas block cold winds from the north and feed rivers with snow and rain. That helps India's climate and water supply.

questions.q: Case: A village sits on a steep slope with heavy rain and many landslides. Best help?
questions.why: Planting trees and making terraces holds the soil and slows water on slopes. Cutting forests or removing grass makes landslides worse.

questions.q: Case: A region has flat land, a big river and frequent floods. It is most likely a …
questions.why: A flat land with a big river that often floods is typical of a river plain. Mountains, plateaus and deserts do not fit.

questions.q: Which is correctly matched?
questions.why: The Andes are in South America. The Alps are in Europe, the Aravallis in India and the Rockies in North America.

questions.q: Why is the Deccan's soil black?
options: It formed from ancient lava rocks
questions.why: The Deccan's black soil formed from the weathering of ancient lava (volcanic rock). It is not from coal dust or burning.

questions.q: Case: Tourists dump plastic on a coral island. Long-term harm?
options: Damages reefs, marine life and fishing livelihoods
questions.why: Plastic dumped on a coral island harms coral reefs and marine life. That can damage fishing and tourism for local people.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Timeline and Sources of History
courses.summary: What history is and why we study it, measuring time — years, decades, centuries, millennia, BCE and CE, timelines — and the sources historians use: archaeological, literary and oral, plus how scientists help date the past.
outcomes: Learners can explain what history is and why it matters
Learners can count years in BCE and CE and draw timelines
Learners can classify sources of history
Learners can explain how archaeologists and scientists reconstruct the past

scenes.text: Riya finds a black-and-white photo of Grandpa as a boy.
'That was in 1965 — more than 60 years ago,' he says.
She works out decades and centuries.
History is the story of the past — and she is part of it too.

steps.title: History
steps.body: **History** is the study of the past — people, events, ideas and how things changed. It helps us understand how our present came to be and learn from past mistakes and successes.

steps.title: Units of time
steps.body:
- **Decade** = 10 years · **Century** = 100 years · **Millennium** = 1000 years
- The 21st century runs from 2001 to 2100; the 1900s are the 20th century.

steps.title: BCE and CE
steps.body: Dates in the widely used calendar are counted from a starting year 1. Years before it are **BCE** (Before Common Era), counted backwards (500 BCE is earlier than 100 BCE). Years after are **CE** (Common Era). There is **no year 0**. (Older books use BC and AD.)

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
How many years from 300 BCE to 200 CE?

- 300 + 200 = 500, minus 1 (no year 0) = **499 years**. (For rough work, many teachers accept 500.)

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Which century is 1857 in?

- 1801–1900 → **19th century**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 500 BCE comes after 100 BCE.
- Saying 1950 is in the 'nineteenth century' — it's the 20th.

activity.prompt: Arrange these dates from earliest to latest.

quiz.why: A century is 100 years. A decade is 10 years and a millennium is 1000.

quiz.q: Which is earlier: 600 BCE or 200 BCE?
quiz.why: BCE years are counted backwards, so a bigger number is earlier. So 600 BCE is earlier than 200 BCE.
The 21st century runs from 2001 to 2100, so 2025 falls in it.
A millennium is 1000 years. A century is 100 years.
CE stands for Common Era. It is used for years after year 1, in place of AD.

scenes.text: Arjun pegs cards on a string: born 2014, school 2018, first prize 2023.
Equal gaps for equal years.
Teacher shows a class timeline of Indian history.
Seeing events in order makes the story clear.

steps.title: Timeline
steps.body: A **timeline** is a line showing events in time order, with equal spaces for equal periods. Earliest on the left (or bottom). For BCE–CE timelines, BCE numbers decrease towards the centre (year 1 CE).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Draw a scale for 3000 BCE to 2000 CE in 10 cm.

- Total 5000 years → **1 cm = 500 years**; 1 CE sits at 6 cm from the left.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Place: Harappan cities (~2600 BCE), Buddha (~5th century BCE), India's independence (1947 CE).

- Left to right in that order.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Uneven spacing on a timeline.
- Placing BCE dates in increasing order towards the right (wrong).

events.text: Time of the Buddha and Mahavira
Constitution of India comes into force

quiz.why: A timeline needs equal spaces for equal amounts of time, so it shows events in proportion. Random gaps would mislead.

quiz.q: On a BCE–CE timeline, 1000 BCE is … 500 BCE
quiz.why: On a timeline, earlier events go to the left. 1000 BCE is earlier than 500 BCE, so it is left of it.
The Constitution of India came into force on 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day.
10 cm cover 2000 years, so 1 cm stands for 2000 ÷ 10 = 200 years.
2600 BCE is the earliest, since BCE years come before CE years. The others (1526, 1857, 1947) are all CE.

scenes.text: At the National Museum, Delhi, Neha sees pottery, coins and a stone inscription.
A guide reads lines from an old manuscript.
In her village, Grandma sings songs about a local hero.
All are clues — sources — to the past.

steps.title: Types of sources
steps.body:
- **Archaeological**: remains dug up or found — buildings, tools, pottery, ornaments, seals, bones, coins, inscriptions
- **Literary (written)**: texts on palm leaves, birch bark, paper — religious texts, epics, poems, travellers' accounts, court histories (manuscripts are hand-written)
- **Oral**: stories, songs, legends passed by word of mouth

steps.title: Inscriptions and coins
steps.body: Inscriptions are writings on stone, metal or walls (Ashoka's edicts). Coins show rulers, dates, symbols and trade links.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Classify: a copper coin, a song about a battle, a palm-leaf manuscript.

- Archaeological, oral, literary.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why do historians compare many sources?

- Each source may be incomplete or one-sided; comparing gives a fuller, more reliable picture.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing every old text is literally accurate — historians check sources carefully.
- Ignoring oral traditions — they preserve the past of communities who didn't write.

quiz.why: A manuscript is a handwritten text, often on palm leaf or birch bark. It is not printed by machine.
Ashoka's edicts are inscriptions, messages carved on rocks and pillars.
Oral sources are stories, songs and sayings passed from person to person by word of mouth.
Coins tell us about rulers, their titles and trade, as well as metals used. They do not tell about weather.
Comparing sources helps historians get a more reliable picture, since one source may be wrong or biased.

scenes.text: At a site in Haryana, archaeologists dig carefully with brushes and small trowels.
They record each layer and the objects in it.
Bits of charcoal are sent to a lab for dating.
Slowly a picture of a 4,500-year-old town appears.

steps.title: Archaeologists
steps.body: **Archaeologists** study the past by excavating (digging) sites and studying remains. They note the **layer** where each object is found: lower layers are usually older.

steps.title: Science helps
steps.body:
- **Radiocarbon (carbon) dating** estimates the age of once-living material (wood, bone, charcoal) up to about 50,000 years old.
- DNA studies of ancient bones, study of seeds and pollen tell us about diet, health and climate.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Pottery A is found 1 m deep; pottery B 3 m deep at the same undisturbed site. Which is likely older?

- **B** (lower layer).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why can't carbon dating date a stone tool directly?

- Stone was never alive; scientists date organic material found with it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking archaeologists hunt for 'treasure' — they record everything, even broken pots.
- Removing objects from sites — it destroys evidence and is illegal at protected sites.

items: Interview an elder about their childhood (oral source)
Find the oldest object at home and guess its age
Look at an old coin or stamp and note what it shows
Make a timeline of your family over three generations
Write what each source tells you and what it doesn't

quiz.q: Lower layers in an undisturbed site are usually …
quiz.why: In an undisturbed site, newer layers form on top of older ones, so lower layers are usually older.
Carbon dating works on things that were once alive, such as wood, bone or cloth. It does not work on stone, metal or plastic.
Excavation means carefully digging at a site to find remains of the past.
Rakhigarhi, a Harappan site, is in Haryana.

quiz.q: Why record the layer of each object?
quiz.why: Recording the layer of each object helps date it and understand its context. Loose objects tell much less.

questions.q: History is the study of …
questions.why: History is the study of the past, of people and what happened to them. It is not only about kings or wars.

questions.q: A decade is …
questions.why: A decade is 10 years. A century is 100 years.

questions.q: Song passed down through generations is a(n) … source
questions.why: A song passed down through generations is an oral source, passed by word of mouth. It is not written or dug up.

questions.q: Which is earlier?
questions.why: BCE years are counted backwards, so 100 BCE came before 100 CE. So 100 BCE is earlier.

questions.q: 1757 is in the … century
questions.why: 1757 is in 1701–1800, which is the 18th century.

questions.q: Coins are … sources
questions.why: Coins are material remains found by digging, so they are archaeological sources. Books are literary sources.

questions.q: Manuscripts were written on …
questions.why: Old manuscripts were written on palm leaves and birch bark. Plastic, steel and glass were not used.

questions.q: Assertion (A): There is no year 0 between 1 BCE and 1 CE. Reason (R): The calendar jumps from 1 BCE to 1 CE.
questions.why: Both are true: the calendar goes from 1 BCE straight to 1 CE, so there is no year 0. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Carbon dating can date …
questions.why: Carbon dating works on once-living material such as wood. A wooden beam can be dated, but gold, glass and granite cannot.

questions.q: Case: Two pots at 0.5 m and 2 m depth in undisturbed layers. Which is older?
questions.why: In undisturbed layers, deeper means older. So the pot at 2 m is older than the one at 0.5 m.

questions.q: Why do historians use many sources?
questions.why: Historians use many sources to cross-check facts and fill gaps. A single source may be incomplete or biased.

questions.q: Case: A timeline of 10 cm covers 1000 BCE to 1000 CE. Where is 1 CE?
questions.why: The timeline runs from 1000 BCE to 1000 CE, which is 2000 years, and 1 CE is almost exactly halfway. So it is at about 5 cm.

questions.q: Years from 250 BCE to 250 CE (exact, no year 0)?
questions.why: With no year 0, 250 BCE to 1 BCE is 250 years and 1 CE to 250 CE is 250 years, but counting from 250 BCE to 250 CE gives 250 + 250 − 1 = 499 years.

questions.q: Which is a literary source?
questions.why: A traveller's written account is a literary (written) source. A burial site, clay seal and Ashoka's rock edict are archaeological or inscription sources.

questions.q: Case: An inscription mentions a king and a year; a coin of the same king shows a different title. A historian should …
options: compare with other sources and explain the difference
questions.why: When sources disagree, a historian should compare them with other sources and explain the difference. Ignoring one or inventing a story is not good history.

questions.q: How many centuries from 500 BCE to 1500 CE (approx.)?
questions.why: From 500 BCE to 1500 CE is about 2000 years, which is about 20 centuries.

courses.title: Ch 5 · India, That Is Bharat
courses.summary: The many names of our land through time — Bharata and Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa, Hind and Hindustan, India — where they come from, how others described India, and what the Constitution says.
outcomes: Learners can explain the origins of the names Bharat, Jambudvipa, Hind/Hindustan and India
Learners can describe how ancient texts described the extent of Bharatavarsha
Learners can quote Article 1 of the Constitution
Learners can appreciate how names reflect history and contact with other peoples

scenes.text: Aditi notices her passport says 'Bharat Ganarajya' in Hindi and 'Republic of India' in English.
'Why two names?' she asks her mother.
Her mother opens a book about ancient texts.
The names carry thousands of years of history.

steps.title: The Bharatas
steps.body: The **Rigveda**, one of the oldest texts in the world, mentions the **Bharatas**, a prominent people (clan) in north-west India. Over time, the land came to be called after them.

steps.title: Bharatavarsha
steps.body: Later texts such as the **Vishnu Purana** describe **Bharatavarsha** as the land lying **north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains (Himalayas)**, whose people are called Bhāratī. The name also became linked with stories of a legendary king Bharata.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
According to the Vishnu Purana, what are Bharatavarsha's boundaries?

- **The ocean in the south and the Himalayas in the north**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why are names useful to historians?

- They show how people saw their land and who they were in contact with.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'Bharat' is a recent name — it is very old.
- Thinking only one story explains the name; several traditions exist.

statements.s: The Rigveda mentions a people called the Bharatas.
Bharatavarsha was described as lying between the ocean and the Himalayas.
'Bharat' first appeared in the 20th century.
Our Constitution uses both 'India' and 'Bharat'.

quiz.why: The Bharatas, an ancient group of people, are mentioned in the Rigveda. The Constitution and Akbarnama are much later.
The Vishnu Purana describes Bharatavarsha as the land south of the Himalayas (the snowy mountains) and north of the ocean.
The Vishnu Purana calls the people of Bharatavarsha Bhāratī, meaning people of Bharata.

options: show views and contacts of people
quiz.why: The names for a land show how people saw it and who they were in contact with. So they are evidence for historians.
The Vishnu Purana is a Purana, an ancient Sanskrit text. It is not a coin, map or inscription.

story.title: The island of the jamun tree

scenes.text: Sameer's grandmother hands him jamun fruits from their tree.
'Did you know an old name for our land comes from this tree?'
'Jambudvipa — the island of the jambu (jamun) tree.'
Sameer is amazed.

steps.title: Jambudvipa
steps.body: An old name meaning 'the island/continent of the **jambu** (jamun) tree'. It appears in early texts and in **Ashoka's** inscriptions (3rd century BCE), and in Buddhist and Jain traditions, where it often referred to the Indian subcontinent or a larger region.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which emperor's inscription mentions Jambudvipa?

- **Ashoka** (Mauryan).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
What tree gives the name Jambudvipa?

- The **jamun** tree (Syzygium cumini).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking 'dvipa' means only a small island — here it means a large landmass/continent.

quiz.why: Jambu is the Sanskrit name for the jamun tree. The word 'Jambudvipa' is based on it.
Jambudvipa, the name for the land of the jamun tree, appears in the inscriptions of the emperor Ashoka. Akbar, Tipu Sultan and Shivaji lived much later.
'Dvipa' means a large landmass or island-continent. So Jambudvipa was 'the landmass of the jamun tree'.
Ashoka was a Mauryan emperor who ruled in the 3rd century BCE. He did not live in the 5th or 15th century CE.

quiz.q: Jambudvipa is used in Buddhist texts?
quiz.why: Yes. Jambudvipa is also used in Buddhist texts, besides Ashoka's inscriptions, for the land of the Indian subcontinent.

scenes.text: Long ago, Persian traders reached the great river Sindhu.
In their language 'S' became 'H': Sindhu → Hindu.
Greek travellers then called it Indos — the land became India.
One river gave names in many languages!

steps.title: From Sindhu
steps.body:
The river **Sindhu** (Indus) gave rise to many names:

- Old Persian: **Hindu** ('S' sounds became 'H') → later **Hind**, **Hindustan** ('land of Hind')
- Greek: **Indos/Indikē** (the river and land) → Latin **India**
- Chinese travellers used names like **Yintu/Yindu**, and **Tianzhu**

steps.title: How outsiders described India
steps.body: Ancient Persian inscriptions (Darius I, ~6th century BCE) list 'Hidu' as a region. Greek writer **Megasthenes** wrote *Indika* about the Mauryan court. Chinese pilgrim **Xuanzang** (7th century CE) studied at Nalanda and described India.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why did the Persians say 'Hindu' instead of 'Sindhu'?

- In their language the 'S' sound often became 'H'.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Who wrote *Indika*?

- **Megasthenes**, Greek ambassador at Chandragupta Maurya's court.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking 'Hindustan' was originally a religious term — it began as a geographical name from the river.

activity.prompt: Match the name to its origin.

quiz.q: Names Hind and India come from the river …
quiz.why: The names Hind and India come from the river Sindhu (Indus). The Persians and Greeks changed the sound of 'Sindhu' in their own languages.
Megasthenes, a Greek ambassador at the Mauryan court, wrote 'Indika', an account of India. The other books were written by other authors.
Xuanzang was a Chinese Buddhist monk who travelled to India in the 7th century CE. He studied here and wrote about what he saw.
The Persians pronounced the 'S' of 'Sindhu' as 'H', giving 'Hindu' and 'Hind'. This sound change happened in Persian, not Latin or Greek.
Hindustan originally meant the land of Hind, a place name coming from Sindhu. It was a geographical name and not a religion.

lessons.title: India, that is Bharat — the Constitution

scenes.text: On 26 January, the school principal reads the Constitution's first line.
'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.'
Students repeat it proudly.
Two names, one nation.

steps.title: Article 1
steps.body: Article 1 of the **Constitution of India** says: “**India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.**” Both names are official. In Hindi the country is **Bharat Ganarajya**.

steps.title: Why names matter
steps.body: Names connect us to history, geography and to the peoples who met India. They show India's long civilisation and its links with the world.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
When did the Constitution come into force?

- **26 January 1950** (Republic Day).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Give three names of India and their language origin.

- Bharat (Sanskrit/Indian texts), Hindustan (Persian), India (Greek/Latin).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking only one name is official — the Constitution uses both.

activity.text: "India, that is ___, shall be a Union of ___."

quiz.q: Article 1 says India is a Union of …
quiz.why: Article 1 of the Constitution says 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'. So India is a Union of States.
The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, which we celebrate as Republic Day. It was adopted earlier, on 26 November 1949.
The official Hindi name of the Republic is Bharat Ganarajya. Aryavarta and Jambudvipa are older names for the land.
Article 1 gives both India and Bharat as official names of the country. Neither is banned or only foreign.
The name India came to English through Greek (Indos) and Latin, which took it from the river Sindhu. It did not come from Japanese or Tamil.

questions.q: 'India, that is Bharat' is from Article … of the Constitution
questions.why: 'India, that is Bharat' is from Article 1 of the Constitution. It declares India a Union of States.

questions.q: The name 'India' comes from the river …
questions.why: The name India comes from the river Indus (Sindhu), through Persian and Greek. It does not come from the Ganga or Kaveri.

questions.q: Jambudvipa is named after the … tree
questions.why: Jambudvipa is named after the jamun (jambu) tree. Peepal, neem and mango are not the source.

questions.q: The Bharatas are mentioned in the …
questions.why: The Bharatas, an ancient group of people, are mentioned in the Rigveda. The Constitution and Indika are much later.

questions.q: Megasthenes was from …
questions.why: Megasthenes came from Greece and visited the Mauryan court as an ambassador. He wrote Indika.

questions.q: Jambudvipa appears in inscriptions of …
questions.why: Jambudvipa appears in the inscriptions of Ashoka. Harsha, Raja Raja Chola and Akbar came later.

questions.q: Bharatavarsha lies between …
questions.why: The Vishnu Purana places Bharatavarsha between the ocean in the south and the Himalayas in the north.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Persians called the land 'Hind'. Reason (R): The 'S' in Sindhu became 'H' in their language.
questions.why: Both are true: the Persians called the land 'Hind' because they pronounced the 'S' of Sindhu as 'H'. The reason explains the name.

questions.q: Xuanzang studied at …
questions.why: Xuanzang, the Chinese pilgrim, studied at Nalanda, a great centre of learning in Bihar.

questions.q: Which is a Chinese name for India?
questions.why: Tianzhu is a Chinese name for India. Indikē is Greek, and Hidu is Old Persian.

questions.q: Case: A textbook says 'Hindustan' began as a religious word. Correction?
options: It began as a geographical name meaning land of Hind (from Sindhu)
questions.why: Hindustan began as a geographical name meaning land of Hind, which comes from Sindhu. It was not originally a religious word.

questions.q: Why did different peoples give India different names?
options: They met it through different languages and routes
questions.why: Different peoples reached India by different routes and spoke different languages, so they gave it different names. The names show their contacts.

questions.q: Order these from earliest: Rigveda's Bharatas, Ashoka's Jambudvipa, Constitution's 'Bharat'
questions.why: The Rigveda is the oldest, Ashoka's Jambudvipa comes from the 3rd century BCE, and the Constitution's 'Bharat' is from 1950. So the order is Rigveda, Ashoka, Constitution.

questions.q: A Persian inscription listing 'Hidu' as a region is from about …
questions.why: The Old Persian inscription listing 'Hidu' is from the time of Darius I, around the 6th century BCE. It is one of the earliest mentions of the name.

questions.q: Which statement is accurate?
options: Both India and Bharat are official names
questions.why: Article 1 uses both 'India' and 'Bharat' as official names. Hindustan is not the official name.

courses.title: Ch 6 · The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation
courses.summary: From early farming to India's first cities: the Harappan (Sindhu–Sarasvati) civilisation — its major sites, planned cities, drains and water management, crafts, seals and script, trade, daily life, and the reasons for its decline.
outcomes: Learners can explain what a civilisation is and how farming led to towns
Learners can locate and describe key Harappan sites
Learners can describe town planning, water management, crafts and trade
Learners can discuss theories of decline and the civilisation's legacy

scenes.text: About 9,000 years ago at Mehrgarh (in present-day Pakistan), people began growing barley and wheat.
They kept cattle, sheep and goats.
Villages grew; extra food let some people become potters and traders.
Over thousands of years, cities rose along great rivers.

steps.title: What is a civilisation?
steps.body: A **civilisation** is a complex society with cities, organised government or rules, specialised jobs (crafts, trade), writing or record-keeping, and shared culture.

steps.title: Early farming
steps.body: **Mehrgarh** (Baluchistan) shows early farming and herding in the subcontinent from about 7000 BCE. Surplus food allowed villages to grow into towns.

steps.title: The Harappan civilisation
steps.body: Named after **Harappa**, the first site excavated (1920s). Also called the **Indus** or **Sindhu–Sarasvati** civilisation because many sites lie along the Indus and the Ghaggar–Hakra river (often identified with the ancient Sarasvati). Its mature urban phase was about **2600–1900 BCE**.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why did cities grow near rivers?

- Water for farming, drinking and transport; fertile soil.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Which was found first, Harappa or Dholavira?

- **Harappa** (1920s); Dholavira was excavated much later.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the civilisation was only along the Indus — many sites are in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab.
- Confusing Mehrgarh (early farming village) with a Harappan city.

quiz.why: The Harappan civilisation is named after Harappa, the first site where its remains were excavated. It was named after a place, not a person.
The mature Harappan phase lasted from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. 500 BCE and 1000 CE are much later.
Mehrgarh, in present-day Pakistan, shows some of the earliest farming in South Asia. Railways, printing and steel came much later.
A civilisation usually has cities and people with specialised jobs. It does not have only hunters or no settlements.
The dried-up Ghaggar–Hakra river is often identified with the Sarasvati of the Vedic texts. Many Harappan sites lie along it.

scenes.text: Imagine walking a straight street of baked bricks, 4,500 years ago.
Under the street, covered drains carry waste water away.
On the citadel stands the Great Bath, lined with waterproof bricks.
City planners of the past were brilliant.

steps.title: Major sites
steps.body:
- **Harappa** (Punjab, Pakistan) and **Mohenjo-daro** (Sindh, Pakistan)
- **Dholavira** (Kutch, Gujarat) — huge reservoirs; UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021)
- **Lothal** (Gujarat) — a dock-like basin and bead-making
- **Kalibangan** (Rajasthan) — ploughed field, fire altars
- **Rakhigarhi** (Haryana) — one of the largest sites

steps.title: Town planning
steps.body:
- Streets in a **grid**, crossing at right angles
- Standard-sized **baked bricks** (ratio about 1 : 2 : 4)
- Many cities divided into a raised **citadel** and a **lower town**
- Houses around courtyards, with wells and bathrooms

steps.title: Water management
steps.body: Covered **drains** along streets with inspection holes; wells; Dholavira's stone **reservoirs** stored rain water; the **Great Bath** at Mohenjo-daro (likely for special/ritual bathing) was made watertight with bricks and bitumen.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
What does the 1:2:4 brick ratio show?

- **Standardisation** — common rules across far-off cities.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why were Dholavira's reservoirs vital?

- Kutch is dry; storing monsoon water helped the city survive.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the Great Bath a swimming pool — its exact use isn't known; experts think it was for special bathing.
- Placing Mohenjo-daro in India — it's in present-day Pakistan.

activity.prompt: Match the site to its feature.

quiz.q: Harappan streets were laid in a …
quiz.why: Harappan streets were laid out in a grid, crossing at right angles. This shows careful town planning.
The Great Bath is at Mohenjo-daro, in present-day Sindh, Pakistan. It was a large water tank built with bricks.
Dholavira is in Kutch, Gujarat. It is a Harappan site known for its water reservoirs.
Harappan drains were covered, which kept the streets clean. This is a sign of good planning.
Harappan bricks were made in a fixed ratio, showing standardisation across towns. It suggests common planning and rules.

scenes.text: A craftsman carves a tiny square steatite seal with a bull and some signs.
Traders press it into clay on goods bundles.
Boats carry beads and cotton to faraway Mesopotamia.
Even today, no one can read the signs!

steps.title: Crafts
steps.body: Beads of **carnelian** and other stones, shell bangles, copper and bronze tools, pottery painted in red and black, cotton textiles, the famous bronze 'dancing girl' figure from Mohenjo-daro.

steps.title: Seals and script
steps.body: Small, square **seals** usually of steatite, carved with animals (humped bull, 'unicorn', elephant, tiger) and signs of the **Harappan script**. The script has **not been deciphered** yet. Seals were probably used to mark goods.

steps.title: Weights and trade
steps.body: Standardised cube-shaped stone **weights**. Trade within the subcontinent and with **Mesopotamia** (whose texts mention a land called '**Meluhha**', probably the Harappan region) and the Gulf.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
How do we know Harappans traded with Mesopotamia?

- Harappan seals and beads have been found in Mesopotamia, and Mesopotamian texts mention Meluhha.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why is the script still a mystery?

- Inscriptions are very short and no bilingual text (like a translation) has been found.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying we know the Harappans' kings' names — without a deciphered script, we don't.
- Calling seals 'coins' — they were not money.

statements.s: The Harappan script has been fully deciphered.
Seals were often made of steatite.
Mesopotamian texts may refer to the region as Meluhha.
Harappans used standard weights.

quiz.why: Most Harappan seals were made of steatite, a soft stone that is easy to carve. They were not made of gold, iron or plastic.

quiz.q: A famous bronze figure is the …
quiz.why: The 'dancing girl' is a famous small bronze figure from Mohenjo-daro. The Ashoka lion and Nataraja are from later times.

quiz.q: Meluhha is mentioned in texts from …
quiz.why: Meluhha is mentioned in Mesopotamian texts and is thought to mean the Harappan land. It shows trade between the two.
Carnelian, a red stone, was used for making beads. It was not used for roofs, bricks or weapons.
Seals were probably used to stamp and mark goods, showing who owned or sent them. They were not used for cooking.

scenes.text: By about 1900 BCE, people slowly left many big cities.
The Ghaggar–Hakra river was drying up; rains may have weakened.
Families moved to smaller villages further east and south.
Their skills and ideas lived on in later Indian life.

steps.title: Daily life
steps.body: Farmers grew wheat, barley, pulses, sesame, cotton and possibly some rice; kept cattle; used ploughs (Kalibangan field). People wore cotton and ornaments; children played with toy carts and whistles.

steps.title: Decline (c. 1900 BCE)
steps.body: Scholars suggest several causes together: **climate change** and weaker monsoons, **drying of rivers** (Ghaggar–Hakra), floods in some areas, decline of long-distance trade. Cities shrank; people moved to villages — it was a gradual change, not a sudden end.

steps.title: Legacy
steps.body: Continuities seen later: certain weights and measures, bangles and sindoor-like ornaments, ploughing, bullock carts, some craft styles, worship of trees and animals, yoga-like postures on some seals (interpretations differ).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why do historians speak of 'decline' rather than 'disappearance'?

- People and skills continued in smaller settlements.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Give one Harappan item still used in Indian villages.

- **Bullock cart** (toy models found).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing one single disaster ended it all — evidence points to many slow causes.
- Presenting guesses as certain facts; historians mark them as 'likely' or 'possibly'.

items: I can explain town planning in 3 points
I can give 2 pieces of evidence for trade
I can list 2 possible reasons for decline
I can name 1 legacy in today's life

quiz.why: The Harappan cities began to decline around 1900 BCE. 10,000 BCE is far too early and 500 CE too late.
Drying rivers and climate change are likely causes of the decline. Railways, gunpowder and printing did not exist then.
A ploughed field from Harappan times was found at Kalibangan. It shows that they farmed with ploughs.
Toy models of bullock carts have been found at Harappan sites. Cars, planes and bicycles did not exist.

quiz.q: Harappan people wore clothes made of …
quiz.why: Harappans grew cotton and wore cotton clothes. Polyester, nylon and plastic were invented much later.

questions.q: First Harappan site excavated?
questions.why: Harappa was the first site of this civilisation to be excavated, in the 1920s, so the civilisation was named after it.

questions.q: Great Bath is at …
questions.why: The Great Bath is at Mohenjo-daro. It is not at Harappa, Kalibangan or Lothal.

questions.q: Harappan script is …
questions.why: The Harappan script has not been deciphered yet, so we cannot read what the seals say.

questions.q: Dockyard-like basin found at …
questions.why: A large brick basin like a dockyard was found at Lothal, in Gujarat. It suggests Harappans traded by sea.

questions.q: Seals were usually made of …
questions.why: Harappan seals were usually made of steatite, a soft stone. Paper and wood would not last.

questions.q: Dholavira is a UNESCO World Heritage Site since …
questions.why: Dholavira became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

questions.q: Harappan streets were …
questions.why: Harappan streets were in a grid pattern, which shows town planning. They were not random or circular.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Harappans traded with Mesopotamia. Reason (R): Harappan seals have been found in Mesopotamia.
questions.why: Both are true: Harappans traded with Mesopotamia, and Harappan seals found in Mesopotamia are the evidence. The reason supports the assertion.

questions.q: Brick ratio 1:2:4 shows …
questions.why: A fixed brick ratio of 1:2:4 means bricks were made to the same standard everywhere. This is standardisation.

questions.q: Early farming at Mehrgarh began about …
questions.why: Early farming at Mehrgarh began about 7000 BCE. The Harappan cities came much later, around 2600 BCE.

questions.q: Which site is in Haryana?
questions.why: Rakhigarhi is a Harappan site in Haryana. Dholavira and Lothal are in Gujarat and Mohenjo-daro is in Pakistan.

questions.q: Case: A city has a raised area with large buildings and a lower area with houses. This shows …
questions.why: A raised area with large buildings (citadel) and a lower area with houses shows town planning. Many Harappan cities had this layout.

questions.q: Case: In a dry region, a city built stone reservoirs. Best conclusion?
options: They managed water to survive dry periods
questions.why: Stone reservoirs in a dry region show that people stored and managed water to last through dry periods. It does not mean it never rained.

questions.q: Why do historians say the end was gradual?
options: People moved to smaller settlements over time
questions.why: Historians say the end was gradual because people moved to smaller settlements over time. There is no evidence of one flood or asteroid.

questions.q: Which is NOT a likely reason for decline?
questions.why: Railways did not exist in Harappan times, so they cannot be a reason. Weaker monsoons, a drying river and lower trade are possible.

questions.q: Why is the script hard to decipher?
options: Short inscriptions and no bilingual text
questions.why: The inscriptions are very short, and no bilingual text, like the Rosetta Stone, has been found. This makes the script hard to decipher.

courses.title: Ch 7 · India's Cultural Roots
courses.summary: The ideas and traditions at the roots of Indian culture: the Vedas and the seers who composed them, the Upanishads and schools of thought, Buddhism and Jainism, and folk and tribal traditions — presented respectfully as part of a shared heritage.
outcomes: Learners can describe the Vedas and name the four Vedas
Learners can explain key ideas of the Upanishads in simple words
Learners can outline the teachings of the Buddha and Mahavira
Learners can appreciate folk and tribal traditions' respect for nature

scenes.text: At a village gurukul-style school, children recite verses exactly as their teacher does.
They learn by listening and repeating, not from books.
'These verses were passed down orally for thousands of years,' says the teacher.
UNESCO recognises Vedic chanting as an intangible heritage.

steps.title: What are the Vedas?
steps.body: Ancient collections of hymns and verses in early **Sanskrit**, composed by many **rishis** (seers), including some women seers (**rishikas**) such as **Ghosha** and **Lopamudra**. The four Vedas: **Rigveda** (oldest), **Samaveda** (melodies), **Yajurveda** (ritual formulas), **Atharvaveda** (daily life, healing, charms).

steps.title: Oral tradition
steps.body: They were preserved for centuries by careful memorisation with special recitation methods, long before being written down. **Vedic chanting** is on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage (2008).

steps.title: Ideas
steps.body: Hymns praise nature forces (Agni – fire, Indra, Varuna, Ushas – dawn), and express ideas like **ṛta** (cosmic order) and the famous line that truth is one, though the wise call it by many names.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which Veda is linked with music?

- **Samaveda** — many of its verses are set to melodies.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How were the Vedas preserved without writing?

- Through **oral** transmission with strict recitation techniques.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Vedas were written on paper first.
- Thinking only men composed hymns — rishikas did too.

activity.prompt: Match the Veda to its focus.

quiz.why: The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas. Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda came later.
The Vedas were first preserved orally, by memorising and chanting. They were written down much later.

quiz.q: A woman seer of the Rigveda?
quiz.why: Ghosha was a woman seer (rishika) who composed hymns in the Rigveda. Razia, Mirabai and Ahilyabai lived much later.
There are four Vedas: Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda.
The Vedas are in an early form of Sanskrit, called Vedic Sanskrit. They are not in English or Persian.

scenes.text: Nachiketa, a boy in an Upanishad story, asks deep questions about life and death.
He doesn't accept easy gifts in place of answers.
Teachers and students in these texts discuss: What is the self? What is reality?
Questioning is part of India's tradition.

steps.title: Upanishads
steps.body: Philosophical texts, often dialogues between teachers and students. Key ideas: **Brahman** (the ultimate reality), **ātman** (the inner self), and that they are connected; the value of knowledge and self-understanding. Women thinkers like **Gargi** and **Maitreyi** appear in debates.

steps.title: Schools of thought (darshanas)
steps.body: Over time, many schools of philosophy developed — such as Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Nyāya (logic), Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta — along with other traditions. They debated openly, showing a culture of discussion.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
What does the Nachiketa story teach?

- The value of seeking **true knowledge** over riches.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Name a woman thinker in the Upanishads.

- **Gargi** (or Maitreyi).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking Indian thought had only one view — many schools debated and differed.

cards.back: Woman philosopher who questioned in a famous debate

quiz.why: The Upanishads are mainly philosophical texts that ask deep questions about life and the self. They are not maps or laws.
Ātman means the inner self or soul. It is not a temple, king or river.
Gargi was a woman thinker who took part in philosophical debates, as recorded in the Upanishads. The others were rulers or leaders of later times.
Nyāya is a school of Indian philosophy that deals with logic and reasoning. It is not about dance, music or medicine.

quiz.q: Many schools show a culture of …
quiz.why: Having many schools of thought shows a culture of discussion and debate, where people questioned and argued.

story.title: The prince who left the palace

scenes.text: Prince Siddhartha of Kapilavastu sees an old man, a sick man and a funeral.
He leaves home to seek why people suffer.
At Bodh Gaya, under a pipal tree, he gains enlightenment and becomes the Buddha.
Around the same time, Mahavira teaches non-violence.

steps.title: The Buddha (c. 5th century BCE)
steps.body:
- Born Siddhartha Gautama at **Lumbini**; enlightenment at **Bodh Gaya**; first teaching at **Sarnath**
- Taught the **Middle Path** (avoid extremes), the causes of suffering and how to end it, kindness and right conduct
- Followers formed the **sangha** (community of monks and nuns); he taught in **Pali/Prakrit**, languages of ordinary people

steps.title: Mahavira and Jainism
steps.body:
- **Vardhamana Mahavira**, regarded by Jains as the **24th tirthankara**
- Key ideas: **ahiṃsā** (non-violence to all living beings), truth, non-stealing, non-attachment; **anekāntavāda** (truth has many sides)

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why did the Buddha's teaching spread widely?

- He taught in people's languages, welcomed all, and the sangha carried it far; later rulers like Ashoka supported it.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
What is the story of the blind men and the elephant used to explain?

- **Anekāntavāda** — each sees only part of the truth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up Bodh Gaya (enlightenment) and Sarnath (first sermon).
- Thinking Jain ahiṃsā is only about humans — it includes all living beings.

quiz.why: The Buddha gained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, in Bihar, under a peepal tree. Sarnath is where he gave his first teaching.

options: walk in the middle of roads
quiz.why: The Middle Path means avoiding extremes, such as too much luxury or too much hardship.
Ahiṃsā means non-violence, which is not harming others. It is a key idea in Buddhism and Jainism.
Mahavira is regarded as the 24th tirthankara of Jainism. Rishabhanatha was the first.
The Buddha taught in the languages ordinary people spoke, such as Pali and Prakrit. This helped his message reach many.

scenes.text: In Meghalaya, Ribor's village protects a forest that no one may cut.
Elders say spirits of nature live there.
The grove is full of rare plants and birds.
Beliefs and conservation go hand in hand.

steps.title: Living traditions
steps.body: Folk and tribal communities across India have their own songs, dances, stories, art (Warli, Gond, Madhubani), festivals and deities, often centred on **nature** — forests, rivers, mountains, animals.

steps.title: Sacred groves
steps.body: Patches of forest protected by communities for religious reasons — e.g., in Meghalaya (Mawphlang), Kerala (kavu), Maharashtra (devrai). They preserve biodiversity.

steps.title: Give and take
steps.body: Folk, tribal and textual traditions influenced each other: many local deities became part of wider traditions, and textual ideas spread through local stories.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why are sacred groves important today?

- They protect rare species, springs and soil.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Name a tribal art form.

- **Warli** (Maharashtra) or **Gond** (Madhya Pradesh).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Treating tribal traditions as 'less advanced' — they hold deep ecological knowledge.

activity.prompt: Is there a festival, song or story in your family or area connected with nature? Describe it.
activity.hint: Think of harvest festivals, river worship, tree planting rituals, or folk songs.

quiz.why: Sacred groves are protected by local communities, who treat them as holy. This keeps the trees safe.
Warli art is a tribal painting style from Maharashtra. It is not from Kerala, Assam or Punjab.
Many tribal traditions centre on nature, such as forests, rivers and animals. They treat nature with respect.
Kavu are sacred groves in Kerala. Other states have sacred groves with different names.
Folk and textual traditions influenced each other over time, sharing stories and ideas. They did not stay separate.

questions.q: Oldest of the Vedas?
questions.why: The Rigveda is the oldest of the Vedas. Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda came after it.

questions.q: The Buddha's first teaching was at …
questions.why: The Buddha gave his first teaching at Sarnath, near Varanasi. He was born at Lumbini and gained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.

questions.q: Ahiṃsā means …
questions.why: Ahiṃsā means non-violence, which is not harming any living being. It does not mean truth, wealth or courage.

questions.q: Vedas were preserved …
questions.why: The Vedas were preserved orally for centuries, by memorising and chanting. Printing and writing came much later.

questions.q: Mahavira is regarded as the … tirthankara
questions.why: Mahavira is regarded as the 24th and last tirthankara of Jainism.

questions.q: Upanishads are mostly …
questions.why: The Upanishads are mostly philosophical dialogues about the self and the universe. They are not battle records or tax lists.

questions.q: A woman seer of the Rigveda?
questions.why: Lopamudra was a woman seer to whom Rigveda hymns are attributed. Avvaiyar, Mirabai and Akka Mahadevi were poets of later times.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Buddha's teachings reached ordinary people. Reason (R): He taught in Pali/Prakrit, not only in a learned language.
questions.why: Both are true: the Buddha taught in Pali/Prakrit, the languages of ordinary people, so his teachings reached them. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Anekāntavāda teaches …
questions.why: Anekāntavāda is the Jain idea that truth has many sides, so no single view shows all of it. It does not teach violence or one correct view.

questions.q: The Buddha was born at …
questions.why: The Buddha was born at Lumbini, now in Nepal. Sarnath and Bodh Gaya are linked with his teaching and enlightenment.

questions.q: Vedic chanting was recognised by UNESCO as …
questions.why: UNESCO recognised Vedic chanting as an intangible cultural heritage in 2008. It is a living tradition, not a monument.

questions.q: Case: A village bans cutting trees in a forest patch dedicated to a local deity. This is a …
questions.why: A forest patch protected because it is dedicated to a local deity is a sacred grove. It keeps trees and wildlife safe.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: The Samaveda is the Veda of melodies, with hymns set to music. The Rigveda is the oldest and Yajurveda and Atharvaveda are Vedas, not Buddhist or Jain texts.

questions.q: Why is debate between schools of thought important?
options: It shows a culture of questioning and many views
questions.why: Debate between schools shows a culture of questioning and many views. It helped ideas grow, and it did not stop learning.

questions.q: Case: In a story, six blind men touch an elephant and describe it differently. Which idea is illustrated?
questions.why: Six blind men each touching a different part of an elephant and describing it differently show that each sees part of the truth. That is Anekāntavāda.

questions.q: Which is NOT a teaching of the Buddha?
options: Extreme self-torture is the only way
questions.why: The Buddha rejected extreme self-torture and taught the Middle Path. So saying that extreme self-torture is the only way is not his teaching.

school-c6-social-b.title: Class 6 Social Science · Exploring Society: India and Beyond (Part B: Ch 8–14 & revision)
school-c6-social-b.description: Every chapter of Class 6 Social Science (Exploring Society: India and Beyond, NCERT 2024 edition onward) — geography, history, culture, governance and economics — in original words with activities, quizzes, chapter tests and mock papers.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'
courses.summary: India's rich diversity — food, clothing and textiles, festivals, languages and arts — and the threads that bind it into one: shared stories like the Ramayana and Mahabharata told in many languages, shared values and the idea of 'many in the One'.
outcomes: Learners can give examples of diversity in food, clothing, festivals and languages
Learners can explain how shared stories and values create unity
Learners can describe regional versions of epics and harvest festivals
Learners can show respect for differences in daily life

scenes.text: Class 6 holds a tiffin festival — each child brings a home dish.
Poha from Indore, appam from Kerala, thepla from Gujarat, momos from Sikkim.
Some wear traditional clothes: a Mekhela sador, a Nauvari sari, a phiran.
Different tastes, one happy class.

steps.title: Food
steps.body: Climate and local crops shape food: rice and fish in the east and coasts, wheat breads in the north, millets in dry areas, coconut in Kerala. Yet many ideas are shared — dal, rice/roti, seasonal vegetables, pickles, sweets at festivals.

steps.title: Clothing and textiles
steps.body: The **sari** is draped in dozens of styles across regions. India's handloom traditions: **Banarasi** (Varanasi), **Kanjivaram** (Tamil Nadu), **Pochampally ikat** (Telangana), **Muga silk** (Assam), **Pashmina** (Kashmir), **Bandhani** (Gujarat/Rajasthan). Unstitched garments like dhoti and sari are common in many regions.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why is coconut used widely in Kerala's food?

- Coconut palms grow abundantly in its coastal climate.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Name two famous silk saris from different states.

- **Kanjivaram** (Tamil Nadu) and **Banarasi** (Uttar Pradesh).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all Indians eat the same food or wear the same clothes.
- Making fun of others' food — every cuisine reflects its environment.

activity.prompt: Match the textile to its region.

quiz.why: Food habits depend largely on climate and the crops that grow locally. That is why people in different regions eat different things.
Muga silk, golden in colour, comes from Assam. It is not from Punjab, Goa or Bihar.
The sari is an unstitched cloth that is draped in many regional styles. It is not stitched like trousers.
Millets are drought-hardy, so they are common in dry regions. They need little water.
Respecting what others eat shows good manners and helps unity. Mocking someone's food is rude.

scenes.text: In January, Harpreet lights a Lohri bonfire in Punjab.
Her cousin in Tamil Nadu boils new rice for Pongal.
In Gujarat, friends fly kites on Uttarayan; in Assam, people feast at Magh Bihu.
All celebrate the harvest and the Sun.

steps.title: Festivals
steps.body: Festivals mark seasons, harvests and stories: around mid-January — **Makar Sankranti**, **Pongal**, **Lohri**, **Magh/Bhogali Bihu**, **Uttarayan**; in April — **Baisakhi/Vaisakhi**, **Bohag Bihu**, **Vishu**, **Puthandu**; **Onam** in Kerala (Aug–Sept). Many festivals of different faiths are celebrated together by neighbours.

steps.title: Languages
steps.body: India has hundreds of languages and many scripts. The Constitution's **Eighth Schedule** lists **22 languages**. Many Indians are bilingual or multilingual, and languages borrow words from each other.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
What is common to Pongal, Lohri and Bihu?

- They are **harvest festivals** celebrated around the same time of year.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How many languages are in the Eighth Schedule?

- **22**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking India has one or two languages only.
- Thinking festivals belong only to one community — many are shared across communities.

quiz.why: Pongal, a harvest festival, is celebrated in Tamil Nadu in mid-January.
There are 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.
Lohri is a harvest festival of Punjab, celebrated with bonfires in January.
