Onam is the harvest festival of Kerala. It is not from Gujarat, Assam or Bengal.
Many Indians speak more than one language, which shows India's multilingual nature.

lessons.title: Shared stories: the epics in many voices

scenes.text: Nani in Bengal reads the Krittivasi Ramayan.
In Kerala, Kathakali dancers perform episodes from the epics.
In Varanasi, the Ramlila is staged from Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas.
One story, told in many languages and art forms.

steps.title: Epics everywhere
steps.body: The **Ramayana** and **Mahabharata** were retold in many languages: **Kamba Ramayanam** (Tamil, Kamban), **Krittivasi Ramayan** (Bengali), **Ramcharitmanas** (Awadhi, Tulsidas), versions in Telugu, Kannada, Odia, Assamese, Malayalam and more; also in Southeast Asia (Thailand's Ramakien).

steps.title: Other shared stories
steps.body: The **Panchatantra** fables spread across India and the world. Jataka tales (Buddhist) and folk tales carry common values: honesty, courage, kindness, duty.

steps.title: Many in the One
steps.body: Each region adds its own flavour, yet the shared stories and values connect people — this is **unity in diversity**.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Who wrote the Ramcharitmanas and in which language?

- **Tulsidas**, in **Awadhi**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How do shared stories create unity?

- People across regions know the same characters and values, giving a common cultural language.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking there is only one 'correct' version of the epics — many versions coexist.

activity.prompt: Match the retelling to its language.

quiz.why: Kamba Ramayanam is the Ramayana written by Kamban in Tamil.
Ramcharitmanas was written by Tulsidas, in Awadhi. Valmiki wrote the Sanskrit Ramayana and Kamban the Tamil one.
The Panchatantra is a collection of fables, mostly animal stories with morals. It is not a law book or a map.
The Ramakien is the Thai version of the Ramayana. It shows how the story travelled beyond India.
Many versions of the epics in different languages show creativity and a shared culture. They are not mistakes.

scenes.text: Lalremsiami joins a school in Pune.
Some kids ask odd questions about her looks and food.
Aarav invites her to lunch and asks about Mizo festivals.
Soon the class learns Chapchar Kut dance steps.

steps.title: Respect
steps.body: Diversity is a strength when we are curious, kind and fair. Stereotypes ('all people from X are …') are unfair and hurtful.

steps.title: Values that unite
steps.body: Our Constitution guarantees equality and freedom of religion and expression; shared values include respect for elders, hospitality ('Atithi Devo Bhava'), and the idea **Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam** ('the world is one family').

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
What should you do if a classmate is teased for their accent?

- Stand with them, tell the teaser it's hurtful, and inform a teacher if it continues.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Give an example of 'many in the One' in your school.

- An assembly where students greet in different languages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Laughing at accents, names or food.
- Thinking 'unity' means everyone must become the same.

a.text: A new classmate from another state brings unfamiliar food. Some kids say it smells 'weird'. What do you do?

choices.label: Laugh along
choices.feedback: This hurts your classmate and spreads prejudice.

choices.label: Ask about the dish and sit with them

b.text: Your classmate eats alone and feels unwelcome. Later you realise you could have helped. You can still apologise and invite them tomorrow.

c.text: You learn it's a festival dish from their home. Next week, the class holds a 'food from home' day. Everyone feels included.

quiz.why: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam means 'the world is one family'. It is a phrase from the Maha Upanishad.

options: an unfair fixed idea about a group
quiz.why: A stereotype is an unfair, fixed idea about a group of people. It is not a fact, and it ignores individual differences.
Unity in diversity means people stay different in language, food and faith, yet live together. It does not mean everyone becomes the same.
Atithi Devo Bhava means 'the guest is like God'. It stands for treating guests with respect.

quiz.q: Best response to teasing about accent?
quiz.why: If someone is teased about their accent, the right response is to support them and report it. Joining in or laughing hurts them.

questions.q: Harvest festival of Tamil Nadu?
questions.why: Pongal is the harvest festival of Tamil Nadu. Onam is from Kerala, Bihu from Assam and Lohri from Punjab.

questions.q: Number of languages in the Eighth Schedule?
questions.why: The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages.

questions.q: Kanjivaram saris are from …
questions.why: Kanjivaram silk saris come from Kanchipuram in Tamil Nadu.

questions.q: Ramcharitmanas is in …
questions.why: The Ramcharitmanas by Tulsidas is written in Awadhi, a language of eastern Uttar Pradesh.

questions.q: Bihu is celebrated in …
questions.why: Bihu is the festival of Assam, celebrated at harvest and new year times.

questions.q: Panchatantra stories are …
questions.why: The Panchatantra stories are fables with animal characters and a lesson. They are not laws or epics.

questions.q: 'The world is one family' is …
questions.why: 'The world is one family' is Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam. Satyameva Jayate means 'truth alone triumphs'.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Food differs across India. Reason (R): Climate and local crops vary.
questions.why: Both are true: food differs across India because climate and local crops vary. The reason explains the differences.

questions.q: Which epic retelling is Bengali?
questions.why: The Krittivasi Ramayan is the Bengali retelling of the Ramayana. Ramcharitmanas is in Awadhi and Kamba Ramayanam in Tamil.

questions.q: Lohri, Pongal and Magh Bihu all fall around …
questions.why: Lohri, Pongal and Magh Bihu are harvest festivals celebrated around mid-January. They have different names in different regions.

questions.q: Pochampally ikat is from …
questions.why: Pochampally ikat, a type of woven cloth, is from Telangana.

questions.q: Case: A school celebrates festivals of all students' families. This reflects …
questions.why: A school celebrating the festivals of all students' families shows that differences are welcome. That is unity in diversity.

questions.q: Case: Kathakali performs Mahabharata episodes in Kerala, and Ramlila stages the Ramayana in UP. This shows …
options: shared stories in regional art forms
questions.why: Kathakali and Ramlila both retell epic stories in regional art forms. So people share stories while presenting them differently.

questions.q: Which statement is FALSE?
options: All Indians eat the same food
Saris are draped in many styles
questions.why: All Indians do not eat the same food, as it varies with region and climate. So this statement is false.

questions.q: Why do stereotypes harm unity?
options: They judge people unfairly by group
questions.why: Stereotypes judge people unfairly because of the group they belong to. This breaks friendship and unity.

questions.q: Case: Words like 'roti', 'chai' and 'kitab' are used in many Indian languages. This shows …
questions.why: Words like roti, chai and kitab are used in many Indian languages. This shows that languages borrow and share words.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Family and Community
courses.summary: What families are and the many forms they take, roles, care and values learned at home, the community around us and how people cooperate, and the idea of the world as one family.
outcomes: Learners can describe different kinds of families and their roles
Learners can explain values learned in families such as care, sharing and respect
Learners can describe how communities cooperate and support one another
Learners can link family and community values to wider society

scenes.text: Every Sunday, Meher's whole family gathers at her grandparents' house.
Uncles cook, cousins set the table, Dadi tells stories.
Meher's friend lives with just her mother — also a loving family.
Families come in many shapes.

steps.title: Kinds of families
steps.body:
- **Joint / extended family**: grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and cousins living together
- **Nuclear family**: parents (or one parent) and children
- Single-parent families, families with adopted children, families where grandparents raise children — all are families

steps.title: Roles
steps.body: Members care for each other: earning, cooking, cleaning, caring for children, the elderly and the sick, teaching values. Sharing housework fairly — among men, women and children — is important.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Give one advantage each of joint and nuclear families.

- Joint: more people to share work and care. Nuclear: more space and independence.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How can children help at home?

- Tidy their things, help in cooking or shopping, care for younger siblings or elders.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only one type is a 'real' family.
- Thinking housework is only for women.

items.text: Parents and two children in a flat
Grandparents, parents, uncle's family under one roof

quiz.why: A joint family includes grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins living together. A nuclear family has only parents and children.

quiz.q: A single mother and her children are …
quiz.why: A single mother and her children are a family. A family is not defined by having two parents.
Housework should be shared fairly among family members. It should not fall on women alone.
Families teach values like care and respect, which we carry through life. They teach more than rules.

quiz.q: Caring for elders is a role of …
quiz.why: Caring for elders is a role of family members. Doctors help only with health.

scenes.text: There's one mango left and three children.
Mother cuts it into three equal parts.
Little Ravi offers his piece to Grandpa.
Sharing and respect are learned at home.

steps.title: Family values
steps.body: Care, sharing, respect for elders, honesty, responsibility, hard work, gratitude and forgiveness. These shape how we behave outside the home too.

steps.title: Traditions
steps.body: Stories, festivals, recipes, songs passed down generations give a sense of belonging.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
How does sharing at home help in school?

- Children who share learn to cooperate in groups and make friends.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
What tradition might a family pass on?

- A festival recipe, a lullaby, a family story.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking values are taught only by lecturing — mostly by example.

activity.prompt: Which value did you learn at home that you are proud of? Describe a moment you used it.
activity.hint: Think of sharing, honesty, helping, respecting elders …

quiz.why: Values are mostly learned by watching others and doing things ourselves, such as seeing elders be kind.

quiz.q: Offering your share to an elder shows …
quiz.why: Offering your share to an elder shows respect and care. It is not greed.

quiz.q: Passing a recipe down generations is a …
quiz.why: Passing a recipe down the generations is a tradition. A tradition is a custom handed down in a family or community.
Gratitude means being thankful to those who help us.
Responsibility at home means doing your own tasks, like keeping your things tidy. Blaming others avoids responsibility.

scenes.text: The village handpump breaks in summer.
Neighbours meet and collect money and tools.
A mason fixes it; children carry water meanwhile.
Together, the community solves the problem.

steps.title: Community
steps.body: A **community** is a group of people who live in an area or share interests, and help each other: neighbours, a village, a housing society, a school community.

steps.title: Cooperation
steps.body: Communities organise festivals, clean-ups, help in disasters, run cooperatives (like milk cooperatives — Amul began as one in Gujarat), community kitchens (langar at gurdwaras).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
How do communities help during floods?

- Shelter, food, rescue, sharing boats, collecting relief.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
What is a langar?

- A community kitchen at gurdwaras serving free meals to all, regardless of background.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking problems must always wait for government — communities can act too (with authorities).

items: I learned the names of 3 neighbours
I helped in a clean-up or sapling planting
I thanked a community worker (sweeper, guard, postman)
I shared books or toys I don't use

options: people who live together or share interests and help each other
quiz.why: A community is a group of people who live together or share interests and help each other. It is larger than a family.
Langar is a free community kitchen run at gurdwaras, where everyone eats together. It is not a tax or a game.
Amul began as a milk cooperative of farmers in Gujarat. It is owned by the farmers, not by one person.
Cooperation means working together for a shared goal. Competing or fighting is the opposite.
During disasters, communities help each other with food, shelter and rescue. That shows community spirit.

scenes.text: After an earthquake abroad, Indian rescue teams fly out to help.
Students collect blankets for people in need.
Teacher writes 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' on the board.
Care that starts at home can reach the world.

steps.title: Widening circles
steps.body: Family → neighbourhood → village/town → state → nation → world. The same values of care and respect apply at every level.

steps.title: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam
steps.body: An ancient phrase meaning **the world is one family** — India used 'One Earth, One Family, One Future' as the theme of its G20 presidency (2023).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
How can a student act on 'the world is one family'?

- Respect people of all backgrounds, help in relief drives, care for the environment.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why is caring for the environment a 'family' duty?

- Everyone shares the Earth; our actions affect others and future generations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking care stops at our own family.

activity.prompt: Arrange from smallest circle to largest.

options: One Earth, One Family, One Future
quiz.why: India's G20 presidency in 2023 had the theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future'. It is based on Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam.

options: at every level from family to world
quiz.why: Values like care apply at every level, from family to community to the whole world. They are not limited to school or home.

quiz.q: Helping in a relief drive shows …
quiz.why: Helping in a relief drive shows care for others. It is not indifference, fear or greed.
The circles widen from family to village to state to world, and the world is the largest circle.
Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam is an ancient Indian phrase meaning 'the world is one family'. It is not a city, law or festival.

questions.q: A nuclear family usually has …
questions.why: A nuclear family usually has parents and their children. A joint family also has grandparents and cousins.

questions.q: A community kitchen at gurdwaras?
questions.why: A community kitchen at a gurdwara is called a langar, where free meals are served to all.

questions.q: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam means …
questions.why: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam means 'the world is one family'. Satyameva Jayate means truth wins.

questions.q: Housework should be shared …
questions.why: Housework should be shared fairly by all members. It should not fall only on mothers or daughters.

questions.q: Amul is an example of a …
questions.why: Amul is a cooperative owned by milk producers. It is not a government ministry or a private palace.

questions.q: Values are best taught by …
questions.why: Values are best taught by example, since children copy what they see. Shouting or fines do not teach values well.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Communities can solve local problems together. Reason (R): Cooperation pools people's skills and resources.
questions.why: Both are true: communities can solve local problems together because cooperation pools skills and resources. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is NOT a type of family?
questions.why: Nuclear, joint and single-parent are types of families. A cricket team is a group, not a family.

questions.q: Case: After a cyclone, neighbours share food and shelter. This shows …
questions.why: Neighbours sharing food and shelter after a cyclone shows community cooperation. It is the opposite of isolation or selfishness.

questions.q: Case: A grandmother teaches grandchildren a folk song. This passes on …
questions.why: A grandmother teaching a folk song passes on a tradition. Traditions are handed down through generations.

questions.q: One advantage of joint families?
options: more people share care and work
questions.why: In a joint family, more people share care and work. This helps children and elders.

questions.q: Case: A student says families with one parent are 'incomplete'. Best response?
options: Explain all loving families are real families
questions.why: A family with one parent can still be loving and complete. The best reply is to explain that all loving families are real families.

questions.q: India's G20 presidency year?
questions.why: India held the G20 presidency in 2023, with the theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future'.

questions.q: Which shows care at the world level?
options: Sending disaster relief to another country
questions.why: Sending disaster relief to another country shows care at the world level. Littering, fighting and wasting water do not.

questions.q: Why do family values matter for society?
options: People carry them into schools, workplaces and communities
questions.why: Family values matter for society because people carry them into schools, workplaces and communities. So good values at home spread outward.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Grassroots Democracy — Part 1: Governance
courses.summary: What government and governance mean, democracy and the right to vote, the three levels of government (Union, State, Local) and the three organs — legislature, executive and judiciary — with the separation of powers.
outcomes: Learners can explain what government does and why rules are needed
Learners can describe democracy and universal adult franchise
Learners can name the three levels of government and give examples of their work
Learners can explain the roles of the legislature, executive and judiciary

scenes.text: At break, two groups both want the football field.
Pushing starts; nobody gets to play.
The class monitor calls a vote and a timetable is made.
Rules decided together bring order — that's governance.

steps.title: Government and governance
steps.body: A **government** is the system that makes decisions and rules for a country, state or local area and carries them out — roads, schools, hospitals, security, water, justice. **Governance** is how these decisions are made and implemented.

steps.title: Democracy
steps.body: In a **democracy**, people choose their representatives through **elections**. India follows **universal adult franchise**: every citizen aged **18 or above** can vote, regardless of religion, caste, gender, wealth or education. Elections are held regularly (usually every 5 years) and votes are secret.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why are rules needed?

- To keep order, protect rights and settle disputes fairly.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Who can vote in India?

- Citizens aged **18+** registered as voters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking democracy means 'anyone can do anything' — it means rule by people through fair rules.
- Thinking only educated or rich people can vote.

statements.s: In India, citizens aged 18 and above can vote.
Only property owners can vote.
Votes in Indian elections are secret.
Government provides services like roads and schools.

quiz.why: The voting age in India is 18. At 18 a citizen can vote in elections.
Universal adult franchise means all adult citizens can vote, whatever their wealth, gender or caste.
In a democracy people choose their representatives by voting. They are not ruled by a king alone.
Elections in India are usually held every 5 years. After that the people can choose again.

options: how decisions are made and carried out
quiz.why: Governance is how decisions are made and carried out. It is not a festival or a game.

scenes.text: A pothole appears in Nidhi's lane.
Her uncle complains about a train delay.
Her aunt visits a state-run hospital.
Each problem is handled by a different level of government!

steps.title: Levels
steps.body:
- **Union (Central) government**: whole country — defence, railways, currency, foreign affairs; led by the Prime Minister; Parliament in New Delhi
- **State government**: a state — police, state roads, hospitals, school education (shared); led by the Chief Minister; State Legislative Assembly
- **Local government**: villages (panchayats) and towns/cities (municipalities) — water, sanitation, streetlights, local roads

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Who handles a broken streetlight in a city lane?

- **Local government** (municipality).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Who prints currency notes?

- **Union** (through the Reserve Bank of India).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Writing to the Prime Minister for a broken streetlight — go to the local body first.

quiz.why: The Prime Minister is the head of the Union government. The Chief Minister heads a State government and the Sarpanch a village.
The Chief Minister is the head of a State government. The Prime Minister heads the Union government.
Defence is a Union subject, handled by the Union government for the whole country. States do not run the army.
Streetlights in towns are looked after by local government, such as the municipality.
Parliament sits in New Delhi, the national capital.

lessons.title: Three organs and separation of powers

scenes.text: Parliament passes a law to make helmets compulsory for two-wheeler riders.
Traffic police enforce it and issue fines.
A rider who feels wrongly fined goes to court.
Three organs, three jobs.

steps.title: Organs of government
steps.body:
- **Legislature**: makes laws (Parliament at the Union; Legislative Assemblies in states)
- **Executive**: implements laws and runs the government (Prime Minister/Chief Minister with ministers, and officials like police and civil servants)
- **Judiciary**: interprets laws, settles disputes, protects rights (courts — Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in states, lower courts)

steps.title: Separation of powers
steps.body: Each organ has its own role and checks the others so that no one has unlimited power. Courts are independent.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
A new road-safety rule is passed, enforced and challenged. Match organs.

- Passed → legislature; enforced → executive; challenge heard → judiciary.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why must courts be independent?

- To judge fairly even when the government is a party.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the police make laws — they enforce them.
- Thinking judges make laws — they interpret and apply them.

activity.prompt: Match the organ to its job.

quiz.why: The legislature makes laws, such as Parliament. The executive carries them out and the judiciary settles disputes.
The police enforce laws, so they are part of the executive. The legislature makes laws and the judiciary decides cases.
The Supreme Court is the highest court of India.

options: any one organ having all power
quiz.why: Separation of powers prevents any one organ of government from having all the power. This protects against misuse.
Disputes are settled by courts, which are the judiciary. Parliament makes laws.

scenes.text: Kiran's colony has had no water for a week.
Her father files a written complaint at the municipal office and gets a receipt number.
He follows up on the city's grievance portal.
Repairs start in three days. Citizens make governance work.

steps.title: Good governance
steps.body: Governments should be **transparent** (open about decisions), **accountable** (answerable to people), **responsive**, fair and efficient.

steps.title: Citizens' role
steps.body:
- Vote in every election (when 18+)
- Follow laws, pay taxes
- Raise problems through proper channels: complaints, grievance portals, gram sabha / ward meetings
- The **Right to Information Act, 2005** lets citizens ask government offices for information
- Respect others' rights; take part in community work

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
How can a citizen find out how money for a village road was spent?

- File an **RTI** application or ask at the gram sabha.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why should complaints be written?

- They create a record and can be followed up.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking governance is only the government's job — citizens' participation is essential.

items: I know who my local representative is
I can name one way to file a complaint
I follow traffic and safety rules
I encourage adults at home to vote

quiz.why: The Right to Information (RTI) Act was passed in 2005. It lets citizens ask for government information.
An accountable government is answerable to the people. It must explain and justify its actions.

quiz.q: A way to raise a local problem?
quiz.why: A written complaint or a grievance portal is the proper way to raise a local problem. Vandalism or shouting on the road is not.
Good citizens vote, follow the laws and take part in community life. Ignoring elections or avoiding taxes harms democracy.
Transparency means openness about decisions, so people can see how things are done. Hiding information is the opposite.

questions.q: Voting age in India?
questions.why: The voting age in India is 18. The age used to be 21 until it was lowered in 1989.

questions.q: Laws are made by the …
questions.why: The legislature makes the laws. The executive carries them out and the judiciary applies them in cases.

questions.q: Courts belong to the …
questions.why: Courts belong to the judiciary, which settles disputes and checks that laws are followed.

questions.q: Railways are run by the … government
questions.why: Railways run across the whole country, so they are run by the Union government.

questions.q: Chief Minister heads the … government
questions.why: A Chief Minister heads a State government.

questions.q: Universal adult franchise means …
questions.why: Universal adult franchise means every adult citizen has the right to vote. It does not depend on money, gender or education.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Courts must be independent. Reason (R): They often judge cases involving the government.
questions.why: Both are true: courts must be independent because they often judge cases involving the government. They need to be fair and free from pressure.

questions.q: Garbage collection in a city is handled by …
questions.why: Garbage collection in a city is done by the municipality, the local government. It is not a job for the army or Parliament.

questions.q: Which is an executive action?
questions.why: Enforcing a rule, like the helmet rule, is done by the police, which belong to the executive. Debating a bill is legislature and hearing a case is judiciary.

questions.q: Case: A citizen thinks a new law violates her rights. She should approach …
questions.why: A citizen who thinks a law violates her rights can approach a court. Courts are the judiciary that protects rights.

questions.q: Separation of powers means …
options: each organ has its role and checks others
questions.why: Separation of powers means each organ has its own role and checks the others. So no one can control everything.

questions.q: Case: A village needs a new handpump. First approach?
questions.why: A village's first approach is to the gram panchayat, the local government. It looks after local needs like handpumps.

questions.q: Which is NOT a function of government?
questions.why: Governments provide roads, run schools and maintain law and order. Choosing your friends is a personal choice.

questions.q: Why does India hold regular elections?
options: So people can choose and change representatives
questions.why: Regular elections let people choose and also change their representatives. This keeps the government accountable.

questions.q: Which pair is wrong?
questions.why: The judiciary settles disputes and does not collect taxes. That is done by the executive.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Grassroots Democracy — Part 2: Local Government in Rural Areas
courses.summary: Panchayati Raj in villages: the gram sabha, gram panchayat and sarpanch, the three tiers (gram panchayat, panchayat samiti, zila parishad), the 73rd Constitutional Amendment, reservation for women and others, and how panchayats work for people.
outcomes: Learners can explain the roles of the gram sabha and gram panchayat
Learners can describe the three-tier Panchayati Raj system
Learners can state key facts about the 73rd Amendment
Learners can describe how villagers participate and hold panchayats accountable

scenes.text: Under the big banyan tree, villagers of Hardi gather for the gram sabha.
Women ask for a new handpump near their homes; farmers ask about canal water.
The sarpanch reads out last year's spending.
Everyone 18+ on the voters' list can speak and vote here.

steps.title: Gram sabha
steps.body: All adults (**18+**) whose names are on the village voters' list form the **gram sabha**. It meets regularly to discuss plans, approve the budget, choose beneficiaries of schemes, and check the panchayat's work — the base of grassroots democracy.

steps.title: Gram panchayat
steps.body: An elected body for a village or group of villages: **ward members (panch)** and a head — **sarpanch/pradhan/mukhiya**. A **panchayat secretary** (appointed by the government) keeps records. Elections every **5 years**, conducted by the **State Election Commission**.

steps.title: Work of the panchayat
steps.body: Drinking water, village roads, drains, streetlights, cleanliness, public buildings, implementing schemes (housing, employment like MGNREGA work), registering births and deaths. Funds come from taxes (house/market), government grants and schemes.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Who can attend the gram sabha?

- Every adult (18+) on the village voters' list.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Who keeps panchayat records?

- The **secretary**, appointed by the state government.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Confusing the gram sabha (all adult voters) with the gram panchayat (elected representatives).

pairs: All adult voters of the village

options: all adult voters of the village
quiz.why: The gram sabha includes all adult voters of the village. It is not limited to the sarpanch or to men.
The sarpanch is the head of the gram panchayat. A mayor heads a city and a collector heads a district.
Panchayat elections are held every 5 years.
Panchayat elections are conducted by the State Election Commission. The Election Commission of India handles Parliament and State assembly elections.
A panchayat looks after village roads and water. Currency, foreign policy and defence belong to the Union government.

scenes.text: Hardi's panchayat can repair its well, but a bridge across the river connects 12 villages.
The block-level panchayat samiti plans the bridge.
The zila parishad at the district approves funds.
Three tiers work together.

steps.title: The three tiers
steps.body:
- **Gram panchayat** — village level
- **Panchayat samiti** (block/taluka level) — members include elected representatives; coordinates the gram panchayats of a block
- **Zila parishad** (district level) — plans and coordinates development across the district

Names vary by state (e.g., mandal parishad, taluka panchayat).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
A school building for many villages of a block is planned by …

- the **panchayat samiti**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why have three tiers?

- Some problems are village-sized, others need block- or district-level planning and money.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking the zila parishad is part of the State Assembly — it is a local body.

activity.prompt: Arrange the tiers from the smallest area to the largest.

quiz.why: The panchayat samiti is the block-level body. The gram panchayat is the village level and the zila parishad the district level.
The zila parishad is the district-level body of the panchayati raj system.
The panchayati raj system has 3 tiers: village, block and district.
The gram panchayat is the village-level body. Parliament and the High Court are not village bodies.
The names of the tiers may vary from state to state. The three-tier structure is similar.

scenes.text: Kamla Devi never thought she'd lead her village.
When the seat was reserved for women, she contested and won.
She focused on water, girls' schooling and toilets.
Today many women lead panchayats across India.

steps.title: 73rd Amendment
steps.body: The **73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992)**, in force from **24 April 1993** (celebrated as **National Panchayati Raj Day**), gave panchayats constitutional status: regular elections every 5 years, State Election Commissions, State Finance Commissions, and the three-tier system.

steps.title: Reservation
steps.body: At least **one-third** of seats (and of sarpanch posts) are reserved for **women**; many states have raised it to **50%**. Seats are also reserved for **Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes** in proportion to population.

steps.title: Making it work
steps.body: Villagers attend gram sabhas, ask questions, check accounts (social audits), and vote. Problems: 'proxy' sarpanch (a husband running affairs for an elected woman), low attendance — awareness fixes these.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
When is National Panchayati Raj Day?

- **24 April**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why reserve seats for women?

- To ensure women's voices in decisions about water, health, schooling — issues they often know best.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking panchayats existed in the Constitution from 1950 — constitutional status came in 1992–93 (village councils existed long before).

statements.s: The 73rd Amendment came into force in 1993.
At least one-third of panchayat seats are reserved for women.
Panchayat elections can be postponed forever.
Social audits help villagers check panchayat spending.

quiz.why: National Panchayati Raj Day is observed on 24 April. It marks the date the 73rd Amendment came into force.

quiz.q: Women's reservation in panchayats: at least …
quiz.why: At least one-third of panchayat seats are reserved for women. Some states have set aside more.
The 73rd Amendment to the Constitution is about rural local government, the panchayats. The 74th is about urban bodies.

options: someone else runs affairs for the elected person
quiz.why: A 'proxy sarpanch' problem is when someone else, such as a relative, runs the affairs for the elected person. It defeats the purpose of election.
A social audit checks how money was spent on public programmes. The people of the village take part in it.

questions.q: Gram sabha consists of …
options: all adult voters of the village
questions.why: The gram sabha is made up of all adult voters of the village. It is not only elected members or officers.

questions.q: Head of a gram panchayat?
questions.why: The sarpanch is the head of a gram panchayat.

questions.q: District-level panchayat body?
questions.why: The zila parishad is the district-level body. The panchayat samiti is the block level.

questions.q: Panchayat elections are conducted by …
questions.why: Panchayat elections are conducted by the State Election Commission, not by the police.

questions.q: Block-level body?
questions.why: The panchayat samiti works at the block level. The gram panchayat is the village level.

questions.q: The 73rd Amendment was passed in …
questions.why: The 73rd Amendment was passed in 1992 and came into force in 1993.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Gram sabha keeps the panchayat accountable. Reason (R): It reviews plans and spending.
questions.why: Both are true: the gram sabha reviews plans and spending, so it keeps the panchayat accountable. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Panchayat secretary is …
questions.why: The panchayat secretary is a government official appointed by the state government. The sarpanch is elected.

questions.q: Seats for SC/ST in panchayats are reserved …
questions.why: Seats for SC and ST in panchayats are reserved in proportion to their population in the area. This gives them a fair voice.

questions.q: Case: A bridge is needed to link 15 villages of a block. Best body to plan?
questions.why: A bridge linking 15 villages of a block is a block-level project, so the panchayat samiti is best placed to plan it. One gram panchayat covers only one village.

questions.q: Case: Villagers want to know how road funds were used. They can …
options: raise it in gram sabha or file an RTI
questions.why: Villagers can raise the question in the gram sabha or file an RTI application to learn how funds were used. Vandalism does not help.

questions.q: Which is NOT a function of a gram panchayat?
questions.why: Printing currency is done by the Union government. Water supply, street lighting and registering births are local tasks.

questions.q: National Panchayati Raj Day marks the date …
questions.why: National Panchayati Raj Day marks 24 April 1993, when the 73rd Amendment came into force.

questions.q: Case: A woman sarpanch's husband attends meetings and decides for her. Why is this a problem?
options: It defeats the purpose of women's reservation
questions.why: If her husband decides for her, the woman sarpanch is not really using her power. This defeats the purpose of women's reservation.

questions.q: Correct order of tiers (lowest to highest)?
options: gram panchayat → panchayat samiti → zila parishad
questions.why: From lowest to highest the tiers are gram panchayat (village), panchayat samiti (block) and zila parishad (district).

courses.title: Ch 12 · Grassroots Democracy — Part 3: Local Government in Urban Areas
courses.summary: How towns and cities govern themselves: municipal corporations, municipal councils and nagar panchayats, wards and councillors, the mayor and commissioner, the 74th Amendment, the services urban local bodies provide, how they raise money, and how citizens take part.
outcomes: Learners can name the types of urban local bodies
Learners can explain the roles of ward councillors, mayor and commissioner
Learners can list services provided and sources of funds
Learners can describe how citizens raise and solve civic issues

scenes.text: Priya lives in Bengaluru — a huge city with a municipal corporation.
Her cousin in a smaller town has a municipal council.
Another cousin's growing town, once a village, has a nagar panchayat.
The size of the town decides the type of body.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Municipal Corporation (Nagar Nigam)** — large cities (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru …)
- **Municipal Council (Nagar Palika / municipality)** — smaller cities and towns
- **Nagar Panchayat** — areas changing from rural to urban

Cities are divided into **wards**; each ward elects a **councillor** (corporator).

steps.title: 74th Amendment
steps.body: The **74th Constitutional Amendment (1992)**, in force from **1 June 1993**, gave urban local bodies constitutional status: regular elections every 5 years, reservation of seats for women (at least one-third), SCs and STs.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which body governs Mumbai?

- A **municipal corporation** (Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
What is a ward?

- A smaller area of a city that elects its own councillor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Confusing the 73rd (rural) and 74th (urban) Amendments.

quiz.why: Large cities have a municipal corporation. Smaller towns have a municipality, and transitional areas a nagar panchayat.

quiz.q: City areas that elect councillors are …
quiz.why: A city is divided into wards, and each ward elects a councillor.
The 74th Amendment is about urban local bodies. The 73rd is about panchayats.
Areas changing from rural to urban (transitional areas) have a nagar panchayat.

quiz.q: Women's reservation in urban bodies: at least …
quiz.why: At least one-third of seats in urban local bodies are reserved for women.

story.title: Who's in charge of the city?

scenes.text: The mayor cuts a ribbon at a new park.
The municipal commissioner, a senior officer, oversees the departments.
Ward councillor Mr. Khan listens to residents' complaints.
Elected leaders decide; officials implement.

steps.title: Elected wing
steps.body: Ward **councillors** form the council; they discuss and decide on budgets and policies, raise ward problems. The **mayor** (in corporations) or **chairperson/president** (in councils) heads the council (chosen directly or indirectly depending on the state).

steps.title: Administrative wing
steps.body: The **municipal commissioner** (often an IAS officer, appointed by the state) and staff — engineers, health officers, sanitation workers — **implement** decisions. Committees (water, health, works) handle specific tasks.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
A resident's street has overflowing drains. Who to approach first?

- The **ward councillor** or the ward office/helpline.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Who prepares and implements the budget's works?

- The **commissioner** and departments, after council approval.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking the mayor personally fixes every pothole — departments do the work.

pairs: Handle specific areas like water or health

quiz.why: A ward councillor is elected by the people of the ward. Courts do not appoint councillors.
The municipal commissioner is an appointed official, a government officer. Councillors and mayors are elected.
The mayor heads the municipal corporation council of a city.
Elected leaders mainly decide policies, such as what the city will spend on.
Officials mainly carry out the decisions made by elected leaders. They do not make laws or win elections.

scenes.text: Garbage piles up near Asha's colony market.
Residents report it on the municipal app with photos.
They also start segregating wet and dry waste.
The spot becomes a small garden.

steps.title: Services
steps.body: Water supply, sewerage and drains, solid waste management, street lighting, roads and footpaths, parks, public health and dispensaries, fire services, primary schools (in many cities), birth and death certificates, building permissions, markets.

steps.title: Money
steps.body: **Property tax**, water charges, fees for licences and permissions, advertisement fees, and grants from state and Union governments.

steps.title: Citizens' role
steps.body: Pay taxes, segregate waste, avoid littering, save water, report problems on helplines/apps, attend ward/area sabhas where they exist, vote in municipal elections.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Name two sources of a municipality's income.

- **Property tax** and **water charges** (also grants).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How does waste segregation help the city?

- Wet waste can be composted; dry waste recycled; less goes to landfills.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking services are 'free' — they are paid for by taxes and charges.
- Leaving sanitation workers to handle unsegregated, sharp or hazardous waste.

items: I separate wet and dry waste at home
I never litter or spit in public
I report a civic problem through the proper channel
I save water and switch off unused lights
I thank the sanitation workers in my area

quiz.why: The main tax of municipalities is property tax, paid by owners of buildings and land.

quiz.q: Birth certificates in cities are issued by …
quiz.why: Birth certificates in cities are issued by the municipality, a local government body.
Segregating waste means separating wet and dry waste, which makes recycling and disposal easier.
Municipal services are paid for by taxes, user charges and grants from the state and Union governments. They cannot run on donations alone.
A good citizen duty in cities is to avoid littering, to keep public places clean. Parking anywhere or wasting water harms others.

questions.q: Large cities are governed by a …
questions.why: Large cities are governed by a municipal corporation. A gram panchayat is for villages and a zila parishad for districts.

questions.q: City areas electing councillors?
questions.why: A city is divided into wards, and each ward elects one councillor. Villages and blocks belong to rural government.

questions.q: 74th Amendment is about …
questions.why: The 74th Amendment is about urban local government. The 73rd is about rural panchayats.

questions.q: Main source of municipal income?
questions.why: The main source of municipal income is property tax, paid on land and buildings. Income tax and customs go to the Union government.

questions.q: The commissioner is …
questions.why: The municipal commissioner is an appointed government official who carries out the council's decisions. Councillors are the elected members.

questions.q: A nagar panchayat is for …
options: areas changing from rural to urban
questions.why: A nagar panchayat is for areas changing from rural to urban. Mega-cities have municipal corporations.

questions.q: 74th Amendment came into force on …
questions.why: The 74th Amendment came into force on 1 June 1993. The 73rd came into force on 24 April 1993.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Waste segregation reduces landfill load. Reason (R): Wet waste can be composted and dry waste recycled.
questions.why: Both are true: segregating waste lets wet waste be composted and dry waste recycled, so less goes to landfill. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is NOT a municipal service?
questions.why: Water supply, parks and streetlights are municipal services. Defence is run by the Union government.

questions.q: Who heads a municipal corporation council?
questions.why: The mayor heads the council of a municipal corporation. A sarpanch heads a village panchayat.

questions.q: Case: A colony's drain overflows for days. Best first step?
options: Complain to the ward councillor / civic helpline
questions.why: A blocked drain is a local problem, so the first step is to complain to the ward councillor or the civic helpline. Writing to the President or blocking roads does not help.

questions.q: Case: A city's budget for new parks is approved by councillors and built by engineers. This shows …
options: elected wing decides, administrative wing implements
questions.why: Councillors decide the budget and plans, and engineers build the parks. So the elected wing decides and the administrative wing carries out.

questions.q: Difference between the 73rd and 74th Amendments?
options: 73rd for rural panchayats, 74th for urban bodies
questions.why: The 73rd Amendment is for rural panchayats and the 74th is for urban local bodies. Both are about local government, not Parliament or courts.

questions.q: Case: A town wants more money for water pipelines. Possible source?
options: State grant or higher water charges
questions.why: A town can get money for pipelines through a state grant or by raising water charges. Customs duty and currency printing are not for municipalities.

questions.q: Why should citizens vote in municipal elections?
options: Councillors decide local services that affect daily life
questions.why: Councillors decide local services like water, roads and waste, which affect daily life. So citizens should vote in municipal elections.

courses.title: Ch 13 · The Value of Work
courses.summary: Why people work, economic and non-economic activities, paid and unpaid work (including care work at home), the dignity of all work, volunteering and seva, and how work creates value for people and society.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish economic from non-economic activities
Learners can recognise unpaid care work and its value
Learners can explain the dignity of labour
Learners can give examples of volunteering and community service

scenes.text: Rekha cooks in a restaurant and earns a salary.
At home in the evening, she cooks dinner for her family — no pay.
Same work, but one is paid.
Economists call the first an economic activity.

steps.title: Economic activities
steps.body: Activities done to **earn money (income)** or produce goods and services for sale/exchange — farming for the market, working in a factory, teaching in a school, running a shop, driving a taxi.

steps.title: Non-economic activities
steps.body: Activities done out of love, care, duty or social/religious reasons **without payment** — cooking for one's family, caring for a sick relative, helping a neighbour, volunteering, prayer.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
A doctor treats patients at her clinic and also treats her son at home. Classify.

- Clinic: **economic**; at home: **non-economic**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
A farmer grows vegetables to sell at the mandi. Classify.

- **Economic**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking non-economic activities are unimportant — they are essential to life.
- Classifying by the type of work instead of the purpose (paid or not).

items.text: Teacher teaching in school for salary
Mother helping her child with homework
Volunteering at a blood donation camp

quiz.why: Economic activities are done to earn income, such as a job or business. Sleeping and praying are not done for income.
Cooking for one's own family without pay is a non-economic activity. It is not done to earn income.

quiz.q: A bus driver driving for wages is …
quiz.why: A bus driver drives for wages, so the activity is economic.
What decides the category is the purpose: whether the work is done to earn or not. Time, place or clothes do not matter.
Volunteering is done without pay, so it is non-economic.

lessons.title: Unpaid care work and dignity of labour

scenes.text: Arjun lists everything done at home in a day.
Cooking, cleaning, washing, shopping, caring for Dadi, helping with homework.
His mother and grandmother do most of it — unpaid.
Arjun decides to share some tasks.

steps.title: Unpaid care work
steps.body: Household and care work — cooking, cleaning, fetching water, caring for children, the elderly and the sick — is often done by women and girls without pay. It is real **work** that keeps families and the economy running, though it is not counted in GDP.

steps.title: Dignity of labour
steps.body: All honest work deserves **respect** — sanitation workers, farmers, domestic workers, porters, engineers, teachers. Mahatma Gandhi stressed doing one's own cleaning and respecting manual work.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why should unpaid care work be shared?

- It's fair, gives everyone time to study, work and rest, and teaches life skills.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Give an example of showing dignity of labour.

- Greeting and thanking the sanitation worker; not littering to make their work harder.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling some jobs 'low' — every job contributes.
- Saying a homemaker 'does nothing'.

activity.prompt: List the unpaid work done in your home in one day. Who does most of it? What one task will you take on?
activity.hint: Think of cooking, cleaning, water, shopping, care for elders and children.

options: caring for the elderly at home
quiz.why: Caring for the elderly at home is unpaid care work. Working in a bank, driving a taxi and selling vegetables are paid jobs.
Dignity of labour means respecting all honest work, whether manual or office work. No job should be looked down on.

quiz.q: Unpaid care work is often done by …
quiz.why: In most homes, unpaid care work is mostly done by women and girls. This is why sharing it fairly matters.
Yes. Unpaid housework is real work, as it takes time and effort and keeps the family going, even though no wages are paid.
Gandhi encouraged people to respect manual work and do their own tasks. He believed in self-reliance.

scenes.text: Every Saturday, Tara's school club visits an old-age home.
They read newspapers aloud and play carrom with the residents.
No one is paid, but everyone is happier.
Seva builds a caring society.

steps.title: Volunteering
steps.body: Giving time and skills freely for the good of others — teaching younger children, tree planting, disaster relief, blood donation (adults), cleaning drives, langar seva.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Builds community, helps those in need, teaches empathy and skills, and creates value that money doesn't measure.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Is volunteering economic or non-economic?

- **Non-economic** (no payment).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Name a volunteering activity a Class 6 student can safely do.

- Reading to younger children, a supervised clean-up drive, collecting books for a library.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Volunteering in unsafe situations without adult guidance.

items: Pick a cause (environment, elders, animals, education)
Ask a parent/teacher to help plan
Give at least one hour this month
Invite a friend to join next time

quiz.why: Volunteering means giving your time freely to help others. It is not done for wages.

options: volunteer service in a community kitchen
quiz.why: Langar seva is volunteer service in a community kitchen, such as cooking and serving food at a gurdwara.
Volunteering builds empathy and community spirit. It brings people together and does not cause fights or debt.
Students should volunteer safely with adult guidance. Going to dangerous places or alone at night is unsafe.
The value created by volunteering is real, even though it is not paid. It meets needs and helps society.

story.title: What do you want to be?

scenes.text: In class, students share dream jobs: pilot, farmer, coder, nurse, artist.
Teacher asks: 'What skills does each need?'
Learning, practice, honesty and teamwork come up again and again.
Every job needs skills — and every skill can be learned.

steps.title: Work gives
steps.body: Income, purpose, identity, skills, social connections, and value for others.

steps.title: Skills for work
steps.body: Reading, writing, numbers, digital skills, communication, teamwork, problem-solving, honesty and punctuality. Vocational skills (carpentry, tailoring, plumbing, coding) are valuable.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Name two skills a nurse needs.

- Care and communication; knowledge of health and hygiene.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why is honesty a work skill?

- People trust honest workers; trust builds businesses and careers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Believing only a few jobs are 'good'. Choose based on interest, skill and service.

activity.prompt: Match the job to a key skill.
pairs: Knowledge of soil, seeds and weather

quiz.why: Work gives people income and also a sense of purpose. It is more than just money.

quiz.q: A skill useful in every job?
quiz.why: Communication is a skill useful in every job, because we need to talk, listen and write clearly. Whistling and juggling are not general skills.
Vocational skills are practical skills for particular jobs, such as carpentry or tailoring. They are valuable and legal.
Honesty at work builds trust with customers and co-workers. Dishonesty brings confusion and loss of trust.
Choose work based on your interest, skill and the service you can give. Choosing only by what friends say or luck is less wise.

questions.q: Selling vegetables at a market is …
questions.why: Selling vegetables in a market is done to earn income, so it is economic.

questions.q: Caring for a sick grandparent at home is …
questions.why: Caring for a sick grandparent at home is unpaid, so it is non-economic. It is still valuable work.

questions.q: Dignity of labour means …
questions.why: Dignity of labour means respecting all honest work, not just desk jobs. Manual work deserves respect too.

questions.q: Volunteering is …
questions.why: Volunteering is unpaid service given to help others. It is not a tax, a crime or a salaried job.

questions.q: Unpaid care work is counted in GDP?
questions.why: Unpaid care work is usually not counted in GDP, since GDP counts paid goods and services. Yet it has great value.

questions.q: A doctor treating her own child at home is …
questions.why: A doctor treating her own child at home is not working for income, so the activity is non-economic. If she were paid, it would be economic.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Homemakers do valuable work. Reason (R): Their unpaid care keeps families and the economy running.
questions.why: Both are true: homemakers do valuable work, because their unpaid care keeps families and the economy running. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is economic?
options: A volunteer reading at a library
questions.why: A tutor teaching for fees is earning income, so it is economic. The other cases are unpaid.

questions.q: Which shows dignity of labour?
questions.why: Thanking sanitation workers shows respect for all work. Mocking porters or calling jobs 'low' goes against dignity of labour.

questions.q: Case: A carpenter makes a chair for his home and another to sell. Classify.
questions.why: The chair made for his own home is for his use, so it is non-economic. The chair made to sell is for income, so it is economic. The purpose decides.

questions.q: Case: A survey shows girls in a village spend 3 hours a day fetching water. A good solution?
options: Village water supply and sharing tasks
questions.why: A village water supply saves girls' time, and sharing tasks reduces their burden. Skipping school or ignoring the problem does not solve it.

questions.q: Why is volunteering valuable even without pay?
options: It meets needs and builds community
questions.why: Volunteering meets people's needs and builds community, even though it is unpaid. Its value is social.

questions.q: Which is NOT a work skill?
questions.why: Teamwork, punctuality and honesty are work skills. Cheating is not a skill, it is wrong.

questions.q: Case: Two families — in one, all members share chores; in the other, one person does all. Likely outcome in the first?
options: Fairer, more time for everyone to study and rest
questions.why: When all members share chores, it is fairer and everyone gets time to study and rest. One person doing it all is a heavy, unfair load.

questions.q: Economic vs non-economic activity is decided by …
options: whether it is done for income/exchange
questions.why: Whether an activity is economic is decided by its purpose, whether it is done for income or exchange. Hardness, place or age do not decide it.

courses.title: Ch 14 · Economic Activities Around Us
courses.summary: Primary, secondary and tertiary economic activities with Indian examples, how the three sectors depend on one another (from cotton field to shirt to shop), and how economic activities change with technology.
outcomes: Learners can classify activities into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors
Learners can trace a product through all three sectors
Learners can explain interdependence among sectors
Learners can describe how technology changes work

scenes.text: Ramu grows cotton in Vidarbha.
His neighbour keeps cows for milk; another family fishes in the river.
Nearby, miners dig coal.
All take things directly from nature — primary activities.

steps.title: Primary sector
steps.body: Activities that use **natural resources directly**: farming, animal rearing (dairy, poultry), fishing, forestry (collecting wood, honey, tendu leaves), mining.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Is collecting honey from a forest primary?

- **Yes** — taken directly from nature.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why is farming called primary?

- It produces raw materials directly from land and water.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Calling a sugar mill primary — it is secondary (it processes sugarcane).

statements.s: Fishing is a primary activity.
Mining coal is primary.
Making jam in a factory is primary.
Dairy farming is primary.

quiz.why: Primary activities use natural resources directly, such as farming, fishing and mining. Machines and banks come in other sectors.
Fishing takes a resource directly from nature, so it is primary. Banking and teaching are services, and a textile mill is secondary.
Forestry is a primary activity, such as collecting wood and honey from forests. Transport and IT are services, and car making is secondary.
Mining takes resources out of the earth, so it is a primary activity.

quiz.q: A dairy farmer is in the … sector
quiz.why: A dairy farmer rears animals and gets milk directly from them, so this is primary.

scenes.text: Ramu's cotton travels to a spinning mill in Gujarat.
It becomes yarn, then cloth on power looms.
A garment unit stitches shirts.
Turning raw materials into goods — secondary activities.

steps.title: Secondary sector
steps.body: Activities that **process raw materials into finished goods** — manufacturing and construction: textile mills, sugar mills, steel plants, food processing (jam, pickles), handicrafts, building houses and bridges.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Classify: making furniture from wood.

- **Secondary** (processing).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Is building a dam secondary?

- **Yes** — construction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking only big factories count — a potter or a weaver at home is also doing secondary work.

quiz.why: Secondary activities process raw materials into goods, like making cloth from cotton. Extracting resources is primary.

quiz.q: A potter shaping clay pots is …
quiz.why: A potter turns clay into pots, which is making goods from raw materials. So it is secondary.
Construction makes buildings and roads from materials, so it is a secondary activity.
Making pickles from mangoes processes a raw material into a product, so it is secondary. Growing the mangoes is primary.
Steel is made from iron ore, which comes from mines. Milk, cotton and honey are not raw materials for steel.

scenes.text: Trucks carry shirts from the factory to cities.
A bank loan helped the shop owner buy stock.
Priya buys a shirt; the shopkeeper uses a mobile payment app.
Every sector needed the others.

steps.title: Tertiary sector
steps.body: Activities that provide **services** rather than goods: transport, trade (shops), banking, communication, teaching, health care, tourism, IT, delivery, repair.

steps.title: Interdependence
steps.body: Farmers need seeds, tools and fertilisers (secondary) and transport, banks, markets (tertiary). Factories need raw materials (primary) and transport, power, banks (tertiary). Services need goods and food from the other two.

steps.title: Example 1 — trace a product
steps.body: Wheat (farmer, primary) → flour mill and bakery (secondary) → truck, shop, delivery app (tertiary) → your bread.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why would a bad monsoon affect a biscuit factory?

- Less wheat and sugarcane → raw materials cost more → production and jobs suffer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking services are not 'real work' because they make no goods.

activity.prompt: Order the journey of a cotton shirt.
items: Ginning and spinning mill makes yarn

quiz.why: Banking is a service, so it is tertiary. Primary uses nature directly and secondary makes goods.
A truck carrying goods provides transport, which is a service. So it is tertiary.
Interdependence means the sectors depend on each other. For example, factories need raw materials from farms.
Teaching is a service, so it is tertiary.

quiz.q: A bad monsoon can hurt factories because …
quiz.why: A bad monsoon reduces crops, so factories that use farm products get fewer raw materials. This shows the link between sectors.

scenes.text: Ramu now hires a tractor instead of bullocks.
He checks mandi prices on his phone.
A drone sprays crops in a neighbour's field.
Technology changes how every sector works.

steps.title: Technology changes work
steps.body: Machines and digital tools raise productivity — tractors and drip irrigation (primary), automated looms and robots (secondary), UPI payments and online services (tertiary). Some jobs change or disappear; new jobs appear, needing new skills.

steps.title: India's sectors
steps.body: A large share of India's workers is in agriculture, while services contribute the largest share of the economy's output. Manufacturing is being expanded through skill training.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
How does UPI help a small vegetable seller?

- Quick, cash-free payments and a record of sales.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Name a new job created by technology.

- Drone operator, app developer, data entry operator.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking technology only removes jobs — it also creates new ones that need new skills.

activity.prompt: Match the technology to its sector.

quiz.why: UPI is used for digital payments, which is part of banking services.

options: changes jobs and needs new skills
quiz.why: Technology changes jobs and creates a need for new skills. It does not end all work.
A drone operator is a job created by new technology. A drone operator is not a crop or a mineral.

quiz.q: Largest share of India's output comes from …
quiz.why: The largest share of India's output (GDP) comes from services, such as banking, IT and transport.

quiz.q: A large share of India's workers is in …
quiz.why: A large share of India's workers is in agriculture, even though its share of output is smaller. Space research and aviation employ few people.

questions.q: Farming is a … activity
questions.why: Farming takes crops directly from the land, so it is a primary activity.

questions.q: Textile mill work is …
questions.why: Textile mill work turns cotton into cloth, so it is secondary (manufacturing).

questions.q: A bank provides …
questions.why: A bank provides services such as savings and loans. It does not provide raw materials, crops or minerals.

questions.q: Fishing is …
questions.why: Fishing takes fish from nature, so it is a primary activity.

questions.q: Making furniture is …
questions.why: Making furniture turns wood into goods, so it is secondary.

questions.q: A school teacher works in the … sector
questions.why: A teacher provides a service, so the work is in the tertiary sector.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The three sectors are interdependent. Reason (R): Each needs goods or services from the others.
questions.why: Both are true: the three sectors are interdependent, because each needs goods or services from the others. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is tertiary?
questions.why: Transporting vegetables is a service, so it is tertiary. Mining and growing are primary and pickling is secondary.

questions.q: Sugar from sugarcane is made in the … sector
questions.why: Making sugar from sugarcane in a mill is processing, so it is secondary. Growing the cane is primary.

questions.q: Case: A drought reduces cotton. Which is hit next?
questions.why: A drought reduces cotton, which is the raw material for textile mills. So textile mills are hit next.

questions.q: Case: Trace bread. Correct order?
questions.why: The bread starts with the farmer who grows wheat, then the mill or bakery makes bread, and then the shop sells it. That is primary, secondary, tertiary.

questions.q: Which is a new job due to technology?
questions.why: An app developer is a job created by technology. Hand-copying books mostly disappeared with printing.

questions.q: Construction of a bridge is …
questions.why: Constructing a bridge makes a structure from materials, so it is a secondary activity.

questions.q: Case: A fisherwoman sells fish on a mobile app and gets UPI payments. Sectors involved?
questions.why: Fishing is primary, and selling by app and getting UPI payments are services (trade and payments), which are tertiary. So two sectors are involved.

questions.q: Why do farmers need the tertiary sector?
options: For transport, markets, banking and information
questions.why: Farmers need transport, markets, banking and information, which are services of the tertiary sector. Farming alone is not enough.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 6 Social Science
courses.summary: Theme-wise fact sheets for all 14 chapters of Exploring Society: India and Beyond, map and timeline practice, answer-writing tips, and two mock papers.
outcomes: Learners can recall key facts from each theme
Learners can practise map, time-zone and timeline questions
Learners can write clear, structured answers
Learners can self-test with mock papers

scenes.text: Ishaan pastes a world map and a timeline on his wall.
He marks the Tropics, Prime Meridian and IST meridian.
He sticks Harappan sites on a small India map.
Seeing it daily, he remembers it all.

steps.title: Geography (Ch 1–3)
steps.body:
- Map components: distance (scale), direction, symbols; physical/political/thematic maps
- Equator 0°, Tropics 23½° N/S, polar circles 66½°; Prime Meridian 0° (Greenwich); ancient reference at Ujjain
- 15° = 1 hour, 1° = 4 min; IST at 82½° E = GMT + 5:30
- 71% water; 7 continents (Asia largest, Australia smallest); 5 oceans (Pacific largest/deepest, Arctic smallest)
- Tides (Moon), currents (warm/cold), tsunami (undersea quake)
- Mountains (Himalayas, Kangchenjunga 8,586 m), plateaus (Deccan black soil, Chota Nagpur minerals), plains (Indo-Gangetic)

steps.title: History (Ch 4–6)
steps.body:
- Decade 10, century 100, millennium 1000 yrs; BCE counts backwards; no year 0
- Sources: archaeological, literary, oral; carbon dating for once-living material
- Names: Bharata (Rigveda), Bharatavarsha (Vishnu Purana), Jambudvipa (Ashoka), Hind/Hindustan (Persian), India (Greek); Article 1 'India, that is Bharat'
- Harappan: mature c. 2600–1900 BCE; Harappa, Mohenjo-daro (Great Bath), Dholavira (reservoirs), Lothal (dock), Kalibangan (ploughed field), Rakhigarhi; grid streets, drains, seals, undeciphered script, trade with Mesopotamia (Meluhha)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up latitude and longitude
- Placing BCE dates wrongly on a timeline

quiz.why: The Tropic of Cancer is at 23½° North. The Tropic of Capricorn is at 23½° South.
Australia is the smallest continent.
A dock-like basin has been found at Lothal in Gujarat, a Harappan port town.
A folk song passed from person to person is an oral source. A manuscript, inscription and coin are written or material sources.
'Hind' comes from the Persian pronunciation of Sindhu, the Indus. The Persians said 'H' for 'S'.

lessons.title: Fact sheet: Culture, Governance and Economics (Ch 7–14)

scenes.text: Two teams race to answer flash cards.
'73rd Amendment?' 'Panchayats, 1992!'
'Three sectors?' 'Primary, secondary, tertiary!'
Revision becomes a game.

steps.title: Culture (Ch 7–8)
steps.body:
- Four Vedas (Rigveda oldest), oral preservation; rishikas Ghosha, Lopamudra; Upanishads — Brahman, ātman; Gargi, Maitreyi
- Buddha: Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Middle Path; Mahavira: 24th tirthankara, ahiṃsā, anekāntavāda
- Diversity in food, textiles (Banarasi, Kanjivaram, Pochampally, Muga), festivals (Pongal, Lohri, Bihu, Onam), 22 Eighth-Schedule languages; epics in many languages (Kamban, Krittivas, Tulsidas)

steps.title: Governance (Ch 9–12)
steps.body:
- Family types; community cooperation; Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam
- Voting age 18; levels: Union, State, Local; organs: legislature, executive, judiciary; separation of powers; RTI 2005
- Rural: gram sabha (all adult voters), gram panchayat (sarpanch), panchayat samiti (block), zila parishad (district); 73rd Amendment 1992 (in force 24 Apr 1993); ≥ 1/3 seats for women
- Urban: municipal corporation, municipal council, nagar panchayat; wards & councillors; mayor; commissioner; 74th Amendment (in force 1 Jun 1993); property tax

steps.title: Economics (Ch 13–14)
steps.body:
- Economic (for income) vs non-economic (unpaid) activities; unpaid care work; dignity of labour; volunteering
- Primary (farming, fishing, mining), secondary (manufacturing, construction), tertiary (services); interdependence; technology changes work

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body:
Classify: weaving a sari for sale, teaching for salary, catching fish.

- Secondary, tertiary, primary (all economic).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing gram sabha with gram panchayat
- Mixing 73rd (rural) and 74th (urban) Amendments

pairs: All adult voters of a village

quiz.why: The panchayat samiti works at the block level. The gram sabha is at the village and the zila parishad at the district.
The legislature makes laws. The executive carries them out and the judiciary applies them.
Langar is a community kitchen that serves free food, run by volunteers. It is not a tax or a court.
Transport is a service, so it is in the tertiary sector.
Bodh Gaya is where the Buddha gained enlightenment. Lumbini is his birthplace and Sarnath is where he gave his first teaching.

scenes.text: Riya reads: 'Explain three features of Harappan town planning.'
She writes three numbered points with an example each.
For the map question, she labels neatly with a key.
Clear structure earns full marks.

steps.title: Answer-writing tips
steps.body:
- Use points or short paragraphs; one idea per point
- Add an example or a place/date for each point
- For maps: neat labels, a key, north arrow if drawing
- For time questions: show the steps (degrees × 4 minutes)

steps.title: Q1. Three features of Harappan planning
steps.body:
1. Grid streets crossing at right angles
2. Covered drains with inspection holes
3. Standard baked bricks (1:2:4); citadel and lower town

steps.title: Q2. Time at 45° E when it is 6:00 am at Greenwich
Q3. Difference between gram sabha and gram panchayat
steps.body: Gram sabha: all adult voters, reviews plans and spending. Gram panchayat: elected council headed by the sarpanch that carries out work.

steps.title: Q4. Name the five oceans in decreasing size
steps.body: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic

steps.title: Q5. Give one example each of primary, secondary and tertiary activity
steps.body: Fishing; making steel; banking

quiz.why: The mature Harappan phase lasted from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. 7000 BCE is the time of early farming at Mehrgarh.
The Equator divides the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. The Prime Meridian divides it into East and West.
The Supreme Court is the highest court in India.
Ladakh is India's cold desert. Thar and Kutch are hot or salty deserts.
'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States' is in Article 1 of the Constitution.
Kanjivaram silk saris come from Tamil Nadu.

scenes.text: A week before exams, Kabir does mock 2 under timed conditions.
He finds he still confuses the 73rd and 74th Amendments.
He writes a memory trick: '3 = gram (village), 4 = city (four walls)'.
He's ready.

steps.title: Q1. Explain the three organs of government with one example each
steps.body: Legislature makes laws (Parliament passes a road-safety law); executive implements (police enforce it); judiciary interprets/settles disputes (court hears a challenge).

steps.title: Q2. Why are plains densely populated?
steps.body: Fertile alluvial soil, water, flat land for farms, roads and cities.

steps.title: Q3. Name four sources of history with an example of each
steps.body: Archaeological (pottery), inscription (Ashokan edict), literary (manuscript), oral (folk song).

steps.title: Q4. Give two teachings each of the Buddha and Mahavira
steps.body: Buddha: Middle Path; kindness/right conduct. Mahavira: ahiṃsā; anekāntavāda.

steps.title: Q5. Trace a cotton shirt through the three sectors
steps.body: Cotton farming (primary) → spinning, weaving, stitching (secondary) → transport and shop (tertiary).

steps.title:
- 'Everest is in India' ✗ (Nepal–China)
- Writing 'BC/AD' is acceptable but be consistent; prefer BCE/CE
- Calling the Great Bath a swimming pool
steps.body: Common slips

activity.prompt: Which theme needs one more revision session? Plan when and how you'll do it.
activity.hint: E.g., Governance — make a chart of rural vs urban local bodies.

quiz.why: The 74th Amendment is about urban local bodies like municipalities. The 73rd is about panchayats.
The Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica.

quiz.q: Mock: Lower layers at a site are usually …
quiz.why: In undisturbed layers, the lower ones were laid down earlier, so they are usually older.
Pongal is the harvest festival of Tamil Nadu.
Unpaid care work is real work, even though it is mostly unpaid. It takes time and effort and supports families.

quiz.q: Mock: 1 hour of time = ? degrees of longitude
quiz.why: Earth turns 15° each hour (360° ÷ 24), so one hour of time equals 15° of longitude.

questions.q: Prime Meridian is at …
questions.why: The Prime Meridian is at 0° longitude. It passes through Greenwich.

questions.q: Largest ocean?
questions.why: The Pacific is the largest ocean. The Arctic is the smallest.

questions.q: Head of gram panchayat?
questions.why: The sarpanch is the head of the gram panchayat. A mayor heads a city and a collector heads a district.

questions.q: Fishing is in the … sector
questions.why: Fishing takes a resource directly from nature, so it is a primary activity.

questions.q: Which is a political map feature?
questions.why: Political maps show state and country boundaries. Rainfall, ocean depth and heights are other kinds of maps.

questions.q: A millennium is …
questions.why: A millennium is 1000 years, and a century is 100 years.

questions.q: Buddha's first teaching?
questions.why: The Buddha gave his first teaching at Sarnath. He was born at Lumbini and gained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.

questions.q: Judiciary …
questions.why: The judiciary interprets and applies laws, deciding cases in courts. The legislature makes laws.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Places east of Greenwich are ahead in time. Reason (R): The Earth rotates from west to east.
questions.why: Both are true: places east of Greenwich are ahead in time because the Earth rotates west to east. The Sun reaches the east first.

questions.q: Dholavira is famous for …
questions.why: Dholavira is famous for its water reservoirs and water management in a dry region. Lothal has the dockyard and Mohenjo-daro the Great Bath.

questions.q: Which is a secondary activity?
questions.why: Making sugar is processing a raw material, so it is secondary. Growing cane is primary and banking and selling are services.

questions.q: Gram sabha includes …
options: all adult voters of the village
questions.why: The gram sabha has all the adult voters of a village. It is not made up only of women or officials.

questions.q: Case: It is 2:00 pm at Greenwich. Time at 82½° E?
questions.why: 82½° E is 82.5 × 4 = 330 minutes, or 5 h 30 min, ahead of Greenwich. So 2:00 pm becomes 7:30 pm.

questions.q: Case: A city's garbage problem should first be raised with …
questions.why: A city garbage problem is a local one, so raise it first with the ward councillor or the municipal helpline. The Prime Minister or the army would not handle it.

questions.q: Case: A timeline of 12 cm covers 3000 BCE to 3000 CE. Scale?
questions.why: The timeline covers 3000 BCE to 3000 CE, which is 6000 years. Divided over 12 cm, that is 500 years per cm.

questions.q: Which correctly matches?
questions.why: Kamba Ramayanam is the Tamil Ramayana by Kamban. Ramcharitmanas is in Awadhi, Ramakien is Thai and Krittivasi is Bengali.

questions.q: Case: A town with a growing population, once a village, would usually have a …
questions.why: A place changing from a village into a town would usually have a nagar panchayat, the body for transitional areas. A corporation is for large cities.

questions.q: Time difference between 15° W and 75° E?
questions.why: 15° W and 75° E are 90° apart. At 4 minutes per degree that is 360 minutes, which is 6 hours.

questions.q: Which statement is FALSE?
options: The Harappan script has been deciphered
questions.why: The Harappan script has not been deciphered, so saying it has been is false. Lothal's basin, trade with Mesopotamia and covered drains are all true.

questions.q: Case: A farmer sells milk via a cooperative that processes it into butter and delivers to shops. Sectors involved?
questions.why: Milk from the farm is primary, processing it into butter is secondary and delivering it to shops is a service, which is tertiary. So all three sectors are involved.
